neighbors.heading: a candle on a candlestick
neighbors.text: Today the arti flame left the shrine and reached every face in the room. Christians pass a flame too: at many candlelight services, one candle lights the next, row by row. Jesus said: "Ye are the light of the world... Neither do men light a candle, and put it under a bushel, but on a candlestick; and it giveth light unto all that are in the house."
neighbors.difference: In arti, light is offered before the image of God and comes back as blessing. For Christians, the light is Christ, and the people who carry it are asked to shine it outward in good deeds.
neighbors.shared: a small flame is meant to reach everyone in the room.

neighbors.heading: light upon light
neighbors.text: Today a small flame was held up to the one all light comes from. The Qur'an reaches for a lamp too: "Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth. The similitude of His light is as a niche wherein is a lamp." A few lines on come three words: "Light upon light."
neighbors.difference: Arti waves a real lamp before an image of God. Muslims pray without images, and the lamp in this verse is a likeness only; the Qur'an also says nothing is like God.
neighbors.shared: light is one of the first words we reach for when we mean God.

neighbors.heading: beads in the hand
neighbors.text: Today the beads moved one by one, so the mind could stay with the name. Catholics know that feeling. The rosary is a loop of beads, and on most of them a prayer that begins with the angel's greeting to Mary: "Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee: blessed art thou among women." The hand keeps count; the heart keeps company.
neighbors.difference: Japa repeats a mantra or a name of God. The rosary repeats prayers addressed to God and to Mary, asking her to pray for us, while the mind rests on scenes from the life of Jesus.
neighbors.shared: a hand on a string of beads can carry a whole prayer.

neighbors.heading: remember, remember
neighbors.text: Today you met japa: a name of God said again, so it stays. Sikhs call it naam simran, remembering the Name, and the Guru Granth Sahib keeps returning to it. One hymn opens, in plain words: remember, remember, remember God, and find peace. Many Sikhs repeat Waheguru, sometimes with a mala, often with none.
neighbors.difference: Japa is often counted, and the Gita names it among offerings. The Sikh Gurus asked that the Name be held in the heart all day, while working and living, more than counted on beads.
neighbors.shared: a name said with love can steady a whole day.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 262, Sukhmani Sahib (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: two at a table
neighbors.text: Today the first domino was who you sit with. Jews say it too. Proverbs puts it plainly: "He that walketh with wise men shall be wise." And an old rabbinic teaching says that when two people sit together and words of Torah pass between them, the Divine Presence rests between them.
neighbors.difference: In Bhaja Govindam, good company leads step by step to freedom while still alive. In Jewish teaching, company is for learning Torah and living it together, here, in this world, with the presence of God among the learners.
neighbors.shared: who you sit with changes who you become.
neighbors.sources: Proverbs 13:20 (KJV) · Pirkei Avot 3:2 (paraphrase; 3:3 in some editions)

neighbors.heading: the whole of the path
neighbors.text: Today good company started the whole chain. A sutta tells of it. Ananda, the Buddha's companion, says good friendship is half of the spiritual life. The Buddha corrects him: not half. Good friends, good companions, are the whole of it, because with them a person walks the path.
neighbors.difference: For Hindus, satsang is the company of what's true, often of people turned toward God. The Buddha's good friend points toward the end of suffering, and the path he teaches doesn't rest on a creator God.
neighbors.shared: nobody climbs alone; good friends are part of the climb.

neighbors.heading: kindness to parents
neighbors.text: Today Ganesha won by circling his mother and father. Muslims hold parents close too. The Qur'an says: "Thy Lord hath decreed, that ye worship none save Him, and (that ye show) kindness to parents." When they grow old, it says, don't even sigh at them, but speak a gracious word. A famous hadith names the mother three times before the father.
neighbors.difference: Ganesha's parents are Shiva and Parvati, so his circle honors God too. In Islam, kindness to parents comes right after worshipping God alone: parents are honored and served, never worshipped.
neighbors.shared: the people who raised you are a whole world.
neighbors.sources: Qur'an 17:23 (Pickthall 1930) · Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Good Manners (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a thank-you list
neighbors.text: Today the whole world was right there in two people. A Roman emperor felt something like it. Marcus Aurelius opened his private notebook not with big ideas but with a list: what he learned from his grandfather, his mother, his teachers, his friends. Gentleness from one, honesty from another. Before thinking about the universe, he thanked the people close by.
neighbors.difference: Ganesha's walk is worship: his parents are divine, and the circle is a sacred act. Marcus is giving thanks to human teachers and family, as a habit of a good mind, without making it a rite.
neighbors.shared: the people close by deserve your thanks first.

neighbors.heading: water for everyone
neighbors.text: Today Hanuman flew a mountain to save one wounded man. Sikhs tell of Bhai Kanhaiya, who carried water across a battlefield to the wounded, friend and enemy alike. When some complained, Guru Gobind Singh asked him why. He answered that he saw no enemy, only the Guru in every face. The Guru, the story goes, then gave him balm for their wounds too.
neighbors.difference: Hanuman's rescue is for Rama's brother, as love and loyalty to Rama. Bhai Kanhaiya's seva crosses the battle line on purpose: the soldiers trying to kill his own side got water too.
neighbors.shared: when someone is hurting, you bring what heals.
neighbors.sources: Sikh tradition, the story of Bhai Kanhaiya (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: oil and wine on the road
neighbors.text: Today Hanuman didn't stop to ask which herb; he brought what was needed. Jesus told a story like that. A man lies beaten by the road. A Samaritan, a stranger, stops: he "went to him, and bound up his wounds, pouring in oil and wine, and set him on his own beast, and brought him to an inn, and took care of him."
neighbors.difference: Hanuman is a divine hero with powers no one else has, and many Hindus pray to him as sankat mochan. The Samaritan is an ordinary traveler in a parable, and Jesus ends it with: go, and do thou likewise.
neighbors.shared: the one who stops for the wounded is the hero.

neighbors.heading: a prince walks out
neighbors.text: Today a prince gave up a crown and walked into the forest. Buddhists know a prince who did that too. The Buddha remembers it himself: while still young, with his mother and father weeping, he shaved his hair and beard, put on the ochre robe, and went forth from home into homelessness, to find a way beyond suffering.
neighbors.difference: Rama leaves to keep his father's word: it's his dharma, and he'd rather stay. Siddhartha leaves by his own choice, against his parents' wishes, to search for freedom from suffering.
neighbors.shared: sometimes the bravest step is walking away from a throne.

neighbors.heading: not my will
neighbors.text: Today Rama heard the worst news and said, in effect, so be it. Catholics remember a night like that in a garden. Jesus, knowing what was coming, prayed: "Father, if thou wilt, remove this chalice from me: but yet not my will, but thine be done." Then he stood up and walked toward it.
neighbors.difference: Rama accepts to keep a promise made by his father, a king. For Catholics, Jesus accepts the will of God the Father, and the cross that follows is understood as the way he saves the world.
neighbors.shared: saying yes to what's hard can be a kind of courage.

neighbors.heading: weep, don't wail
neighbors.text: Today a king died of missing his son. A Roman thinker wrote to a grieving friend about tears. Seneca didn't tell him to stop crying. He wrote: "Let not the eyes be dry when we have lost a friend, nor let them overflow. We may weep, but we must not wail."
neighbors.difference: The Ramayana holds up Dasharatha's grief, even the grief that kills him, as love. Seneca, a Stoic, honors tears but asks for measure, so grief doesn't swallow the one still living.
neighbors.shared: tears for someone you love are nothing to be ashamed of.
neighbors.sources: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 63 (Gummere)

neighbors.heading: my son, my son
neighbors.text: Today a father's grief for his son ended his life. The Hebrew Bible keeps a father's grief too. When King David hears his son Absalom is dead, he climbs to a room over the gate and weeps: "O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! would God I had died for thee, O Absalom, my son, my son!"
neighbors.difference: In the Ramayana, Dasharatha's grief arrives as the fruit of an old curse. David's grief is for a son who rose against him. Jewish mourning has its own shape: seven days of shiva, and the Kaddish.
neighbors.shared: a parent's grief is love with nowhere to go.

neighbors.heading: two small coins
neighbors.text: Today a forest woman gave Rama berries she'd tasted, and he ate them gladly. Christians tell of a poor widow at the temple, dropping in two tiny coins while the rich gave plenty. Jesus noticed her: "Verily I say unto you, That this poor widow hath cast more in, than all they which have cast into the treasury."
neighbors.difference: Shabari gives directly to Rama, whom many Hindus honor as God in human form. The widow gives to the temple treasury, and it's Jesus, watching, who says her gift counts most.
neighbors.shared: a small gift, given with your whole heart, is never small.

neighbors.heading: what reaches God
neighbors.text: Today Rama ate berries that broke the rules, because of the love in them. The Qur'an says something close about offerings. Speaking of animals sacrificed at the pilgrimage and shared with the poor, it says: "Their flesh and their blood reach not Allah, but the devotion from you reacheth Him." The thing is given away; the heart is what arrives.
neighbors.difference: In the story, God in human form sits and eats what Shabari offers. In Islam, God needs nothing and eats nothing: the meat feeds people, and only the devotion reaches Him.
neighbors.shared: what counts in a gift is the love it carries.

neighbors.heading: the little way
neighbors.text: Today a squirrel carried sand while monkeys carried boulders, and Rama noticed. Catholics have a saint who lived like that squirrel. Thérèse of Lisieux, a young nun, felt too small for great deeds. So she chose what she called her little way: not letting a single small sacrifice slip, a glance, a word, each one done for love.
neighbors.difference: In the story, Rama himself picks up the squirrel and blesses it. Thérèse offered her small acts to God trusting she was seen, without a sign, and the Church later named her a saint.
neighbors.shared: small things, done with love, are never too small.
neighbors.sources: Thérèse of Lisieux, Story of a Soul (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a basket of earth
neighbors.text: Today the whole army built a bridge, stone by stone, and even a squirrel helped. Sikhs know that picture. They call it kar seva: volunteers carrying earth in baskets, hand to hand, to dig and clean the sacred pool at the Golden Temple. The Guru Granth Sahib says, in plain words: serve in this world, and you'll find a place in God's court.
neighbors.difference: The bridge was built for Rama's war to bring Sita home. Sikh kar seva is ongoing community work at a gurdwara, open to anyone, with no hero at the center, only the sangat.
neighbors.shared: every pair of hands counts, even the smallest.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 26 (paraphrase) · Sikh tradition of kar seva (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: no song at the sea
neighbors.text: Today the story stopped its cheering to let Ravana's wife weep. Jews say it too. Proverbs: "Rejoice not when thine enemy falleth, and let not thine heart be glad when he stumbleth." And the rabbis tell that when Egypt's army drowned, the angels wanted to sing, and God said: my creatures are drowning, and you would sing?
neighbors.difference: In the Ramayana, it's Ravana's wife who mourns, and Rama who says hostility ends at death. In the rabbinic story, it's God who refuses the victory song, for the enemy's sake.
neighbors.shared: even an enemy was someone's whole world.

neighbors.heading: an old rule
neighbors.text: Today Rama said the fight ends at death: give him his rites. Buddhists keep an old line about ending enmity. The Dhammapada says: "For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love, this is an old rule." It doesn't pretend the wrong didn't happen. It just won't carry the hate any further.
neighbors.difference: The Ramayana honors Ravana with funeral rites after a war it calls righteous. The Dhammapada asks that hatred be let go all along the way, not only once the fighting is over.
neighbors.shared: hate stops somewhere; let it stop with you.

neighbors.heading: every soul will taste
neighbors.text: Today the yaksha asked about the greatest wonder: people die all around us, and we live as if we never will. The Qur'an names it plainly: "Every soul will taste of death." And a hadith asks Muslims to remember death often; many read it as a call to live the day in front of them well.
neighbors.difference: Yudhishthira's answer sits inside a tradition of rebirth and of the self that doesn't die. In Islam, each person lives one life, and after death comes the Day of Resurrection and God's judgment.
neighbors.shared: remembering that life ends can make today count.

neighbors.heading: ten thousand years
neighbors.text: Today's riddle: we see death every day and act as if it won't come for us. A Roman emperor wrote himself the same reminder, in a notebook meant for no one else: "Do not act as if thou wert going to live ten thousand years. Death hangs over thee. While thou livest, while it is in thy power, be good."
neighbors.difference: Yudhishthira answers a divine spirit's test, and his right answer brings his brothers back to life. Marcus writes it to himself, with no promise of reward: being good now is reason enough.
neighbors.shared: the time to be good is today.

neighbors.heading: fifty-two held his cloak
neighbors.text: Today you met the lamps of Diwali, lit so someone could find the way home. Sikhs light them the same season, for Bandi Chhor Divas. Sikh tradition tells that Guru Hargobind, freed from a fort prison, refused to leave unless the kings imprisoned with him came too. They held the tails of his cloak and walked out together. Amritsar lit lamps to welcome him.
neighbors.difference: Diwali's lamps welcome Rama home, or honor Krishna or Lakshmi, depending on the family. Bandi Chhor's lamps honor a Guru who would not take his own freedom unless others shared it.
neighbors.shared: a lamp in the window says: come home, you're welcome here.

neighbors.heading: one candle more
neighbors.text: Today rows of small lamps were lit against the darkest night. Many Christians light candles in the dark weeks before Christmas, one more each Sunday of Advent, until the wreath is bright. The Gospel of John gives the picture behind it: "And the light shineth in darkness; and the darkness comprehended it not."
neighbors.difference: Diwali's lamps welcome a homecoming, and Lakshmi into an open house. For Christians, the light John means is Christ himself, and the Advent candles count down to his birth.
neighbors.shared: you don't argue with the dark; you light one more candle.

neighbors.heading: a handful of dust
neighbors.text: Today a lopsided clay Ganesha was enough, because love made it. Buddhists tell of a small boy playing in the road when the Buddha walked by begging for food. The boy had nothing, so he scooped up a handful of dust and offered it as if it were a meal. The Buddha accepted it, and the story says that gift grew into a great life.
neighbors.difference: For many Hindus, the murti is a form God can truly be present in. For many Buddhists, a Buddha image recalls a teacher who showed the way, honored with gifts; the Buddha isn't a creator God.
neighbors.shared: what you give with love is never too plain.

neighbors.heading: the Lord beholdeth the heart
neighbors.text: Today the question was whether a lopsided Ganesha is good enough. Catholics keep statues and holy pictures at home too, and some are far from perfect. The Bible is plain about what counts: "man seeth those things that appear, but the Lord beholdeth the heart." And the Church teaches that honor shown to an image passes to the one it shows.
neighbors.difference: Many Hindus understand a murti as a form God can dwell in. Catholics honor a statue as a picture of Jesus, Mary or a saint, never as God's dwelling; they believe Christ is truly present in the Eucharist instead.
neighbors.shared: God isn't grading the art; the love is what's seen.
neighbors.sources: 1 Kings 16:7 (Douay-Rheims; 1 Samuel 16:7 in many Bibles) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 2132 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: I breathe
neighbors.text: Today you met prana, the breath that keeps going whether you choose it or not. The American psychologist William James noticed that when he looked hard for his own mind, he kept finding his breath. He wrote: "The 'I think' which Kant said must be able to accompany all my objects, is the 'I breathe' which actually does accompany them."
neighbors.difference: In the Upanishads, prana is life itself, and breath points toward something deeper, the self. James was describing experience as a scientist, and didn't claim the breath was sacred.
neighbors.shared: your breath has been with you through everything.

neighbors.heading: the breath of life
neighbors.text: Today breath was the one the senses begged to stay. The Torah starts a human life with a breath: "And the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul." The rabbis read a psalm's last line to mean: for every single breath, praise God.
neighbors.difference: In the Upanishads, prana is the life-force, the greatest of the powers in us. In Judaism, breath is a gift God gives each person, and every breath is a reason to say thank you to the Giver.
neighbors.shared: every breath is a small gift worth noticing.

neighbors.heading: pray without ceasing
neighbors.text: Today you met five syllables said over and over: I bow to Shiva. Many Christians, especially in the Orthodox churches, keep one short prayer the same way, often in rhythm with the breath: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me. It grew from an old line, "God be merciful to me a sinner," and from Paul's advice: "Pray without ceasing."
neighbors.difference: Om namah shivaya bows to Shiva, the auspicious one. The Jesus Prayer asks Christ for mercy, and Christians say it to the one they believe is God's Son.
neighbors.shared: a few words, said again and again, can hold a whole heart.

neighbors.heading: hearts find rest
neighbors.text: Today a short mantra rolled through a temple all night. Muslims know that kind of repeating too. They call it dhikr, remembrance: short phrases praising God, said again and again, often counted on beads or fingers. The Qur'an says why: "Verily in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest!"
neighbors.difference: Om namah shivaya bows to Shiva, whom many Hindus worship as the Supreme. Dhikr remembers the one God of Islam, by the names the Qur'an gives Him, with no image.
neighbors.shared: a heart can rest inside a few words of praise.

neighbors.heading: the lamp that stays lit
neighbors.text: Today one small flame made a dark house a home. Catholic churches keep a flame too. Next to the tabernacle, where the consecrated bread is kept, a special lamp, often red, burns day and night. Church law asks it to shine without stopping, to honor Christ present there. In an empty church, that small light says Christ is there.
neighbors.difference: A Hindu home lamp is often lit at dawn and dusk, often first in the puja, before the image of God. The Catholic sanctuary lamp burns without stopping, marking where Catholics believe Christ is present in the Eucharist.
neighbors.shared: one small flame can say: someone holy is here.

neighbors.heading: the sun and moon are lamps
neighbors.text: Today one flame in a clay dish lit the shrine. Sikh tradition says Guru Nanak, the first Sikh Guru, watched a temple arti and sang his own. In plain words: the sky is the plate, the sun and moon are the lamps, and the stars are the pearls. Many Sikhs still sing it at night before sleep.
neighbors.difference: A Hindu home lamp is a real flame offered before God. Guru Nanak's hymn makes the whole sky the arti, and Sikh worship centers on the Guru Granth Sahib, with no image to wave lamps before.
neighbors.shared: every light, small or huge, can be a way of saying thank you.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 663 and Ang 13, Kirtan Sohila (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: first a blessing
neighbors.text: Today the sweet went to the shrine first, then came back to be shared. Jews say a blessing before they eat, and the Talmud explains why with two verses. One says, "The earth is the LORD's, and the fulness thereof." Another says the earth is given to people. Before the blessing, the rabbis say, the food is God's; after it, it's ours.
neighbors.difference: In puja, the food is set before the image of God, then returns as prasad. In Jewish practice today, food isn't set out for God to receive; the blessing itself, said with the food in hand, is the thanks.
neighbors.shared: food tastes different once you've said thank you first.

neighbors.heading: not without sharing
neighbors.text: Today food was offered, then shared with everyone in the house. In many Buddhist lands, people feed the monks who walk by at dawn with their bowls, then share the merit of the gift. The Buddha said, in plain words: if people knew, as he knew, what giving and sharing bring, they wouldn't eat without sharing, not even their last bite.
neighbors.difference: Naivedya is offered to God and comes back as grace. In Buddhism, the food goes to monks and nuns and people in need; the blessing lies in the giving itself, not in a god receiving it.
neighbors.shared: a meal is sweeter when it's shared.

neighbors.heading: your body has a right
neighbors.text: Today the body was a temple worth caring for. Islam has a hadith about that. The Prophet Muhammad heard that a companion was fasting every day and praying all night. He told him to fast some days and eat on others, to pray and also sleep, because, in plain words, your body has a right over you.
neighbors.difference: The Maitreya Upanishad says the one living in the body is Shiva himself. In Islam, God is never inside the body; the body is a trust from God, to be cared for and answered for.
neighbors.shared: caring for your body is part of the spiritual life.

neighbors.heading: if anything is sacred
neighbors.text: Today a poet-saint said his legs were pillars and his head a golden dome. An American poet said it too. Walt Whitman, in a long hymn to the body, wrote: "If any thing is sacred the human body is sacred." Hands, feet, breath, the whole walking person, worth honoring.
neighbors.difference: For Basavanna and the Upanishad, the body is a temple because Shiva lives in it. Whitman found the body sacred in itself, with no single god named inside it.
neighbors.shared: the body you live in is worth honoring.
neighbors.sources: Walt Whitman, "I Sing the Body Electric," Leaves of Grass

neighbors.heading: worn every day
neighbors.text: Today you met the tilak, a mark of what you honor, worn where everyone can see. Sikhs wear their faith in the open too. Many keep their hair uncut and tie a turban, the dastar, every morning. The Sikh code of conduct asks Sikhs to keep their hair whole, and the turban covers it with honor, one wrap at a time.
neighbors.difference: A tilak can change with the day, the temple or the lineage, and many Hindus wear none. For many Sikhs, uncut hair and the turban are part of keeping faith every day, not only on special days.
neighbors.shared: sometimes faith shows on the outside, so you remember it inside.
neighbors.sources: Sikh Rehat Maryada, the Sikh code of conduct (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: ash on the forehead
neighbors.text: Today you met three lines of sacred ash on a forehead. Christians know ash on the forehead too. On Ash Wednesday, at the start of Lent, many churches mark a cross of ash on each person, often with an old line from Genesis: "for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return." Then people walk out into the day, still wearing it.
neighbors.difference: A tilak can mark lineage, devotion or a temple visit, and many wear one often. For Christians who keep it, the ash cross comes once a year, a sign of repentance as Lent begins.
neighbors.shared: a small mark can carry a big remembering.

neighbors.heading: keeping him on the right
neighbors.text: Today you walked around something holy, keeping it on your right. Buddhists do the very same thing. In the old suttas, people who'd visited the Buddha bow, then walk around him, keeping him on their right, before they leave. Today pilgrims still circle stupas and temples clockwise, sometimes with prayer beads, sometimes in silence.
neighbors.difference: For Hindus, the center of the circle is a murti, a sacred tree or a mountain where the divine is present. For Buddhists, it's often a stupa holding relics, honoring the Buddha as a teacher who found the way.
neighbors.shared: walking around what you love is a way of saying it.

neighbors.heading: a prayer you walk
neighbors.text: Today prayer was something you did with your feet. Catholics have walking prayers too. In the Stations of the Cross, people move slowly around the church, stopping at fourteen pictures of Jesus' last day, praying at each one. Processions carry a cross or a statue through the streets. The Church counts these among the old ways people pray.
neighbors.difference: Pradakshina circles a sacred center, keeping it on the right. The Stations follow a road, the path Jesus walked to the cross, so walking them is a way of keeping him company.
neighbors.shared: sometimes the body has to walk for the heart to arrive.

neighbors.heading: I shall not stop
neighbors.text: Today a small boy kept saying the name his father had forbidden. A philosopher on trial did something like it. In Plato's telling, Socrates tells the court of Athens that even if they let him go on the condition that he stop questioning, he won't stop. While he has life and strength, he'll keep searching for what's true.
neighbors.difference: Prahlada's courage is devotion to Vishnu, and Vishnu keeps him safe from every danger. Socrates is loyal to his conscience and his search for truth, and he isn't saved: Athens puts him to death.
neighbors.shared: some things are worth saying even when you're told to stop.

neighbors.heading: but if not
neighbors.text: Today a boy sat in a fire and walked out. The book of Daniel has a fire too. Three young Jews refuse a king's order to bow to his golden statue. They tell him: "our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace." And then: but if not, we still won't bow. They walk out of the flames unharmed.
neighbors.difference: Prahlada's story is retold at a Holika bonfire each year, and Vishnu himself comes to save him. Daniel's three friends say out loud they'd keep faith even if no rescue came.
neighbors.shared: faithfulness can walk straight through the fire.

neighbors.heading: running over
neighbors.text: Today a pot of sweet rice boiled over, and everyone cheered. Jesus used that picture for generosity: "Give, and it shall be given unto you; good measure, pressed down, and shaken together, and running over." Many churches also hold a harvest thanksgiving each autumn, with the altar heaped with bread and fruit, often given away after.
neighbors.difference: At Pongal, the first sweet rice is offered to Surya, the sun, before anyone eats. For Christians, thanks goes to God, and Jesus ties the overflow to how freely you give to others.
neighbors.shared: when there's more than enough, it's meant to spill over to others.

neighbors.heading: I will give you more
neighbors.text: Today the rice came in, and the first of it was given in thanks. The Qur'an ties thanks and harvest together. It says to eat of the crops, "and pay the due thereof upon the harvest day," a share for those in need. And it promises: "If ye give thanks, I will give you more."
neighbors.difference: Pongal's first pot is offered to Surya, the sun, and Mattu Pongal thanks the cattle too. In Islam, all thanks go to God alone, and the harvest's share goes to people in need.
neighbors.shared: a full harvest starts with a thank you.

neighbors.heading: arise and eat
neighbors.text: Today Arjuna sat down and said, I can't, and Krishna said, stand up. Catholics read about a prophet who hit the same floor. Elijah, worn out and afraid, lies under a juniper tree and asks God to take his life. He falls asleep. An angel touches him and says: "Arise and eat." There's bread and water by his head. Then he walks on.
neighbors.difference: Krishna's first words are a jolt that reminds Arjuna who he is. Elijah's angel starts with food and sleep, and only later, on the mountain, does God speak to him, in a gentle breeze.
neighbors.shared: when you can't go on, someone may help you stand.

neighbors.heading: rising spirits
neighbors.text: Today Krishna told his friend, on the floor in tears, to stand up. Sikhs have a word for the spirit he's asking for: chardi kala, rising spirits, hope that keeps climbing even in the worst times. Every Ardas, the Sikh prayer, ends with it, in plain words: Nanak, with the Name comes rising spirits; by your will, may all be well.
neighbors.difference: Krishna lifts Arjuna by reminding him of his duty as a warrior. Chardi kala rests on the Name of God, and the same line asks for the good of all, sarbat da bhala.
neighbors.shared: hope can rise even on the hardest day.

items.lessonTitle: Desire → anger → ruin; the peace at the end (2.62–2.72)

neighbors.heading: thou shalt not covet
neighbors.text: Today the Gita traced wanting to anger to ruin. The Torah puts wanting itself among the Ten Commandments: "Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's house." And an old rabbi warned, in plain words, that envy, craving and chasing honor drive a person out of the world.
neighbors.difference: The Gita maps a chain inside the mind and promises peace to the steady one who breaks it. The Torah gives a commandment, and Jewish life often answers coveting with gratitude, Shabbat and the daily blessings.
neighbors.shared: wanting what isn't yours can quietly steal your peace.
neighbors.sources: Exodus 20:17 (KJV; 20:14 in JPS 1917) · Pirkei Avot 4:21 (paraphrase; 4:28 in some editions)

neighbors.heading: the chain and the blowing out
neighbors.text: Today you heard the slide from dwelling to wanting to anger. Buddhists know that chain well. The Buddha taught that craving is where suffering starts, and the Dhammapada says, in plain words, that from craving come grief and fear, and the one free of craving knows neither. The way out has a name: nirvana.
neighbors.difference: The Gita's last verse of the chapter uses that same word, brahma-nirvana: peace in Brahman. For Buddhists, nirvana is the ending of craving itself, with no Brahman or creator behind it.
neighbors.shared: the chain can be broken, right at its first link.

neighbors.heading: say what you do
neighbors.text: Today Krishna said people copy the one in front, so even he keeps acting. The Qur'an asks a sharp question: "O ye who believe! Why say ye that which ye do not? It is most hateful in the sight of Allah that ye say that which ye do not." And it names a living example: "Verily in the messenger of Allah ye have a good example."
neighbors.difference: In the Gita, God himself acts so the world has someone to follow. In Islam, the example to follow is the Prophet Muhammad, a human messenger, not God, and Muslims follow his way, the sunnah.
neighbors.shared: the people watching you learn more from your hands than your words.

neighbors.heading: they do what you do
neighbors.text: Today Krishna said whatever the best person does, others do the same. Psychology found it in a lab. In Albert Bandura's studies, children watched an adult hit an inflatable doll, then were left alone with it. Many copied the adult, often move for move. Children who watched a calm adult mostly didn't. People learn by watching, long before anyone explains.
neighbors.difference: The Gita gives a reason beyond learning: act for lokasangraha, the holding-together of the world, without craving the fruit or claiming to be the doer. The psychology only describes how copying works; it names no duty.
neighbors.shared: someone small is always watching how you live, not what you say.
neighbors.sources: Bandura, Ross & Ross, "Transmission of aggression through imitation of aggressive models" (1961) (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: nine doors and a tenth
neighbors.text: Today the Gita called the body a city of nine gates, with someone quiet seated inside. Sikhs know that city. In the Guru Granth Sahib the body is a fortress with nine doors, the openings of the senses, and a hidden tenth door, the dasam duar, where the Guru's word is heard and the one Light is met within.
neighbors.difference: In the Gita, the one seated in the city is the self, who neither acts nor makes anything act. Gurbani speaks of the Creator's Light found within through the Name and the Guru's grace, and adds a tenth door the Gita doesn't name.
neighbors.shared: your body has busy doors and a quiet center worth visiting.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, hymns of Guru Amar Das and others on the nine doors and the tenth door (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a temple, not a city
neighbors.text: Today the Gita said the body is a city, and someone lives inside. Christians picture a building too. Paul writes to the church at Corinth: "What? know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you, which ye have of God, and ye are not your own?" The body is honored because of who dwells there.
neighbors.difference: For the Gita, the one inside is the self, untouched by what the body does. For Christians, the one who dwells within is the Holy Spirit, God's gift, not the person's own self, which is why Paul says "ye are not your own."
neighbors.shared: your body is a place where something holy lives.

neighbors.heading: the mind at the end
neighbors.text: Today the Gita said the last thought is made of all the ordinary ones. Buddhist teaching says something close. The Abhidhamma lists kinds of karma that can shape what comes after death: a weighty deed, a deed recalled near death, and habitual action, what a person did again and again. And the Buddha urged his monks to practice mindfulness of death now, breath by breath.
neighbors.difference: The Gita asks the dying to remember Krishna and speak Om, and so reach God. Buddhism names no God to remember and no lasting self that travels on; what continues is a stream of causes, and the goal is nirvana.
neighbors.shared: the last breath is shaped by all the ordinary days before it.
neighbors.sources: Abhidhammattha Sangaha ch. 5, kinds of karma by order of ripening (paraphrase) · Anguttara Nikaya 6.19, mindfulness of death (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: now, and at the hour
neighbors.text: Today the Gita said you can't cram for the last thought; it's written every day. Catholics pray toward that hour in the Hail Mary, said over and over in the rosary: "Holy Mary, Mother of God, pray for us sinners, now and at the hour of our death." Now, and at the hour, in one breath. Saint Benedict's Rule tells monks to keep death daily before their eyes.
neighbors.difference: In the Gita, remembering Krishna at death leads beyond rebirth. Catholics believe in one life, then judgment, and hope for heaven through Christ's mercy; they ask Mary to pray for them, honoring her, never worshipping her.
neighbors.shared: the last hour is made of all the small hours before it.
neighbors.sources: the Hail Mary (traditional English text) · Rule of Saint Benedict 4.47 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a job, or a calling
neighbors.text: Today the Gita put lunch next to sacrifice: whatever you do, make it an offering. Researchers saw something like it at work. Amy Wrzesniewski and colleagues found that people in the very same job describe it differently: as a job, a career, or a calling. Hospital cleaners who saw their work as part of caring for patients shaped their days around it.
neighbors.difference: The Gita turns the whole day toward Krishna; the offering has someone who receives it, and it frees you from the bonds of action. The research names no one receiving; it finds that meaning changes with how a person frames their work.
neighbors.shared: an ordinary chore can be pointed somewhere that matters.
neighbors.sources: Wrzesniewski, McCauley, Rozin & Schwartz, "Jobs, careers, and callings" (1997) (paraphrase) · Wrzesniewski & Dutton, "Crafting a job" (2001) (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: for the sake of heaven
neighbors.text: Today the Gita said: whatever you do, whatever you eat, offer it. Jewish teachers have their own way of saying it. Rabbi Yose taught: let all your deeds be for the sake of Heaven. And the Talmud says it's forbidden to enjoy anything of this world without a blessing, so an apple, bread or a glass of water each gets a short blessing before the first bite.
neighbors.difference: The Gita asks that every act be offered to Krishna, freeing you from action's fruits. Jewish life does it through commandments and set blessings to the one God; the blessing thanks God as the giver rather than offering the food up.
neighbors.shared: even a glass of water can be a small thank-you.
neighbors.sources: Pirkei Avot 2:12 (paraphrase; 2:17 in some editions) · Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 35a (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a portrait, not a ritual
neighbors.text: Today Krishna ended his chapter on devotion with a portrait: friendly, compassionate, forgiving, the same to friend and foe. Christians have a portrait too. Paul writes: "But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, Meekness, temperance: against such there is no law." Not a list of rituals. A face you'd want to sit beside.
neighbors.difference: For the Gita, these qualities make someone dear to Krishna. For Christians, they're called fruit because the Holy Spirit grows them in a person who belongs to Christ: more gift than achievement.
neighbors.shared: you can tell real devotion by how someone treats everyone else.

neighbors.heading: they answer: peace
neighbors.text: Today Krishna described the one dear to him: hating no being, afraid of no one, frightening no one. The Qur'an paints its own portrait: "The (faithful) slaves of the Beneficent are they who walk upon the earth modestly, and when the foolish ones address them answer: Peace." The verses go on: they pass the night in prayer, and they spend neither wastefully nor stingily.
neighbors.difference: In the Gita, the portrait is of a devotee of Krishna, God who speaks as a friend in a human form. In the Qur'an, they are servants of Ar-Rahman, the Most Merciful, who has no partner and no likeness.
neighbors.shared: a gentle answer to a harsh word is part of loving God.

neighbors.heading: the light in everyone
neighbors.text: Today the Gita said one sun lights the whole world, and one knower lights every field: look at anyone, and look for the light. The Gospel of John opens with a light like that: "That was the true light, which enlighteneth every man that cometh into this world." The Church teaches that every person is made in God's image, so no one is beneath your notice.
neighbors.difference: For the Gita, the light in every body is the self or the Lord within, never stained. For Catholics, the light is Christ, the Word, shining on each person, who remains a creature and not God, yet bears his image.
neighbors.shared: look at anyone today, and look for the light.
neighbors.sources: John 1:9 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 1700 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: one light in all
neighbors.text: Today the Gita said one light shines in every field. Sikhs sing a close picture at night, in the Sohila: Guru Nanak says that within all is the Light, and You are that Light; by its shining, all are lit. It's one reason the gurdwara kitchen, the langar, seats everyone side by side on the floor, at the same height.
neighbors.difference: The Gita's schools differ: one self in all, or one Lord within many selves. Sikhs honor the one formless Creator's Light in every being, and live it out as equality, with no caste at the langar.
neighbors.shared: the same light shines in the person you find hardest to like.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 13 (Dhanasari, Guru Nanak, in the Sohila) (paraphrase)

items.lessonTitle: Food, sacrifice, austerity, gift — three kinds each (17.7–17.22)

neighbors.heading: the best way to give
neighbors.text: Today the Gita sorted gifts: the clear one is given because it should be, to someone who can't repay you, at the right time and place. Jewish law sorts giving too. Maimonides lists eight levels of tzedakah. High on the list: giver and receiver don't know each other. Highest of all: helping someone stand on their own, with a loan, a partnership or a job.
neighbors.difference: The Gita weighs the giver's state of mind, and the clear gift asks nothing back. For Maimonides, tzedakah is justice, a duty owed to the poor, and the highest level ends the need, so the person no longer has to receive.
neighbors.shared: how you give matters as much as what you give.
neighbors.sources: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Laws of Gifts to the Poor 10:7–14 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the good person's gift
neighbors.text: Today the Gita said a gift comes in three kinds, depending on what's in the hand along with it. The Buddha said something close. He described how a good person gives: with confidence, with respect, at the right time, with a heart that holds nothing back, and without harming themselves or anyone else. Giving, dana, heads the lists of perfections Buddhists cultivate.
neighbors.difference: The Gita's clear gift is given as duty, and in its wider frame as an offering. In Buddhism the gift is offered to no creator; its fruit is a lighter heart and less grasping, a step toward letting go.
neighbors.shared: a gift given with a free heart lightens both hands.

items.lessonTitle: "I have told you. Now do as you choose." (18.59–18.66)

neighbors.heading: no compulsion
neighbors.text: Today, after all the teaching, Krishna handed the choice back: reflect fully, then do as you wish. The Qur'an makes room for choice too: "There is no compulsion in religion. The right direction is henceforth distinct from error." Another verse: "Say: (It is) the truth from the Lord of you (all). Then whosoever will, let him believe, and whosoever will, let him disbelieve."
neighbors.difference: Krishna wraps his handing-back in tender words: you are dear to me. The Qur'an pairs the freedom with plain words about where each choice leads in the life to come, and leaves the guiding of hearts to Allah.
neighbors.shared: real faith is chosen, never forced.

neighbors.heading: chosen, not pushed
neighbors.text: Today Krishna taught everything he could, then said: reflect fully, then do as you wish. Psychologists Edward Deci and Richard Ryan study why that matters. Their self-determination theory finds that people hold on to what they choose for their own reasons, and let go of what they're pressured into. Autonomy, they argue, is a basic human need, alongside feeling capable and connected.
neighbors.difference: The Gita's freedom comes inside a relationship: the Lord in every heart, and a promise of love. The psychology names no God; it finds that choices made freely tend to outlast ones made under pressure.
neighbors.shared: the people who love you most let you decide.
neighbors.sources: Ryan & Deci, "Self-determination theory and the facilitation of intrinsic motivation, social development, and well-being" (2000) (paraphrase)

items.lessonTitle: "Abandon all dharmas, come to me alone" (18.66–18.72)

neighbors.heading: the Guru's sanctuary
neighbors.text: Today Krishna gave his last instruction: come to me for refuge, and do not grieve. Sikhs know that word. In the Guru Granth Sahib, saran, sanctuary, comes back again and again: the singer sets down cleverness and every other prop, comes to the Lord's door, and asks to be kept there. Guru Arjan's hymns often end with Nanak seeking the Lord's sanctuary.
neighbors.difference: In the Gita, refuge is in Krishna, God who speaks in a friend's form. Sikhs seek refuge in the one formless Creator, Waheguru, through the Guru's word, and don't believe God takes birth in a body.
neighbors.shared: when you can't carry it anymore, you can set it down.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, hymns of Guru Arjan on saran, sanctuary (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: come unto me
neighbors.text: Today Krishna said: let go of every other support, come to me for refuge, do not grieve. Christians hear an invitation shaped like it, from Jesus: "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest." And a little later: "For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light." Not more effort. Rest.
neighbors.difference: In the Gita, Krishna promises to free the one who takes refuge from all wrongs. Christians believe Jesus is God made flesh, once, who died for sin and rose again; the rest he offers comes through trusting him.
neighbors.shared: you were never meant to carry everything alone.

items.lessonTitle: Isha Upanishad (18 verses, one week): "all this is pervaded by the Lord" (2 of 7)

neighbors.heading: whose, really?
neighbors.text: Today the Isha asked: whose, indeed, is wealth? The Dhammapada asks it even more sharply: "'These sons belong to me, and this wealth belongs to me,' with such thoughts a fool is tormented. He himself does not belong to himself; how much less sons and wealth?" Loosen the grip of mine, and the torment loosens too.
neighbors.difference: The Isha answers its own question: all this belongs to the Lord, so you hold things as a guest. Buddhism names no owner at all; things are impermanent and not-self, and seeing that clearly is what loosens the grip.
neighbors.shared: hold what you love with an open hand.

neighbors.heading: the earth is the Lord's
neighbors.text: Today the Isha said all this is pervaded by the Lord, so enjoy by letting go. A psalm sings: "The earth is the Lord's and the fulness thereof: the world, and all they that dwell therein." Job, after losing everything, says: "the Lord gave, and the Lord hath taken away." The Church calls an owner a steward, a lot like Gandhi's trustee.
neighbors.difference: The Isha says the Lord pervades all this. Catholics say God made the world and is present in it, but creation is not God; Job blesses a Creator who stays distinct from what he gave.
neighbors.shared: everything you hold was a gift first.
neighbors.sources: Psalm 23:1 (Douay-Rheims; Psalm 24:1 in many Bibles) · Job 1:21 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 2404 (paraphrase)

items.lessonTitle: Kena Upanishad (one week): who impels the mind? (5 of 7)

neighbors.heading: this victory is ours
neighbors.text: Today the gods won and said: this victory is ours. Then fire couldn't burn a blade of grass. Psychologists have a name for the gods' slip: the self-serving bias. Many studies find people tend to credit their wins to their own skill and blame their losses on luck or circumstance. It protects our pride, and it quietly hides how much help we had.
neighbors.difference: The Kena says the power was on loan from Brahman, the one by whom fire burns. The psychology names no lender; it points to teammates, timing and luck, and asks only that you see your success honestly.
neighbors.shared: no win was ever only yours.
neighbors.sources: Miller & Ross, "Self-serving biases in the attribution of causality" (1975) (paraphrase) · Mezulis, Abramson, Hyde & Hankin, "Is there a universal positivity bias in attributions?" (2004) (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: my power and my hand
neighbors.text: Today the gods said: this victory is ours. Moses warns Israel of the same slip, for the day the houses are built and the herds grow: "and thou say in thy heart: 'My power and the might of my hand hath gotten me this wealth.' But thou shalt remember the LORD thy God, for it is He that giveth thee power to get wealth."
neighbors.difference: The Kena's power belongs to Brahman, the mind of the mind, glimpsed like lightning. For Jews, the giver is the one God of the covenant, and the remembering became grace after meals, drawn from a verse in the same chapter.
neighbors.shared: every strength you have was handed to you.
neighbors.sources: Deuteronomy 8:17–18 (JPS 1917) · Deuteronomy 8:10, the source of grace after meals (paraphrase)

items.lessonTitle: Katha Upanishad (one week): Nachiketa and Death (3 of 7)

neighbors.heading: the whole world
neighbors.text: Today Death offered Nachiketa everything, and the boy chose the good over the pleasant. Christians tell of a similar offer: in the wilderness, the devil shows Jesus all the kingdoms of the world and their glory, and Jesus refuses. Later he asks his friends: "For what is a man profited, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?"
neighbors.difference: Nachiketa turns down the bribe, and Death teaches him a self that is not born and does not die. Christians believe Jesus went through death and rose, and that each soul is created by God and given eternal life by him.
neighbors.shared: the best thing isn't always the shiniest thing on the table.

neighbors.heading: better and more lasting
neighbors.text: Today Nachiketa told Death: these last only till tomorrow; keep your horses. The Qur'an speaks to the same choice. People prefer the life of this world, it says, although "the Hereafter is better and more lasting." Another verse says wealth and children adorn this life, but good deeds that endure are better in your Lord's sight.
neighbors.difference: Nachiketa's good leads to knowing the self beyond birth and death. In the Qur'an, the lasting good is faith and good deeds, weighed by Allah, with its reward in the one life to come, not in a cycle of rebirth.
neighbors.shared: choose what will still matter tomorrow.

items.lessonTitle: Mandukya Upanishad (12 verses, one week): the four states; om, letter by letter (1 of 7)

neighbors.heading: in the beginning, a word
neighbors.text: Today the Mandukya said: om, this syllable, is all this, past, present, future and beyond. A Gospel opens with a word too: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God." John adds that "all things were made by him." A word out of silence, and everything after it.
neighbors.difference: For the Mandukya, om is the sound that is all reality, pointing to the silent fourth. For Catholics, the Word is not a syllable but a person, the Son, who "was made flesh" in Jesus; creation comes through him and is not him.
neighbors.shared: there's something sacred in a word spoken out of silence.

neighbors.heading: one, then onkar
neighbors.text: Today the Mandukya gave all of reality to one syllable, om. The Guru Granth Sahib opens with a word many hear as kin to it: Ik Onkar. Guru Nanak puts the numeral one in front of it, so the scripture's first words say: there is one Creator, present in all. It's written as a single symbol, ੴ, at the top of the scripture.
neighbors.difference: The Mandukya maps om's sounds onto waking, dream and deep sleep, and the silence after onto the fourth. Sikhs read Ik Onkar first as a declaration: one Creator, then named as truth, fearless, without hate.
neighbors.shared: one sound can hold everything you mean by one.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1, the Mul Mantar

items.lessonTitle: Karma yoga deep-dive: action as offering; Karma Yoga as taught by Vivekananda; work as worship (7 of 7)

neighbors.heading: a handful of flour
neighbors.text: Today a mongoose searched for a gift as great as four small portions of barley flour. Jewish teachers prized a poor person's flour too. The meal offering was the gift of someone who couldn't afford an animal, and the Talmud says God counts it as though the giver had offered their very soul.
neighbors.difference: In the Mahabharata, the gift goes to a starving guest who turns out to be Dharma himself. In Jewish tradition, the poor person's flour was a Temple offering to the one God; since the Temple fell, prayer and kindness stand in its place.
neighbors.shared: a small gift from a full heart is never small.

neighbors.heading: giving from little
neighbors.text: Today the smallest gift, fully given, outweighed a king's great sacrifice. A verse in the Buddhist scriptures says it plainly: some give from the little they have, others won't give from plenty, and an offering given from little is worth a thousand times its size. Elsewhere the Buddha says that if people knew the fruit of giving, they wouldn't eat without sharing.
neighbors.difference: In the Mahabharata, the guest is Dharma himself, and a god honors the gift. In Buddhism, no god weighs it; its worth comes from the giver's intention and loosened grip, and it ripens as good karma.
neighbors.shared: it's not the size of the gift, but the heart behind it.

items.lessonTitle: Bhakti yoga: the nine forms of devotion; the Alvars and Nayanars; Mirabai, Tulsidas, Surdas; kirtan as method (7 of 7)

neighbors.heading: hearts find rest
neighbors.text: Today Chaitanya led a whole town singing the names of Krishna, and the repeating quieted the mind. Muslims remember God by repeating his names and short phrases, dhikr, alone or together. The Qur'an says: "Verily in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest!" In Sufi circles, people may repeat one line until the room goes quiet inside.
neighbors.difference: Kirtan sings Krishna's names with drums and dancing, and Chaitanya's followers say God is present in the name. Dhikr remembers Allah, who has no form or likeness, and Muslims differ on whether music belongs in it at all.
neighbors.shared: saying a holy name again and again can quiet a busy mind.

neighbors.heading: the ice-breaker effect
neighbors.text: Today a whole street sang together, and the group carried everyone's shyness. Researchers tested something like it. In a 2015 study of adult evening classes, people who sang together felt close to their classmates faster than people in crafts or creative-writing classes, though the other groups caught up over the months. The researchers called it the ice-breaker effect.
neighbors.difference: For kirtan, the goal is God: the name is sung as devotion itself, and the quiet that comes is grace. The research looks only at people, measuring how fast strangers start to feel like a group.
neighbors.shared: singing with others turns strangers into a circle.
neighbors.sources: Pearce, Launay & Dunbar, "The ice-breaker effect: singing mediates fast social bonding" (2015) (paraphrase)

items.lessonTitle: Jnana yoga: neti neti in practice; Shankara's method; the Ashtavakra Gita opening (2 of 7)

neighbors.heading: know your own source
neighbors.text: Today a man counted nine friends and forgot to count himself: you are the tenth. Sikhs sing a line with the same turn toward the one who's looking. Guru Amar Das says, in effect: O my mind, you are the very form of the divine Light; recognize your own source. Nothing new is found. You just stop leaving yourself out.
neighbors.difference: Advaita says you are that: the self is Brahman once ignorance falls away. Sikhs say the mind carries the Creator's Light, but the Creator is within all and beyond all, met through the Guru's word and the Name, with ego the veil.
neighbors.shared: what you're looking for may be the one who's looking.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 441 (Asa, Guru Amar Das) (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: lo here, lo there
neighbors.text: Today the leader looked everywhere for the missing tenth, except at the one doing the counting. Jesus turns a crowd's eyes the same way. Asked when the kingdom of God would come, he says: "The kingdom of God cometh not with observation: Neither shall they say, Lo here! or, lo there! for, behold, the kingdom of God is within you."
neighbors.difference: Advaita says the seeker is the self, one with Brahman. Christians read the kingdom as God's reign, near and within (some translate "among you"); the person is God's beloved creature, not God.
neighbors.shared: stop searching over there for a moment, and look here.

items.lessonTitle: Advaita (Shankara): not-two; rope and snake in full; the Vivekachudamani opening (4 of 7)

neighbors.heading: the turtle and the yoke
neighbors.text: Today the crest-jewel opened by counting how rare a human birth is. The Buddha gave a picture for it. A yoke with one hole drifts on the great ocean, and a blind turtle comes up once every hundred years. Sooner, he said, would the turtle put its neck through that hole than a being lost in the lower worlds would be born human again.
neighbors.difference: For the Vivekachudamani, the luck of human birth opens the way to knowing the self as Brahman. For the Buddha, it's the chance to see the four noble truths and be free, with no lasting self to find.
neighbors.shared: you being here at all is a rare gift; use it gently.

neighbors.heading: what is man?
neighbors.text: Today the crest-jewel asked you to feel the luck of being human before anything else. A psalm stops in the same wonder: "What is man that thou art mindful of him?" Then it answers that God made him a little less than the angels and crowned him with glory and honor. The Church teaches that God willed each person for their own sake.
neighbors.difference: The Vivekachudamani counts a human birth as rare among many births, a chance to discern the self. Catholics believe each person lives one life, created by God, and their worth comes from being loved by him.
neighbors.shared: before anything else: you're here, and that's a gift.
neighbors.sources: Psalm 8:5–6 (Douay-Rheims; Psalm 8:4–5 in many Bibles; second line paraphrased) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 356 (paraphrase)

items.lessonTitle: Dvaita and beyond (Madhva, Ramanuja): the lover and the beloved stay two; why devotion needs difference (3 of 7)

neighbors.heading: one, and still two
neighbors.text: Today the gopis told the philosopher: we don't want the self of all. We want him. The psychologist Erich Fromm wrote about love in a similar way. Mature love, he argued, is a union that keeps each person whole: two beings become one and yet remain two. Love that swallows the other, or loses itself, isn't the real thing.
neighbors.difference: The gopis' beloved is Krishna, God himself, and the devotional schools say that love grows forever. Fromm wrote about love as an art practiced between people; he wasn't describing a soul's love for God.
neighbors.shared: real love lets the other stay themselves.
neighbors.sources: Erich Fromm, The Art of Loving (1956) (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: I am my beloved's
neighbors.text: Today the gopis said they'd rather taste sugar than become sugar: love needs two. The Song of Songs sings that kind of love: "I am my beloved's, and my beloved is mine, that feedeth among the lilies." Rabbinic tradition reads the song as the love between God and Israel, and Rabbi Akiva called it the holy of holies among the writings.
neighbors.difference: The gopis love Krishna, God in a human form, the cowherd of their village. Jews read the Song as love between the one God, who has no body or form, and his people: a covenant in which each stays itself.
neighbors.shared: the space between two who love each other is holy.

items.lessonTitle: Patanjali 1.1–1.16: "now, yoga"; yoga is the stilling of the mind's turnings; practice and non-attachment (6 of 7)

neighbors.heading: in due season
neighbors.text: Today Patanjali said a practice holds when it's kept up a long time, without break, with care, and he promised ground, not fireworks. Paul writes to the Galatians in the same spirit: "And let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not." The harvest comes later than the planting. You keep sowing anyway.
neighbors.difference: Patanjali's practice steadies the mind until the seer rests in itself. Paul's well doing is love lived in Christ, and the harvest he means is life from the Spirit, given by God, not built by effort alone.
neighbors.shared: small, steady days add up to solid ground.

neighbors.heading: small, and steady
neighbors.text: Today Patanjali gave three conditions for a practice that holds: a long time, without break, with care. A hadith says it in one sentence. Aisha reports the Prophet saying that the deeds most loved by Allah are the ones done regularly, even if they're small. Five daily prayers, a little Qur'an each day: a rhythm, not a rush.
neighbors.difference: Patanjali's practice is a method for stilling the mind's turnings. In Islam, the steady deed is worship of Allah and loved by him; the aim is his pleasure, not a particular state of mind.
neighbors.shared: a little, every day, beats a lot, once.
neighbors.sources: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, from Aisha (paraphrase)

items.lessonTitle: karma: the Gita's ch. 3 revisited · bhakti: the Bhagavata Purana's Krishna stories (the…

neighbors.heading: theirs, not ours
neighbors.text: Today the Gita called anyone who takes the world's gifts and gives nothing back a thief. A Catholic voice is just as blunt. The Catechism quotes Saint John Chrysostom: not to let the poor share in our goods is to steal from them, because the goods we hold are not ours, but theirs. The Church calls it the universal destination of goods.
neighbors.difference: In the Gita, the circle runs through offering, rain and the gods, and giving back frees action from binding. For Catholics, the earth is given by one Creator to all people, and sharing is a duty of justice and charity.
neighbors.shared: what reaches your table was meant to keep moving.
neighbors.sources: Catechism of the Catholic Church 2446, quoting St. John Chrysostom (paraphrase) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 2402 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: earn, and share
neighbors.text: Today the Gita said food comes through a circle, and whoever only takes breaks it. Guru Nanak names the one who keeps it turning: whoever eats what they've earned by honest work, and gives some of it away, has recognized the path. Sikhs call the sharing vand chhakna, and the gurdwara's langar feeds whoever walks in.
neighbors.difference: The Gita's circle runs through yajna, offering to the gods, and giving back can be a ritual. Sikh teaching sets fire offerings aside and lives the circle through honest work, remembering the Name, and sharing with anyone hungry.
neighbors.shared: send something back into the circle today.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245 (Sarang ki Var, Guru Nanak) (paraphrase)

items.lessonTitle: karma: Vivekananda's Karma Yoga lectures · bhakti: the Gita Govinda · jnana:…

neighbors.heading: honor at home first
neighbors.text: Today the butcher sent the wandering monk home to his old parents. The commandment says: "Honour thy father and thy mother, that thy days may be long upon the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee." The Talmud spells it out plainly: give them food and drink, clothe them, help them come in and go out.
neighbors.difference: The butcher calls his parents his gods. Jewish teaching honors parents as partners with God in making a child, but never as gods; honoring them runs alongside reverence for the one God, never in place of it.
neighbors.shared: the people at your own door come first.

neighbors.heading: now I'll support them
neighbors.text: Today a butcher told a proud monk that his real practice was waiting at home. The Buddha gave a young man named Sigala advice in the same spirit. Instead of bowing to the six directions as a ritual, honor the people they stand for, starting with your parents: they supported me, so now I'll support them, do their work, and keep the family going.
neighbors.difference: The butcher's teaching is dharma in the Hindu sense: your own duty, done as worship. The Buddha turns a ritual into ethics, serving no god; caring for parents is good conduct that brings good results.
neighbors.shared: your practice may be waiting at your own front door.

items.lessonTitle: karma: seva as a life · bhakti: the Gita Govinda · jnana: Ramana Maharshi's self-inquiry

neighbors.heading: the hidden gift
neighbors.text: Today the Gita said the clear gift isn't given to be seen or repaid. The Qur'an says: "If ye publish your almsgiving, it is well, but if ye hide it and give it to the poor, it will be better for you." A hadith praises the one who gives so quietly that the left hand doesn't know what the right hand gave.
neighbors.difference: The Gita weighs a gift by the giver's state: clear, restless or heavy. Islam also counts giving as worship of Allah, makes zakat a set duty on wealth, and calls open giving good too.
neighbors.shared: the quietest gifts often carry the most love.
neighbors.sources: Qur'an 2:271 (Pickthall 1930) · Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, the seven given shade (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: let the giver forget
neighbors.text: Today the Gita asked what's in the hand along with a gift. The Stoic philosopher Seneca wrote a whole book on giving, and he set a rule for it: the giver should forget the gift at once, and the receiver should never forget it. A kindness you keep reminding people about, he warned, starts to feel like a debt.
neighbors.difference: The Gita adds a reason beyond good manners: action without craving for its fruit doesn't bind the one who acts. Seneca's reason is human: a kindness is a bond of goodwill, and boasting spoils it.
neighbors.shared: give, and let it be finished.

neighbors.heading: without fear, without hate
neighbors.text: Today the raised hand on the shrine said: don't be afraid, and don't answer cruelty with more cruelty. The scripture's opening lines describe the one Creator as nirbhau, without fear, and nirvair, without hate. Guru Arjan sings where that leads: no one is my enemy, and no one is a stranger. Fearless and without hate, together.
neighbors.difference: The abhaya mudra is a gesture on Hindu murtis, a hand offering fearlessness. Sikhs don't use images in worship; for them, fearless and without hate describe Waheguru, and a Sikh grows toward both through the Name.
neighbors.shared: you can stand unafraid without learning to hate.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1 (Mul Mantar) · Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1299 (Kanra, Guru Arjan) (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: called by name
neighbors.text: Today the lesson said your worth isn't up for a vote. In Isaiah, God tells his people, far from home: "Fear not: for I have redeemed thee, I have called thee by thy name; thou art mine." Christians hold that word close. And Paul says what to do with cruelty: "Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good."
neighbors.difference: The lesson grounds worth in the atman, the self no weapon can cut. Christians ground it in being made and loved by God, who calls each person by name: worth given by him, not a divine self within.
neighbors.shared: a stranger's cruelty can't take away who you are.

neighbors.heading: keep going, carefully
neighbors.text: Today, from the top of the first mountain, you saw a whole range ahead, and the Katha said: arise, awake. The Buddha's last words point the same way. Lying between two sal trees at Kusinara, he told his monks: "Decay is inherent in all component things! Work out your salvation with diligence!" No grand ending. Just: keep going, with care.
neighbors.difference: The Katha's path leads to the self that knows no death. The Buddha's diligence works toward nirvana, the end of craving, with no lasting self at the end of the road.
neighbors.shared: there's always more road, and you're ready for the next step.

neighbors.heading: stretching forth
neighbors.text: Today you saw the next peaks behind the first. Saint Paul writes from a ridge like that: he doesn't count himself as having arrived, but one thing he does, "forgetting the things that are behind, and stretching forth myself to those that are before." Saint Augustine said the heart stays restless until it rests in God.
neighbors.difference: The Katha calls the seeker to wake to the self, learning from those who know. Paul presses toward a prize he calls God's call in Christ Jesus, a gift of grace still unfolding, and the road ends in God.
neighbors.shared: look how far you've come, then turn toward the next peak.

neighbors.heading: one stuff under everything
neighbors.text: Today Uddalaka said that in the beginning there was Being alone, one without a second. Philosophers have reached for the same oneness. Baruch Spinoza wrote: "Besides God no substance can be granted or conceived." For him, the chair, the tree and your own hand are all ways the one substance shows itself, which he also called Nature.
neighbors.difference: Uddalaka's Being thinks, let me be many, and sends out heat, water and food. Spinoza's God, or Nature, doesn't choose or wish; everything follows from its nature, the way a triangle's angles follow from being a triangle.
neighbors.shared: under all the different names, one thing holds everything together.
neighbors.sources: Spinoza, Ethics, Part I, Proposition 14 (Elwes translation, 1883)

neighbors.heading: one, without a second
neighbors.text: Today Uddalaka said that in the beginning there was Being alone, one only, without a second. Jews say a line about oneness morning and night: "Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one." And the Torah opens at the very same moment: "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth."
neighbors.difference: In Uddalaka's telling, Being itself grows forth into heat, water and food. In Genesis, God speaks the world into being: made by God, and distinct from him.
neighbors.shared: the whole wide world begins from one.

items.lessonTitle: The salt in water — "taste it here. here. everywhere." (6.13)

neighbors.heading: in every sip
neighbors.text: Today the salt vanished into the water, and still every sip was salty. Christians speak of a God that close. Paul told the people of Athens that God is "not far from every one of us: For in him we live, and move, and have our being." And a psalm asks: "Whither shall I go from thy spirit?"
neighbors.difference: Uddalaka ends with tat tvam asi, you are that, and Hindu schools read it as oneness or as close belonging. For Christians, God is everywhere and holds you up, yet you stay a creature he loves.
neighbors.shared: what matters most is close, even when you can't see it.

neighbors.heading: wherever you turn
neighbors.text: Today the salt vanished into the water, and still every sip was salty. The Qur'an speaks of a nearness like that: "Unto Allah belong the East and the West, and whithersoever ye turn, there is Allah's Countenance." And of each person: "We are nearer to him than his jugular vein."
neighbors.difference: Uddalaka says of the hidden essence: you are that. Muslims hold that Allah is nearer than your own vein, yet beyond everything he created; no creature shares his being.
neighbors.shared: what you're looking for is closer than you think.

items.lessonTitle: The city of Brahman in the heart (8.1)

neighbors.heading: a castle inside
neighbors.text: Today the Upanishad found a small space in the heart, as big as the sky outside. Catholics look inward too. Jesus says in the Gospel: "For lo, the kingdom of God is within you." And Saint Teresa of Avila pictured the soul as a castle of clear crystal with many rooms, and God living in the room at the very center.
neighbors.difference: For the Upanishad, what lives in the heart's space is the self that never ages or dies. For Catholics, God dwells in the soul by grace, as a guest and friend; the soul, however beautiful, is made.
neighbors.shared: the biggest room you'll ever find is inside you.
neighbors.sources: Luke 17:21 (Douay-Rheims) · Teresa of Avila, The Interior Castle, First Mansions, ch. 1 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: why search the forest?
neighbors.text: Today the Upanishad found a small space in the heart that holds heaven and earth. Guru Tegh Bahadur asks a seeker why he goes looking in the forest: the Lord dwells in everything, untouched, and stays right there with you. Again and again the Guru Granth Sahib sings that the One you seek is found within.
neighbors.difference: The Upanishad draws a map: body, lotus-house, inner space. Sikhs keep no map like that. The One is formless and everywhere, met within by remembering the Name and living the Guru's word.
neighbors.shared: you don't have to travel far to find what you're seeking.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 684, Guru Tegh Bahadur (paraphrase)

items.lessonTitle: The gods and demons and the breath (1.3)

neighbors.heading: the breath that stays clean
neighbors.text: Today speech, sight, hearing and mind were all pierced, and only the plain breath stayed clean. Jewish mornings start with a similar hope. The Talmud gives a prayer for waking: my God, the soul you placed in me is pure; you created it, you breathed it into me. In Hebrew, the word for soul, neshamah, is close kin to the word for breath.
neighbors.difference: In the Upanishad, breath stays clean because it took nothing for itself. In the Jewish prayer, the soul is pure because God made it so, and each morning begins with thanks for it.
neighbors.shared: something in you stayed clean, whatever the day has done.

neighbors.heading: the bright mind
neighbors.text: Today the demons pierced speech, sight, hearing and mind, but broke on the plain breath like clay on stone. The Buddha points to something clear underneath too. In a short teaching he says the mind is luminous, and gets stained by troubles that arrive from outside. And his breathing meditation starts simply: breathe in knowing it, breathe out knowing it.
neighbors.difference: The Upanishad's breath wins because it grabs nothing, and carries the senses past death. The Buddha's bright mind isn't a lasting self; it's a mind that can be cleared, moment by moment, through practice.
neighbors.shared: under the noise, there's something clear you can come back to.
neighbors.sources: Anguttara Nikaya 1.49–52 (paraphrase) · Anapanasati Sutta, Majjhima Nikaya 118 (paraphrase)

items.lessonTitle: Maitreyi: "what would I do with wealth if it doesn't make me immortal?" (2.4)

neighbors.heading: what lasts
neighbors.text: Today Maitreyi was offered a share of the property and asked: what would I do with something that won't make me deathless? The Qur'an weighs wealth the same way: "Wealth and children are an ornament of life of the world. But the good deeds which endure are better in thy Lord's sight for reward, and better in respect of hope."
neighbors.difference: Maitreyi asks for knowledge of the self, the thing that doesn't end. The Qur'an points to good deeds that endure, carried before Allah, with hope in his mercy in the life to come.
neighbors.shared: money is fine; just don't let it answer the wrong question.

neighbors.heading: care for the soul
neighbors.text: Today Maitreyi set the money aside and asked for what doesn't end. Socrates, on trial for his life in Athens, asked his city the same kind of question: aren't you ashamed to care so much about money, reputation and honor, and so little about wisdom, truth, and making your soul as good as it can be?
neighbors.difference: Maitreyi wants the deathless, and asks a teacher for it. Socrates asks every citizen to care for the soul right now, and admits he doesn't know for certain what death brings.
neighbors.shared: the best question is often the one underneath the offer.

items.lessonTitle: Uddalaka: the thread and the inner controller (3.7)

neighbors.heading: the knower within
neighbors.text: Today Yajnavalkya named the inner controller, who lives in the earth, the wind and your breath, and rules each from within. Sikhs call the One Antarjami, the knower within every heart, a name the Guru Granth Sahib uses again and again. And the Japji says everyone is within the Hukam, the divine order; no one stands outside it.
neighbors.difference: In the Upanishad, the inner controller is your own self, the deathless. Sikhs speak of the Creator dwelling in all, never born, and the path is living in tune with the Hukam by remembering the Name.
neighbors.shared: a quiet thread runs through everything, including you.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1, Japji pauri 2 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the thread through the beads
neighbors.text: Today Yajnavalkya said a thread holds this world and the next together, like a string through beads, and an inner controller rules each thing from within. Christians say something like it of Christ. Paul writes: "And he is before all things, and by him all things consist." To consist here means to hold together.
neighbors.difference: In the Upanishad, the inner controller is called your self, the deathless. Christians say all things hold together in Christ, the Son through whom God made the world, while each person stays a creature God loves.
neighbors.shared: you're held together by more than you can see.

items.lessonTitle: Janaka and Yajnavalkya: what is the light of man? sun → moon → fire → speech → self (4.3)

neighbors.heading: a lamp for yourself
neighbors.text: Today the sun set, the moon set, the fire went out, speech fell silent, and the self was left as a person's own light. Near the end of his life, the Buddha told his friends not to lean on him once he was gone: be a lamp, an island, for yourselves, with the teaching as your lamp and refuge.
neighbors.difference: Yajnavalkya's light is the self made of knowing, the light within the heart. The Buddha's lamp isn't a lasting self; it's your own effort and the teaching, lit again each day.
neighbors.shared: when the other lights go out, you aren't left in the dark.

neighbors.heading: the light in everyone
neighbors.text: Today, with sun, moon, fire and voice all gone, Yajnavalkya said the self is a person's own light. Catholics speak of a light no night puts out. Saint John's Gospel says of Christ: "That was the true light, which enlighteneth every man that cometh into this world." And Jesus tells his friends: "You are the light of the world."
neighbors.difference: For Yajnavalkya, the light is the self itself. For Catholics, the true light is Christ, God's Word, shining into each person from beyond them; we carry it like a lamp, not as its source.
neighbors.shared: there's a light in you that the dark doesn't reach.
