items.lessonTitle: "As is his desire, so is his will; as his will, so his deed" (4.4)

neighbors.heading: you become what you do
neighbors.text: Today Yajnavalkya said: as a person acts, so they become; doing good, one becomes good. Aristotle said the same about character: "we become just by doing just acts, temperate by doing temperate acts, brave by doing brave acts." Psychologists today call the pattern habit: what you repeat gets easier, and slowly turns into who you are.
neighbors.difference: Aristotle starts with practice and says the right wanting grows from it. Yajnavalkya looks one step further back, to desire itself, and follows the chain past death into the next life.
neighbors.shared: small choices, repeated, quietly build a person.
neighbors.sources: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II.1 (W. D. Ross translation)

neighbors.heading: one good deed pulls the next
neighbors.text: Today Yajnavalkya traced a chain: desire to will, will to deed, deed to what you become. The Mishnah has a chain too. Ben Azzai taught: run to do even a small commandment, and flee from wrongdoing, because one good deed pulls another after it, and one wrong pulls another. The reward of a good deed is the next good deed.
neighbors.difference: Yajnavalkya follows the chain past death into another life, unless desire for the self ends it. Ben Azzai speaks of commandments given by God, done in this life, with the reward left in God's hands.
neighbors.shared: every good thing you do makes the next one easier.

items.lessonTitle: "Do not despise food. Food is Brahman." (3.7–3.10)

neighbors.heading: nothing to be refused
neighbors.text: Today the Taittiriya said: do not despise food; that is the vow. Christians honor food with thanks. Paul writes: "For every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving: For it is sanctified by the word of God and prayer." That's one reason Christian families pause to say grace before eating.
neighbors.difference: The Upanishad calls food Brahman: the chain of eating and being eaten is the holy itself. Christians call food a good gift from God, made holy by thanks, while the Giver stays other than the gift.
neighbors.shared: the plate in front of you deserves a moment of thanks.

neighbors.heading: he never faulted a meal
neighbors.text: Today the Taittiriya said: do not despise food, and never turn away a guest. Muslims remember the same manners in the Prophet. His companion Abu Hurairah said the Prophet never found fault with any food: if he liked it, he ate it, and if not, he left it. The Qur'an adds: "eat and drink, but be not prodigal."
neighbors.difference: For the Upanishad, food is Brahman, the very chain of life. For Muslims, food is rizq, provision from Allah, begun with his name and ended with thanks; the gift is never the Giver.
neighbors.shared: food is a gift; no meal is beneath a thank you.

items.lessonTitle: The person; the gods enter through the doors of the body (1.2)

neighbors.heading: a temple, well made
neighbors.text: Today the gods turned down a cow and a horse, saw a human being and said: well made, indeed! Catholics honor the body too. Genesis says God saw all he had made, "and they were very good." And Saint Paul asks: "know you not, that your members are the temple of the Holy Ghost, who is in you?"
neighbors.difference: In the Aitareya, many gods move in: fire as speech, the sun as sight. Catholics believe in one God, and that the Holy Spirit dwells in the baptized, so the body is honored as his temple.
neighbors.shared: your body isn't a burden; it's a good home.

neighbors.heading: the body the gods long for
neighbors.text: Today the gods saw a human being and said: well made, indeed! Bhagat Kabir sings something close in the Guru Granth Sahib: even the gods long for this human body, so use it to serve and remember the Lord. Guru Amar Das calls the body the Lord's temple, where the jewel of wisdom comes to light.
neighbors.difference: In the Aitareya, the gods move in and become speech, breath and sight. Sikhs worship the One alone; for them, a human birth is a rare chance to meet that One by remembering the Name.
neighbors.shared: this body is a gift worth taking good care of.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1159, Bhagat Kabir (paraphrase) · Ang 1346, Guru Amar Das (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: more than offerings
neighbors.text: Today the Mundaka praised the fire rites as true, then called them unsteady boats. Israel's prophets made a similar turn. Through Hosea, God says: "For I desire mercy, and not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God rather than burnt-offerings." The offerings were commanded and kept, and still the prophets kept asking what they were for.
neighbors.difference: The Mundaka says rites win a heaven that runs out, so the seeker looks past them to the imperishable. Hosea doesn't set the commandments aside; he asks that kindness and knowing God fill them.
neighbors.shared: a ritual is a boat; remember where it's taking you.

neighbors.heading: a raft, not a home
neighbors.text: Today the Mundaka called the rites unsteady boats. The Buddha told a boat story too. A traveler builds a raft to cross a flood. On the far shore, should he carry it on his head? No. The teaching, the Buddha said, is like a raft: for crossing over, not for holding onto.
neighbors.difference: The Mundaka honors the Vedic rites, then points past them to the imperishable. The Buddha counted clinging to rites and rituals among the fetters, and said even his own teaching is a raft to set down.
neighbors.shared: the boat matters; so does knowing when you've reached the shore.

neighbors.heading: truth has come
neighbors.text: Today the Mundaka said: truth alone wins, not untruth. The Qur'an says it just as plainly: "Truth hath come and falsehood hath vanished away. Lo! falsehood is ever bound to vanish." And one of Allah's names is al-Haqq, the Truth: "That is because Allah, He is the Truth."
neighbors.difference: In the Mundaka, satya comes from sat, what is, and truth is a road the sages walk. In Islam, the Truth is a name of Allah himself, and falsehood can't stand before him.
neighbors.shared: what's crooked doesn't last; what's true holds.

neighbors.heading: the long arc
neighbors.text: Today the Mundaka said truth alone wins, and lays the road the sages walk. In 1853 the American minister Theodore Parker said something like it about justice: he couldn't see the whole moral universe, and the arc is long, but from what he could see, he was sure it bends toward justice. Martin Luther King Jr. later made the line famous.
neighbors.difference: The Mundaka sets truth inside the right order of things, and makes it a road to the self. Parker spoke from conscience and the long view of history, without claiming to know how it works.
neighbors.shared: truth can take its time; it still gets there.
neighbors.sources: Theodore Parker, "Of Justice and the Conscience," Ten Sermons of Religion (1853) (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: there is One
neighbors.text: Today the Shvetashvatara said: Rudra is truly one; they do not stand for a second. The Guru Granth Sahib opens on the same number. Its first word is Ik Onkar: there is One. Guru Nanak's Mool Mantar goes on to describe that One: true name, creator, without fear, without hate, beyond time, never born, self-existent.
neighbors.difference: The Upanishad gives the One a name from the old hymns, Rudra, whom Shaiva readers worship as Shiva. Sikhs speak of the One as formless and never born, called by many names, belonging to no single story.
neighbors.shared: you can turn toward the One in your own words.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1, Mool Mantar (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the Lord is one
neighbors.text: Today the Shvetashvatara said Rudra is one, ruling every world from within. Asked which commandment comes first, Jesus quoted Israel's great prayer, the Shema: "Hear, O Israel; The Lord our God is one Lord: And thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart." Christians call him the maker of heaven and earth, near to every creature.
neighbors.difference: The Upanishad gives the one Lord a face and a name, Rudra, later loved as Shiva. Christians believe the one God is Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and came close in Jesus.
neighbors.shared: the One who made the stars still turns toward you.

items.lessonTitle: "Now, yoga." Yoga is the stilling of the turnings of the mind (1.1–1.2)

neighbors.heading: straightening the arrow
neighbors.text: Today Patanjali defined yoga as the stilling of the turnings of the mind. The Buddha watched the same whirl. The Dhammapada says: "As a fletcher makes straight his arrow, a wise man makes straight his trembling and unsteady thought, which is difficult to guard, difficult to hold back." The next verse compares the mind to a fish flapping on dry land.
neighbors.difference: Patanjali stills the mind so the seer can rest in its own nature. The Buddha trains the mind toward freedom without pointing to a lasting seer behind it.
neighbors.shared: a busy mind can learn to settle, a little at a time.

neighbors.heading: be still
neighbors.text: Today Patanjali said yoga is the stilling of the turnings of the mind. Catholics pray a psalm that asks for stillness too: "Be still and see that I am God." Monks and nuns have kept that quiet for centuries, and Catholics today may sit in silent prayer before the Blessed Sacrament, simply resting in God's presence.
neighbors.difference: Patanjali's stillness lets the seer rest in itself, and no god is named yet. In Catholic prayer, the stillness is for meeting God, who is other than you and comes to you as a friend.
neighbors.shared: when the stirring settles, something deeper can be seen.

neighbors.heading: the people you'll meet today
neighbors.text: Today Patanjali gave four keys: friendliness, compassion, gladness, and calm toward those who do wrong. The Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius practiced the fourth. One morning note to himself reads: today I'll meet people who are meddling, ungrateful, arrogant. They can't truly harm me, and I won't be angry with them, because we were made to work together, like two hands.
neighbors.difference: Patanjali offers the four attitudes to clear and settle the mind on the way to stillness. Marcus reasons as a Stoic: all people share one reason, so anger at them is like a hand fighting a foot.
neighbors.shared: how you meet people shapes the mind you carry home.

neighbors.heading: don't cheer when they fall
neighbors.text: Today Patanjali paired four attitudes with four kinds of people, and the hardest was calm toward those who do wrong. Proverbs asks the same: "Rejoice not when thine enemy falleth, and let not thy heart be glad when he stumbleth." And in the Mishnah, Shammai adds a gentler one: greet every person with a cheerful face.
neighbors.difference: Patanjali offers the four keys to make the mind clear and calm. Proverbs grounds it in God: gloating over an enemy displeases the LORD. Jewish teachers add that every person is made in God's image.
neighbors.shared: kindness toward people steadies your own heart.

neighbors.heading: thy will be done
neighbors.text: Today Patanjali named the third part of the yoga of action: surrender to the Lord, offering your actions and letting go of their fruits. The night before he died, Jesus prayed in a garden: "Father, if thou be willing, remove this cup from me: nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done." Christians pray it in the Lord's Prayer: "Thy will be done."
neighbors.difference: Patanjali's Ishvara is a special self, the first teacher, untouched by affliction, and surrender thins the mind's knots. For Christians, surrender is trust in a loving Father, following Jesus, who did it first.
neighbors.shared: you can do your best and then open your hands.

neighbors.heading: the one who surrenders
neighbors.text: Today Patanjali named surrender to the Lord as part of everyday yoga. In Arabic, the word islam itself means surrender, and a muslim is one who surrenders. The Qur'an says: "Nay, but whosoever surrendereth his purpose to Allah while doing good, his reward is with his Lord; and there shall no fear come upon them neither shall they grieve."
neighbors.difference: In the Yoga Sutras, surrender is one practice among three, a way to thin the afflictions. In Islam, surrender to Allah, the One, is the whole of the faith, lived through prayer, fasting and doing good.
neighbors.shared: giving your effort away makes it lighter to carry.

items.lessonTitle: Ignorance — mistaking the passing for the permanent (2.4–2.5)

neighbors.heading: what is seen, what is not
neighbors.text: Today Patanjali named the first mix-up: taking the passing for the permanent. Saint Paul keeps his eyes on the same difference: "we look not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen, are temporal; but the things which are not seen, are eternal."
neighbors.difference: For Patanjali, the deepest mix-up is taking the body and mind for the self, the seer. For Catholics, passing things are still God's good gifts; what lasts is God, and the life he promises.
neighbors.shared: hold the passing things gently; they were never meant to last.

neighbors.heading: whatever is made will pass
neighbors.text: Today Patanjali named the root mix-up: taking what passes for what lasts. Guru Tegh Bahadur says it in his closing verses in the Guru Granth Sahib: whatever has come into being will pass away, today or tomorrow. And he names what stays: the Name stays, the saints stay, the Guru stays.
neighbors.difference: Patanjali's cure is discernment: telling the seer apart from what it sees. The Guru's cure is singing the praises of the One and remembering the Name, which doesn't pass.
neighbors.shared: everything passes, and something worth holding stays.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1429, Saloks of Guru Tegh Bahadur (paraphrase)

items.lessonTitle: Yama — non-harm, truth, non-stealing, restraint, non-grasping (2.30–2.31)

neighbors.heading: five, and ten
neighbors.text: Today Patanjali named five restraints: non-harm, truthfulness, not stealing, restraint, not grasping. Several will sound familiar from Sinai: "Thou shalt not murder. Thou shalt not commit adultery. Thou shalt not steal. Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour." And the last commandment goes inside, like not grasping: "Thou shalt not covet."
neighbors.difference: Patanjali puts non-harm first, as the root of the rest, and makes the five the first limb toward stillness. The Ten Commandments come as God's covenant with Israel, and begin with God before turning to neighbors.
neighbors.shared: a good life starts with how you treat the people around you.

neighbors.heading: the five precepts
neighbors.text: Today Patanjali named five restraints, with non-harm first. Buddhists take five precepts, and they rhyme almost line for line: I undertake to refrain from killing living beings, from taking what isn't given, from sexual misconduct, from false speech, and from drink and drugs that cloud the mind. Buddhists recite them at a temple or at home.
neighbors.difference: Patanjali's fifth is not grasping; the Buddhist fifth is a clear head, free of intoxicants. Buddhists take the precepts as training steps toward awakening; Patanjali calls the five, kept without exception, the great vow.
neighbors.shared: do no harm is a good first step on any path.
neighbors.sources: The five precepts (pañcasīla), as recited in Pali (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a heart at prayer
neighbors.text: Today Patanjali said concentration is binding the mind to one place: it slips, you bring it back. Muslims call the heart's focus in prayer khushu'. The Qur'an opens a chapter with it: "Successful indeed are the believers / Who are humble in their prayers." Teachers say: let the eyes rest on the place of prostration, and the heart on Allah.
neighbors.difference: Patanjali's concentration can rest on any one place, the navel, the heart, the tip of the nose, and leads toward absorption. In Islam, the focus is turning the whole heart to Allah in the daily prayers.
neighbors.shared: each time the mind wanders, you can gently bring it back.

neighbors.heading: bringing it back
neighbors.text: Today Patanjali defined concentration as holding the mind on one place, and bringing it back each time it slips. The psychologist William James wrote: "the faculty of voluntarily bringing back a wandering attention, over and over again, is the very root of judgment, character, and will." An education that trained it, he said, would be the best education there is.
neighbors.difference: Patanjali trains attention as a step toward samadhi, where the sense of me drops away. James studied attention as a scientist, for clearer thinking and a steadier will, without a goal beyond the mind.
neighbors.shared: the coming back is the practice, not the failure.
neighbors.sources: William James, The Principles of Psychology (1890), ch. 11

items.lessonTitle: The powers are obstacles to samadhi (3.37)

neighbors.heading: other tastes
neighbors.text: Today Patanjali turned the list of powers over: seen from samadhi, they're obstacles. Guru Nanak said something close to the wonder-working yogis of his day. In the Japji he sings that the Lord is the true master who holds everything together, and miraculous powers are other tastes, flavors that pull you away from him.
neighbors.difference: Patanjali doesn't call the powers false; he keeps them in their place on the way to freedom. Guru Nanak sets them aside for something sweeter: the Name, and living in the Hukam.
neighbors.shared: the flashy gift isn't the treasure; keep your eyes on what matters.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 6, Japji pauri 29 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: and have not love
neighbors.text: Today Patanjali said the powers are obstacles if the goal is stillness. Saint Paul says gifts can miss the point too: "And though I have the gift of prophecy, and understand all mysteries, and all knowledge; and though I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, and have not charity, I am nothing."
neighbors.difference: For Patanjali, the powers distract from resting as the seer. For Paul, the greatest gift is love, God's own love living in us; without it, even miracles are empty.
neighbors.shared: the most impressive thing isn't always the most important.

items.lessonTitle: Kaivalya — when purity of mind equals purity of self (3.55–3.56)

neighbors.heading: purify the mind
neighbors.text: Today Patanjali said freedom comes when the mind is as clear as the seer: wipe the glass until it adds nothing. The Dhammapada sums up the teaching in one short verse: "Not to commit any sin, to do good, and to purify one's mind, that is the teaching of (all) the Awakened."
neighbors.difference: Patanjali's seer never needed cleaning; only the mind does. The Buddha points to no seer behind it: purifying the mind ends craving, and that ending is itself freedom.
neighbors.shared: clearing the mind is quiet work, and worth it.

neighbors.heading: the clean of heart
neighbors.text: Today Patanjali said freedom comes when the mind is wiped as clean as the seer. Jesus promises something like it in the Beatitudes: "Blessed are the clean of heart: for they shall see God." Catholics speak of purity of heart as a lifelong work of grace: confession, prayer, and letting go of whatever clouds the way we see.
neighbors.difference: For Patanjali, a clean mind lets the seer stand alone, needing nothing. For Catholics, a clean heart is God's gift, and its reward is seeing God face to face, in love.
neighbors.shared: a clear heart sees more truly.

neighbors.heading: looking for a person
neighbors.text: Today Valmiki asked: is there anyone alive who is truthful, kind, grateful, and has conquered anger? A Greek philosopher asked it his own way. Diogenes, the story goes, walked about in broad daylight holding a lit lamp, and told anyone who asked that he was looking for a human being, a real one.
neighbors.difference: Narada answers Valmiki with a name, Rama, and the whole epic becomes the evidence. Diogenes' lamp was a joke with a point: he never claimed to find anyone.
neighbors.shared: good character is rare, and worth looking for.
neighbors.sources: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of the Eminent Philosophers 6.41 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: be the one
neighbors.text: Today Valmiki asked if anyone alive held all sixteen good qualities, and Narada said they're hard to find together. Hillel turned the search around. In the Mishnah he teaches: in a place where there are no worthy people, try to be one yourself. His word is ish, a person who stands up when it counts.
neighbors.difference: Narada names Rama, and the epic tells his story as the answer. Hillel names no hero; he hands the question back to the listener, to be lived out under God's commandments.
neighbors.shared: if you can't find the good person, start becoming one.

neighbors.heading: thy prayer is heard
neighbors.text: Today Dasharatha, the king who had everything but a son, told his counselors his grief and asked for help. Luke's Gospel opens with an old priest, Zacharias, and his wife Elisabeth, who had no child either. While he served in the Temple, an angel said: "Fear not, Zacharias: for thy prayer is heard; and thy wife Elisabeth shall bear thee a son."
neighbors.difference: Dasharatha's sons come through a great sacrifice, and one of them is Vishnu born as a man. Zacharias's son is John the Baptist, a prophet sent to prepare the way for Jesus.
neighbors.shared: it's brave to say out loud what you're longing for.

neighbors.heading: the old man's prayer
neighbors.text: Today Dasharatha admitted the one thing he lacked, a son, and asked for help. The Qur'an tells of Zakariyya praying in secret: "My Lord! Lo! the bones of me wax feeble and my head is shining with grey hair, and I have never been unblest in prayer to Thee, my Lord." And Allah gives him good news of a son, Yahya.
neighbors.difference: Dasharatha seeks sons through a great royal sacrifice with priests and counselors. Zakariyya simply calls on his Lord, alone and in secret; his son Yahya is a prophet and a servant of Allah.
neighbors.shared: an honest ask can open a door you thought was shut.

neighbors.heading: no more force than needed
neighbors.text: Today Rama tried the gentlest way first: take away her power to harm, not her life. Catholic teaching sets the same limit on defending yourself. Following Saint Thomas Aquinas, the Catechism says you may repel force to protect yourself and others, but if you use more violence than is necessary, it becomes wrong.
neighbors.difference: In the Ramayana, the sage finally urges Rama to finish the fight, and the forest is freed. Catholic teaching asks that force be measured, used only as far as defense requires.
neighbors.shared: even when you must stand firm, choose the gentlest way that works.
neighbors.sources: Catechism of the Catholic Church 2264, citing Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae II-II, 64, 7 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the last resort
neighbors.text: Today Rama tried to disarm Tataka before anything harder. Guru Gobind Singh wrote to the emperor Aurangzeb in a Persian letter, the Zafarnama: when every other way has been tried and has failed, then it is right to take up the sword. Sikhs honor the saint-soldier: gentle first, brave when there's no other choice.
neighbors.difference: Rama acts as a prince protecting a sage's rite, at his teacher's word. The Guru speaks of defending the wronged against broken promises, and only after every peaceful means has run out.
neighbors.shared: strength is best when gentleness has had its turn first.
neighbors.sources: Zafarnama of Guru Gobind Singh, verse 22 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a help beside him
neighbors.text: Today Janaka gave Sita to Rama as sahadharmachari, one who walks the path of dharma together with you. The Torah begins marriage with loneliness: "It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him a help meet for him." The Hebrew, ezer kenegdo, means a help who matches him, standing face to face.
neighbors.difference: Rama and Sita circle the fire, and Sita is given as a companion in dharma. A Jewish wedding is a covenant under the chuppah, sealed with a ring and a written ketubah of promises.
neighbors.shared: a good marriage is two people walking the same road.

neighbors.heading: matched in goodness
neighbors.text: Today Janaka called Sita Rama's companion in dharma, one who walks the right way with him. The Buddha once met an old couple, Nakula's parents, who hoped to be together in this life and the next. He told them: if a husband and wife are matched in faith, in virtue, in generosity and in wisdom, they'll see each other again.
neighbors.difference: In the Ramayana, marriage is a sacred rite around the fire. The Buddha laid down no wedding rite; what joins the couple, he said, is shared goodness.
neighbors.shared: love grows strongest when two people walk toward the same good.

neighbors.heading: repel evil with good
neighbors.text: Today Valmiki said one kindness pleased Rama, and a hundred wrongs he didn't count. The Qur'an asks for the same generous memory: "Repel the evil deed with one which is better, then lo! he, between whom and thee there was enmity (will become) as though he was a bosom friend." And of the wronged: "let them forgive and show indulgence."
neighbors.difference: Valmiki shows Rama's generous memory as the sign of a great heart. The Qur'an ties forgiving others to hope in Allah's own forgiveness: forgive, as you long to be forgiven.
neighbors.shared: remember the kindness; let the hurts go uncounted.

neighbors.heading: bad is stronger than good
neighbors.text: Today Valmiki said Rama remembered one kindness and didn't count a hundred wrongs. Psychologists say most of us lean the other way. In a well-known 2001 paper, Roy Baumeister and colleagues found that bad is stronger than good: a harsh word or a hurt sticks longer than a kind one. Rama's memory runs against the grain, and that can be practiced.
neighbors.difference: For Valmiki, Rama's generous memory is part of his goodness, the heart of a dharmic king. Psychology only describes the bias, and suggests noticing good things on purpose, a habit anyone can build.
neighbors.shared: you can choose which memories you keep close.
neighbors.sources: Baumeister, Bratslavsky, Finkenauer and Vohs, "Bad Is Stronger Than Good," Review of General Psychology (2001) (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: sweet is your will
neighbors.text: Today Rama lost a kingdom in one sentence and said, so be it, I'll go. Sikhs have a word for meeting what comes: hukam, the order of God's will running through everything. The Japji says all are within the hukam, and none outside it. Guru Arjan goes further and calls that will sweet. Accepting it, for a Sikh, is trust in the one who sends.
neighbors.difference: Rama bows to a promise his father made, a son keeping a king's human word. For Sikhs, the hukam is God's own will, and accepting it goes hand in hand with standing up for what's right.
neighbors.shared: you can lose something big and still keep your heart steady.
neighbors.sources: Japji Sahib, pauri 2, Guru Granth Sahib Ang 1 (paraphrase) · Guru Arjan, Raag Asa, Guru Granth Sahib (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: not my will
neighbors.text: Today Rama heard he must leave everything, and answered, so be it. Christians remember a night in a garden. Before his arrest, Jesus asked that the cup might pass from him, and then prayed: "nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done." The Gospel doesn't pretend it was easy. He asked first, and then he said yes.
neighbors.difference: Rama keeps his father's promise to Kaikeyi, a son honoring a king's word. Christians hear Jesus speaking to God as Father on the way to the cross, and believe his yes opened salvation to the world.
neighbors.shared: calm can be a choice made while it still hurts.

neighbors.heading: a prince who gave it all
neighbors.text: Today Rama gave his wealth away on the day his life fell apart, and still had a joke for a poor old man. Buddhists tell of a giving prince too. In the Vessantara Jataka, a story of one of the Buddha's past lives, Prince Vessantara gives so freely that he's sent into exile in the forest, and keeps giving there. Buddhists call giving dana.
neighbors.difference: Rama gives before exile so no one who depends on him is left without support, keeping a prince's dharma. Vessantara's giving is told as practice toward awakening, letting go even of what he loves most.
neighbors.shared: grief doesn't have to make your hands close.

neighbors.heading: a cheerful giver
neighbors.text: Today Rama made a poor man throw his staff, gave him every cow up to where it landed, then apologized for the joke. Catholics hear Saint Paul in that: "for God loveth a cheerful giver." The Church counts giving to the poor among the works of mercy, and saints like Francis of Assisi gave away everything they had.
neighbors.difference: Rama gives as a prince leaving home, caring for those who depend on him. For Catholics, a gift to someone in need is also a gift to Christ himself, who said what you do for the least, you do for him.
neighbors.shared: a gift lands best when the other person keeps their dignity.
neighbors.sources: 2 Corinthians 9:7 (Douay-Rheims) · Matthew 25:40 (paraphrase) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 2447 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: another self
neighbors.text: Today Guha, a forest king, came out to meet Rama, and the text calls him a friend as dear as life. Philosophers have tried to name that kind of friend. Aristotle said the best friendship isn't for usefulness or fun, but for the other person's own good, and he called such a friend another self. Guha offers a kingdom and asks nothing back.
neighbors.difference: For many Hindus, Rama is God, and later devotion counts friendship as one way of loving God. For Aristotle, friendship is a human good, part of a well-lived life, that needs nothing beyond itself.
neighbors.shared: the best friends want your good, not your use.

neighbors.heading: loved as his own soul
neighbors.text: Today Guha met Rama at the river, a friend as dear as life. The Hebrew Bible tells of a prince who loved like that. When Jonathan, son of King Saul, met David, "the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul." He gave David his own robe and his sword.
neighbors.difference: Guha offers Rama his kingdom, and Rama turns it down to keep his vow. Jonathan, heir to a throne, knows David will be king one day, and loves him anyway, even against his own father.
neighbors.shared: a true friend is glad to see you rise.

items.lessonTitle: Dasharatha's death and the curse that caused it (Shravana Kumara)

neighbors.heading: honor thy father and mother
neighbors.text: Today a boy with no name in the oldest text became Shravan Kumar, the son who cared for his blind parents. Christians carry a commandment for that love. Paul repeats it to the church at Ephesus: "Honour thy father and mother; which is the first commandment with promise." Elsewhere he asks believers to care for their own families, repaying their parents.
neighbors.difference: Shravan's story grew in later retellings into a byword for a devoted son. For Christians, honoring parents is one of the Ten Commandments given by God, and Jesus also asks that love for him come first.
neighbors.shared: the hands that once carried us deserve to be carried.

neighbors.heading: the wing of mercy
neighbors.text: Today we met the boy later tellings call Shravan Kumar, who carried water to his blind parents. The Qur'an speaks to that same care. When parents grow old, it says, don't speak harshly to them: "lower unto them the wing of submission through mercy," and pray, "My Lord! Have mercy on them both as they did care for me when I was little."
neighbors.difference: For many Hindus, Shravan's devotion is a picture of a son's dharma. In the Qur'an, kindness to parents comes right after the command to worship God alone, so caring for them is part of worship itself.
neighbors.shared: parents growing old is a call to grow gentle.

neighbors.heading: servant of the servants
neighbors.text: Today Bharata ruled for fourteen years and refused to be king, laying every decision before his brother's sandals. Catholics know that shape. Jesus taught that whoever wants to be first must be the servant of the rest. Popes still use an old title, servant of the servants of God, and the Church speaks of keeping watch until Christ comes again.
neighbors.difference: Bharata keeps a throne for a brother who will walk back through the gate. Catholics believe Christ is present now, in the sacraments and the Church, even as they wait for his return.
neighbors.shared: the one in charge can be the one who serves.
neighbors.sources: Matthew 20:26–27 (paraphrase) · servus servorum Dei, a papal title (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the Guru on the throne
neighbors.text: Today a pair of sandals sat on Ayodhya's throne, and Bharata held the royal umbrella over them himself. In a gurdwara, Sikhs see something like it. The Guru Granth Sahib rests on a raised throne under a canopy, and someone waves a whisk, a chaur, above it, as for a sovereign. Tradition says Guru Gobind Singh named the scripture the Guru.
neighbors.difference: The sandals stand in for Rama until he comes home. For Sikhs, the Guru Granth Sahib stands in for no one: it is the living Guru, the word itself, and Sikhs bow to it as such.
neighbors.shared: honoring someone absent can keep them present.

neighbors.heading: no talebearing
neighbors.text: Today Rama stopped his brother mid-sentence: don't speak badly of our middle mother; speak of Bharata. Judaism has a whole teaching about that. The Torah says, "Thou shalt not go up and down as a talebearer among thy people." The rabbis call harmful talk lashon hara, the evil tongue, and warn against it even when it's true.
neighbors.difference: Rama refuses bitterness out of love for a family that wronged him, a son's dharma. Jewish law works it out in detail: what may and may not be said, and when speaking up is needed to protect someone.
neighbors.shared: some words protect a family by never being said.

neighbors.heading: right speech
neighbors.text: Today Lakshmana said one sentence too many about Kaikeyi, and Rama turned the talk back to Bharata. Buddhists count speech as part of the path itself. Right speech, the Buddha taught, means no lying, no talk that divides people, no harsh words, and no idle chatter. What you hear in one place, the suttas say, you don't carry to another to split people apart.
neighbors.difference: Rama guards his words to honor his family and his father's queen. In the Buddha's teaching, right speech is one step of the Eightfold Path, a training of the mind toward freedom from suffering.
neighbors.shared: kind silence about someone can be a gift.
neighbors.sources: Samyutta Nikaya 45.8 (paraphrase) · Digha Nikaya 1, Brahmajala Sutta (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: religion is sincere counsel
neighbors.text: Today an old enemy of Rama told his own king the truth: pleasant speakers are easy to find; people who say hard, good things are rare. Muslims keep a saying of the Prophet close to that: religion is sincere counsel, nasiha. And the Qur'an's short Surah 103 says the ones who aren't lost "exhort one another to truth."
neighbors.difference: Maricha warns Ravana to save his king and his city from ruin. In the hadith, sincere counsel is owed to God, His book, His messenger, leaders and ordinary people alike: honesty, offered with care.
neighbors.shared: the friend who tells you the hard truth is a gift.
neighbors.sources: Sahih Muslim, Book of Faith, hadith of Tamim al-Dari (paraphrase) · Qur'an 103:3 (Pickthall 1930)

neighbors.heading: flatterer or friend
neighbors.text: Today Maricha warned Ravana that people who say pleasant things are easy to find, and people who say hard, useful things are rare. Plutarch, a Greek writer, wrote a whole essay on telling a flatterer from a friend. The flatterer copies you and praises everything, he says; the friend speaks frankly, like a doctor whose medicine stings because it heals.
neighbors.difference: Maricha's warning rests on who Rama is: dharma in bodily form, a truth bigger than any king. Plutarch's test is human and practical: do a friend's words serve your good, or only your mood?
neighbors.shared: honest words, kindly meant, are a rare kind of love.
neighbors.sources: Plutarch, Moralia, How to Tell a Flatterer from a Friend (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a life given for others
neighbors.text: Today an old vulture fought Ravana to protect a woman who wasn't his own, knowing he'd lose. Sikhs remember Guru Tegh Bahadur, the ninth Guru. Tradition says Kashmiri Pandits came to him asking for help to keep their faith, and he went to Delhi and gave his life for their freedom. Sikhs call him Hind di Chadar, the shelter of India.
neighbors.difference: Jatayu fights with beak and talons, an old king keeping faith with his friend's son. At Delhi, Guru Tegh Bahadur didn't fight; he chose death over giving up the freedom to worship, and Sikhs honor him as a martyr.
neighbors.shared: protecting someone who isn't yours is still your business.
neighbors.sources: Bachittar Natak, Dasam Granth (paraphrase) · Sikh tradition

neighbors.heading: greater love
neighbors.text: Today Jatayu, old and outmatched, told Ravana, not while I'm alive, and gave his wings to keep a promise. Christians hear Jesus at the last supper: "Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends." They read it as a picture of the cross, and as a call to costly love.
neighbors.difference: Jatayu dies keeping faith with his friend Dasharatha. Christians believe Jesus laid down his life for everyone, friends and enemies alike, and rose again, and they see every other sacrifice in that light.
neighbors.shared: love keeps its promise even when it knows it'll lose.

neighbors.heading: practice that bears fruit
neighbors.text: Today Shabari, an old woman of the forest, said her years of practice bore fruit the day Rama came. Buddhists keep the verses of their own early women renunciants, the Therigatha. Again and again, these nuns, some old, some once poor or grieving, say in their own words that the long work is done and the mind is free.
neighbors.difference: For Shabari, the fruit is a visit: seeing Rama with her own eyes. In the Therigatha, the fruit isn't anyone's visit; it's freedom won through the nuns' own practice, with the Buddha's teaching pointing the way.
neighbors.shared: years of quiet practice are never wasted.

neighbors.heading: now let your servant go
neighbors.text: Today Shabari, who had waited years, said her practice bore fruit because she had seen Rama. Luke's Gospel has a man who had waited too. Simeon took the baby Jesus in his arms in the Temple and said, "Now thou dost dismiss thy servant, O Lord, according to thy word in peace; because my eyes have seen thy salvation." The Church prays his words at night prayer.
neighbors.difference: Shabari welcomes Rama as an honored guest in her forest hermitage. For Catholics, Simeon holds God made flesh as a child, the long hope of his people arriving.
neighbors.shared: a lifetime of waiting can end in one bright meeting.
neighbors.sources: Luke 2:29–30 (Douay-Rheims) · Liturgy of the Hours, Night Prayer (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: let it ripen
neighbors.text: Today Rama waited out the monsoon in a cave, and Lakshmana told him to save his strength for the time to act. The Stoic teacher Epictetus put it plainly: nothing great comes about suddenly, not even a bunch of grapes or a fig. If you want a fig, he said, let it blossom first, then bear fruit, then ripen.
neighbors.difference: Rama's waiting holds grief and a vow: his wife is a captive and he must keep faith. Epictetus treats patience as reason at work, accepting what isn't in our power and tending what is.
neighbors.shared: waiting well is its own kind of strength.

neighbors.heading: a time to every purpose
neighbors.text: Today Rama couldn't search in the monsoon, so he waited in a cave and watched the rain. The Hebrew Bible makes room for seasons like that: "To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven." Jewish prayer turns with the seasons too, adding words about wind and rain in the rainy months.
neighbors.difference: Rama waits because the roads are flooded and the rains decide. Ecclesiastes sees every season in God's hands, and its teacher admits people can't fully grasp why the times fall as they do.
neighbors.shared: some seasons ask us to wait, and that's allowed.
neighbors.sources: Ecclesiastes 3:1 (JPS 1917) · Ecclesiastes 3:11 (paraphrase) · the Amidah's rain blessing (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: seventy times seven
neighbors.text: Today Sugriva said, I may have slipped, who doesn't, and Rama took him back with an embrace. Christians remember Peter asking Jesus how often to forgive. Seven times? Jesus answered: "I say not unto thee, Until seven times: but, Until seventy times seven." And in the Lord's Prayer, Christians ask to be forgiven as they forgive.
neighbors.difference: Sugriva's apology repairs a pact between friends and allies. For Christians, forgiving others is bound up with being forgiven by God, and many Christians teach it even when the other person never says sorry.
neighbors.shared: a friendship tested and repaired can come back stronger.

neighbors.heading: forgive and overlook
neighbors.text: Today Sugriva owned his slip, and Rama didn't hold the lost weeks against him. The Qur'an asks the same of believers: "Let them forgive and show indulgence. Yearn ye not that Allah may forgive you?" Commentators link the verse to Abu Bakr, who had sworn off helping a relative who wronged him, then forgave him and kept helping.
neighbors.difference: Rama's forgiveness is kshama, a king's patience, like the earth that bears everything. In the Qur'an, forgiving people is tied to hoping for God's forgiveness; one of God's names is Al-Ghafur, the Forgiving.
neighbors.shared: own the mistake, then let the friendship breathe again.

neighbors.heading: hoping for nothing
neighbors.text: Today Svayamprabha fed lost strangers, led them out of her cave, and asked for nothing back. Catholics hear Jesus in Luke's Gospel: "do good, and lend, hoping for nothing thereby: and your reward shall be great." The Church's works of mercy grow from words like these: feed the hungry, give drink to the thirsty, shelter the homeless.
neighbors.difference: Svayamprabha helps by the power of her own austerities, then disappears into the dark. For Catholics, mercy given freely is a way of meeting Christ in the person helped, made possible by God's grace.
neighbors.shared: the kindest help sometimes leaves without waiting for thanks.
neighbors.sources: Luke 6:35 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 2447 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: seva, wanting nothing
neighbors.text: Today a woman in a cave gave food, rest and rescue to lost strangers, and wanted nothing back. Sikhs call that kind of help seva, selfless service. Sukhmani Sahib, a long hymn by Guru Arjan, says the one who serves without desire for reward reaches the Lord. You can see it in the gurdwara kitchen, where volunteers cook for anyone who walks in.
neighbors.difference: Svayamprabha is a solitary ascetic who helps by her own spiritual power. For Sikhs, seva is ordinary and shared, done by householders in kitchens and courtyards, as a way to wear down the ego.
neighbors.shared: help given freely is complete, even if no one remembers.
neighbors.sources: Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan, Guru Granth Sahib (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: mighty man of valor
neighbors.text: Today an old bear walked over to Hanuman and asked: why are you sitting there? The Bible has a scene like it. Gideon is hiding, threshing wheat in a winepress, when an angel greets him: "The LORD is with thee, thou mighty man of valour." Gideon protests that he's the least in his father's house. His strength is named out loud before he feels it.
neighbors.difference: Jambavan reminds Hanuman of strength he was born with, his father the wind's own speed. In Judges, Gideon's strength comes from God being with him, and the story insists the victory is God's.
neighbors.shared: sometimes strength comes back when someone says it out loud.

neighbors.heading: the mind was bright all along
neighbors.text: Today Hanuman sat apart, his strength forgotten, until someone told him his own story. Buddhists have a teaching that sounds close. In the Anguttara Nikaya, the Buddha says the mind is luminous, and it's stained by defilements that arrive from outside. Practice doesn't build the brightness from nothing; it clears away what covered it.
neighbors.difference: Hanuman's strength is a gift from his father, Vayu, and he gets it back by remembering who he is. The Buddha's luminous mind isn't a lasting self or a god's gift; it's clarity uncovered by training.
neighbors.shared: what you've forgotten about yourself may still be there.
neighbors.sources: Anguttara Nikaya, Book of Ones, the luminous mind passage (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: despair not
neighbors.text: Today Hanuman searched every room, found nothing, and fell into despair, then got up again: not giving in to despair is the root of good fortune. In the Qur'an, the prophet Jacob, still grieving his lost son Joseph, sends his sons out searching and tells them, "despair not of the Spirit of Allah."
neighbors.difference: Hanuman talks himself back up and bows to Rama, Sita and the gods before he searches again. For Jacob, hope rests on God's mercy alone, and the verse says only those without faith despair of it.
neighbors.shared: keep looking; giving up isn't the only door left.

neighbors.heading: belief helps create the fact
neighbors.text: Today Hanuman sank into despair in Ravana's palace, and climbed back out more than once. The psychologist and philosopher William James wrote about that climb. In a talk called "Is Life Worth Living?" he said: "Believe that life is worth living, and your belief will help create the fact." For James, hope is partly something you do.
neighbors.difference: Hanuman's hope leans on Rama and the gods; he bows to them before starting again. James grounds hope in what belief does inside a person: courage can open what doubt would have closed.
neighbors.shared: despair can sit with you without making the decision.
neighbors.sources: William James, "Is Life Worth Living?", in The Will to Believe

neighbors.heading: the Name, remembered
neighbors.text: Today Hanuman made sure the first thing Sita heard, frightened and alone, was the name she loved. Sikhs build a whole practice on that: naam simran, remembering the Name of God. Sukhmani Sahib opens by asking you to remember, and remember, and find peace. And the Gurus sang in the everyday languages people spoke, the way Hanuman chose plain words.
neighbors.difference: Hanuman speaks Rama's name to comfort Sita: her husband's name and, for many Hindus, God's. For Sikhs, the Name is God's presence beyond any one form, repeated so the mind stays near it.
neighbors.shared: a loved name, spoken softly, can steady a frightened heart.
neighbors.sources: Sukhmani Sahib, opening, Guru Granth Sahib (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: she heard her name
neighbors.text: Today Hanuman spoke softly from the branches so Sita would hear Rama's name before anything frightening. John's Gospel has a grieving woman in a garden too. Mary Magdalene, weeping at the empty tomb, doesn't know who's speaking, until he says one word: "Mary." She turns and answers, "Rabboni; which is to say, Master."
neighbors.difference: Sita hears her husband's name from a messenger, and learns he's searching for her. Mary hears her own name from Jesus himself, and Christians read it as a first meeting with the risen Christ.
neighbors.shared: being named with love can turn grief toward hope.

neighbors.heading: the snake's old skin
neighbors.text: Today Hanuman, horrified at what his anger nearly did, praised the one who throws off anger the way a snake sheds its old skin. The Buddha used the same picture. The opening verse of the Uraga Sutta, the snake discourse, praises one who checks rising anger the way medicine checks a snake's venom, and lets go of this shore and the far shore, like a snake's worn-out skin.
neighbors.difference: Hanuman condemns his anger because it nearly hurt the one he came to save. For the Buddha, hatred is one of three fires he named, a root of suffering to be uprooted by practice.
neighbors.shared: anger can be set down, the way a snake leaves its skin.

neighbors.heading: be angry, and sin not
neighbors.text: Today Hanuman burned Lanka and then stood on the shore, sick with fear that his fury had harmed Sita. Catholics hear Saint Paul: "Be angry, and sin not. Let not the sun go down upon your anger." The Church counts anger among the capital sins when it becomes a wish for revenge, and teaches that it can be set right.
neighbors.difference: Hanuman learns from his own scare, and relief comes from voices in the sky. For Catholics, sin is healed by God's grace, and in confession anger that did harm can be named and forgiven.
neighbors.shared: the moment after anger is where wisdom can begin.
neighbors.sources: Ephesians 4:26 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 1866, 2302 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: unhistoric acts
neighbors.text: Today a whole army of monkeys and bears built a bridge in five days, and later tellers added a squirrel rolling in sand to help. The novelist George Eliot ended Middlemarch with a line that honors that squirrel's kind of work: "the growing good of the world is partly dependent on unhistoric acts." Small, unseen work holds up big things.
neighbors.difference: In the Ramayana tradition, the bridge is built for Rama, and the squirrel's small gift is told as a lesson in devotion. Eliot's line asks for no particular faith: the good done by quiet, ordinary lives is worth honoring in itself.
neighbors.shared: no gift is too small for the bridge.

neighbors.heading: a mind to work
neighbors.text: Today an army built a bridge across the sea, everyone carrying stones. The Hebrew Bible tells of a whole people rebuilding Jerusalem's wall, many repairing the stretch beside their own homes. Nehemiah sums it up: "So built we the wall... for the people had a mind to work." And the Mishnah adds: you needn't finish the work, but you aren't free to stop.
neighbors.difference: Rama's bridge is built in five days for a rescue, held up by an ocean's promise. Nehemiah's wall is rebuilt to restore a city after exile, and the work goes on under threat.
neighbors.shared: everyone carries a stone, and the bridge holds.
neighbors.sources: Nehemiah 3 (paraphrase) · Nehemiah 4:6 (KJV; 3:38 in Jewish Bibles) · Pirkei Avot 2:16 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: I will in no wise cast out
neighbors.text: Today Rama vowed safety to anyone who comes even once and says, I am yours, even if it were Ravana himself. Christians hear Jesus in John's Gospel: "him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out." And in the Sermon on the Mount he said, "Love your enemies," and pray for those who persecute you.
neighbors.difference: Rama makes his vow as a king and, for many devotees, as God giving refuge, sharanagati. Christians believe that welcome comes through Jesus, whose death and rising they trust opens the door to anyone who turns to him.
neighbors.shared: the door stays open, even for someone from the other side.

neighbors.heading: grant him protection
neighbors.text: Today the enemy king's brother asked for refuge, and Rama said yes, and would have even for Ravana. The Qur'an has a command like it. If one of the idolaters at war with the believers asks for protection, it says, grant it, so he may hear the word of God, then escort him to a place where he is safe.
neighbors.difference: Rama's vow takes in anyone who says, I am yours, and makes him a friend. The Qur'an's protection asks nothing like that: the one who asks hears God's word and is taken safely home.
neighbors.shared: someone asking for safety should find it.

neighbors.heading: the angel who heals
neighbors.text: Today Hanuman carried a mountain of healing herbs through the night, and became the one people pray to when someone they love is sick. Catholics have a healer sent from heaven too. In the Book of Tobit, the angel Raphael travels in disguise, shows young Tobias a remedy, and old Tobit's blindness is cured. Then Raphael reveals who he is.
neighbors.difference: For many Hindus, Hanuman is himself divine and prayed to directly. For Catholics, Raphael is an angel, a creature serving God, honored and asked to pray, while healing comes from God alone.
neighbors.shared: help can arrive at night, just when everyone feels helpless.

neighbors.heading: a Guru's herb garden
neighbors.text: Today Hanuman carried healing herbs through the night and became the one people pray to when someone's in the hospital. Sikhs remember Guru Har Rai, the seventh Guru, who tradition says kept a herb garden and a dispensary. When the emperor's son fell ill and the court's doctors failed, the Guru sent the medicine he needed, though that family had been no friend.
neighbors.difference: Hanuman's flight is a wonder of strength and devotion, a mountain carried in a night. Guru Har Rai's healing is remembered as plain seva: herbs grown and medicine given, to friend or foe.
neighbors.shared: healing belongs to everyone, friend or not.
neighbors.sources: Sikh tradition about Guru Har Rai (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: when your enemy falls
neighbors.text: Today Rama said enmity ends at death, and gave Ravana a king's funeral. The Hebrew Bible says, "Rejoice not when thine enemy falleth." The Talmud tells that when Egypt's army drowned in the sea, the angels wanted to sing, and God stopped them: the work of my hands is drowning, and you would sing?
neighbors.difference: Rama honors Ravana as a great warrior and calls him his own now. The Talmud still celebrates the rescue: Israel sang at the sea. What it refuses is joy at the enemy's death itself.
neighbors.shared: when the fight is over, the hatred can end too.

neighbors.heading: hatred ceases by love
neighbors.text: Today Rama refused to carry hatred one step past Ravana's death, and Sita spared the guards who'd tormented her. The Dhammapada opens close to this. Whoever keeps thinking, he abused me, he beat me, never lets hatred end. Then: "For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love—this is an old rule."
neighbors.difference: Rama honors Ravana with royal rites, a king's duty kept even for an enemy. The Buddha's teaching looks inward: letting go of hatred is part of freeing your own mind, whoever the enemy was.
neighbors.shared: hatred stops where someone finally refuses to pass it on.

neighbors.heading: return the trust
neighbors.text: Today Bharata put the sandals back on Rama's feet and said the kingdom was a deposit left with him; he was giving it back. Muslims call such a trust amanah. The Qur'an says, "Lo! Allah commandeth you that ye restore deposits to their owners," and the Prophet was known, even before his calling, as al-Amin, the trustworthy.
neighbors.difference: Bharata returns a throne to his brother, keeping faith with Rama and their father's word. In Islam, every trust, even your own life and gifts, is held from God, and keeping it is part of worship.
neighbors.shared: what's left in your care deserves to go back whole.
neighbors.sources: Qur'an 4:58 (Pickthall 1930) · Ibn Ishaq, Life of the Messenger of God (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: good faith
neighbors.text: Today Bharata handed back a kingdom he'd held for fourteen years: a promise kept on both sides. The Roman philosopher Cicero wrote that the foundation of justice is good faith, truth and faithfulness to promises and agreements. He even asks when a deposit should be returned, and answers that justice usually means giving back what was trusted to you.
neighbors.difference: Bharata keeps faith out of love and dharma, his whole life shaped around the brother he waits for. Cicero roots good faith in reason and the bonds of society, a duty owed to friend and stranger alike.
neighbors.shared: a promise kept on both sides can feel like coming home.

items.lessonTitle: Janmashtami: the night Krishna was born

neighbors.heading: a child carried to safety
neighbors.text: Today a baby was born at midnight in a tyrant's prison and carried across a river to safety. Christians tell of a child hunted by a king too. After Jesus is born, Joseph is warned in a dream: "Arise, and take the young child and his mother, and flee into Egypt." He leaves by night. Some churches mark Christmas at midnight.
neighbors.difference: For many Hindus, Krishna is God appearing in the world, first in divine form, then as a baby. Christians believe God became human once, in Jesus, fully God and fully human, born to save the world.
neighbors.shared: the good can arrive in the darkest, most locked-up place.

neighbors.heading: the mist cleared
neighbors.text: Today we kept Krishna's birthday, waiting up for the good to arrive in the dark. Sikhs keep birthdays too: Gurpurabs, the Gurus' birthdays, with hymns, prayers and processions. Of Guru Nanak's coming, Bhai Gurdas wrote that when the true Guru Nanak appeared, the mist cleared and light spread through the world.
neighbors.difference: Many Hindus celebrate Krishna's birth as God come down in a body. The Mool Mantar calls God ajooni, beyond birth, and Sikhs honor Guru Nanak as the Guru who brought God's light into the world.
neighbors.shared: a birthday can be a way of saying the light came.
neighbors.sources: Bhai Gurdas, Var 1, pauri 27 (paraphrase) · Mool Mantar, Guru Granth Sahib Ang 1 (paraphrase)

items.lessonTitle: Maha Shivaratri: the great night of Shiva

neighbors.heading: the awakened one
neighbors.text: Today we kept Shivaratri, the night you don't sleep through. Buddhists carry wakefulness in their teacher's very title: Buddha means the awakened one. The Dhammapada says, "Earnestness is the path of immortality (Nirvâna), thoughtlessness the path of death." On observance days, some Buddhists keep extra precepts, and some sit in meditation through the night.
neighbors.difference: On Shivaratri the vigil is devotion: water, bilva leaves and Shiva's name until dawn. For Buddhists, wakefulness is above all a state of mind, clear attention trained day by day, not a night kept for a god.
neighbors.shared: don't sleep through the moments that matter.

neighbors.heading: watch and pray
neighbors.text: Today many Hindus stayed awake for Shiva until dawn. Catholics keep a great night vigil too. On Holy Saturday the Easter Vigil begins in the dark, with a new fire and one candle carried into the church. And Jesus, in the garden before his arrest, asked his friends: "Watch ye, and pray that ye enter not into temptation."
neighbors.difference: Shivaratri honors Shiva with fasting, water and bilva leaves on the lingam. The Easter Vigil keeps watch for Christ's rising from the dead, which Catholics hold as the center of their faith.
neighbors.shared: some nights are worth staying awake for.
neighbors.sources: Matthew 26:41 (Douay-Rheims) · Roman Missal, the Easter Vigil (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: guests in a hut
neighbors.text: Today Ganesha left home for the water, and the crowd shouted, come back soon. Jews keep a festival of a temporary home. At Sukkot the Torah says, "Ye shall dwell in booths seven days." Families build a sukkah, eat in it, and by an old custom welcome honored guests, the ushpizin: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and others. Then it comes down until next year.
neighbors.difference: Ganesha is welcomed home as a divine guest, then released to the water. The sukkah remembers Israel's journey through the wilderness in God's care, and its guests are honored ancestors, welcomed in spirit.
neighbors.shared: you can love something fully and still let it go.
neighbors.sources: Leviticus 23:42 (JPS 1917) · Leviticus 23:43 (paraphrase) · the ushpizin custom, from the Zohar (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: I have given it back
neighbors.text: Today a crowd carried Ganesha into the water, crying, and called out: come back soon. The Stoic teacher Epictetus gave advice for moments like that. Never say of anything, I have lost it, he wrote; say, I have given it back. Enjoy what you have the way a traveler enjoys an inn: fully, knowing it isn't yours to keep.
neighbors.difference: Visarjan is worship: the family offers food, asks forgiveness, and hopes Ganesha will return. Epictetus's letting go is a discipline of reason, accepting that what we love was never ours to control.
neighbors.shared: letting go and looking forward can share one breath.

items.lessonTitle: karma — the Isha Upanishad as a life

neighbors.heading: the earth is the LORD's
neighbors.text: Today the Isha Upanishad asked, whose, after all, is wealth? Christians pray a psalm that answers: "The earth is the LORD's, and the fulness thereof; the world, and they that dwell therein." Jesus told of a rich man who built bigger barns, then heard that his life would be required of him that night. Many Christians call the answer stewardship.
neighbors.difference: The Isha speaks of a world dwelt in by the Lord, and Shankara reads its line as letting go of owning. Christians see a Creator distinct from creation, who entrusts it to people to care for and share.
neighbors.shared: hold what you have like something borrowed, and enjoy it.

neighbors.heading: made trustees
neighbors.text: Today the Isha Upanishad asked, whose, after all, is wealth? The Qur'an answers that everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to God, and tells believers to "spend of that whereof He hath made you trustees." Zakat, a yearly giving, is one of Islam's five pillars, a reminder that wealth was never only yours.
neighbors.difference: The Isha opens a path where, for some readers, letting go of owning leads toward knowing the Self. In Islam, God alone is owner, beyond all creation, and people are trustees who will answer for how they spent.
neighbors.shared: what passes through your hands was lent, not given forever.

items.lessonTitle: bhakti — the Narada Bhakti Sutras opening

neighbors.heading: restless till it rests
neighbors.text: Today Narada said love for God shows in the ache of forgetting him. Catholics hear Saint Augustine, who opens his Confessions speaking straight to God: "Thou madest us for Thyself, and our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee." For Augustine, the ache isn't a failure. It's the heart pointing home.
neighbors.difference: Narada points to the gopis' love for Krishna, and sets several teachers' marks of devotion side by side. Augustine's longing turns toward the God he came to know in Christ, and he tells it as his own life's story.
neighbors.shared: missing God can itself be a kind of love.

neighbors.heading: forgetting, I die
neighbors.text: Today the Narada Bhakti Sutras said real love feels anguish at forgetting the beloved. Guru Nanak sang it in a hymn Sikhs pray in the evening: aakhaa jeevaa, visrai mar jaao. Remembering, I live; forgetting, I die. That's why naam simran, remembering the Name, runs through a Sikh day, from early morning to night prayers.
neighbors.difference: Narada pictures devotion through the gopis' love for Krishna, God with a form and a story. Sikhs love the Formless One, Nirankar, remembered through the Name and the Guru's word.
neighbors.shared: love shows in how much it hurts to forget.
neighbors.sources: Guru Nanak, Raag Asa, in Rehras Sahib, Guru Granth Sahib (paraphrase)

items.lessonTitle: Adi Parva: the snake sacrifice frame

neighbors.heading: the glory of letting it pass
neighbors.text: Today a sage sat with a dead snake on his shoulders and called forgiveness a sage's strength, while his son's curse started a chain. Jewish wisdom says it too. A proverb sings: "it is his glory to pass over a transgression." And the rabbis taught that whoever lets a wrong go, Heaven lets their own wrongs go too.
neighbors.difference: In the epic, forgiveness is a sage's power, a strength his discipline has earned. In Jewish teaching it's also a mirror: as you pass over other people's wrongs, God passes over yours.
neighbors.shared: a chain of hurt can stop with one person who lets go.

neighbors.heading: hatred doesn't end hatred
neighbors.text: Today one insult became a curse, and the curse became a death: a chain, link by link. Buddhists name the way out. The Dhammapada says: "hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love, this is an old rule." Shamika made the same quiet move. He wouldn't add a link.
neighbors.difference: In the epic the curse, once spoken, runs its course, and the story follows the chain to Janamejaya's fire. The Buddha teaches that each link is fed in our own minds, so it can be loosened from the inside.
neighbors.shared: you can be the place where a chain of anger ends.

neighbors.heading: God as your witness
neighbors.text: Today a prince spoke his vow before elders, so he couldn't take it back. Muslims treat a sworn word as weighty too. One chapter of the Qur'an opens: "O ye who believe! Fulfil your undertakings." Another verse warns against breaking an oath once you've made God your surety, the witness to what you promised.
neighbors.difference: Bhishma's witnesses are human elders, and his vow gives away a throne. In Islam the first witness is God, and the Qur'an sets a way to make amends for a broken oath, such as feeding the poor.
neighbors.shared: a promise said out loud is a gift to everyone who heard it.

neighbors.heading: the animal that makes promises
neighbors.text: Today a prince chose to speak his vow before elders, on purpose, so it would hold. Philosophers have marveled at that power. Friedrich Nietzsche called the human being the animal able to make promises: we bind our future selves with words, and other people build their lives on them. Keeping one, he thought, takes a long memory and a steady will.
neighbors.difference: Bhishma's vow belongs to dharma, sealed before elders and honored by the gods in the story. For Nietzsche, a promise is a human achievement, made of memory and will, with no heaven needed to seal it.
neighbors.shared: a promise is how you hand your future self to someone else.
neighbors.sources: Friedrich Nietzsche, On the Genealogy of Morals, second essay, section 1 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: higher still: truthful living
neighbors.text: Today Bhishma said the earth could lose its scent before he would give up truth. Sikhs hold truth that high, and then one step higher. Guru Nanak taught that truth is above everything, and higher still is truthful living. For the Guru, truth isn't only a word kept once; it's a way of living, every day.
neighbors.difference: Bhishma's truth is a vow never to marry or rule. The Gurus taught truthful living inside ordinary life: marrying, working honestly, raising a family and sharing. Two pictures of keeping faith with truth.
neighbors.shared: a life can be the proof of what a person says.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 62, Sri Raag, Guru Nanak (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: let yes be yes
neighbors.text: Today Bhishma would not break his word, even when the woman it was made for asked him to. Jesus spoke about words that hold. "But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay," he says in the Sermon on the Mount. A yes should simply mean yes, with nothing extra needed to prop it up.
neighbors.difference: Bhishma's whole life rests on one great sworn vow. In the same passage Jesus says "Swear not at all," asking for speech so plain that no oath is needed. Christians differ on oaths today; many churches allow them, while Quakers and some others decline them.
neighbors.shared: a word you keep becomes a place others can stand.

neighbors.heading: joy at someone else's good
neighbors.text: Today a boy watched his stronger cousin, and the story says jealousy took hold, until it became poison in the food. Buddhists practice an antidote. Mudita means gladness at another's good fortune, one of four boundless states the Buddha taught, beside loving-kindness, compassion and equanimity. It's grown on purpose, often starting with a dear friend's win.
neighbors.difference: The epic shows envy growing and lets us watch where it leads. Buddhist practice works on it ahead of time, training the mind toward gladness until another's success stops feeling like your loss.
neighbors.shared: a cousin's win doesn't have to be your loss.
neighbors.sources: Digha Nikaya 13, Tevijja Sutta, the four boundless states (Rhys Davids; paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: brothers and envy
neighbors.text: Today a grudge started young, between cousins raised in one palace. Catholics know an old telling of it: Cain and Abel. The Catechism calls envy a capital sin, sadness at another's good, and Scripture says: "But by the envy of the devil, death came into the world." The cure it names is goodwill: learning to be glad for the other.
neighbors.difference: The epic weighs both boys: Bhima's rough play and Duryodhana's jealousy. Catholic teaching treats envy as a sin of one's own heart, to be confessed and healed by God's grace, whatever the other person did.
neighbors.shared: a family grudge is easier to heal while it's still small.
neighbors.sources: Wisdom 2:24 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 2538–2540 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: drawn out of the water
neighbors.text: Today a basket floated down to a couple with no child, and a boy found a home. Jews tell a story with the same river in it. Moses, laid in an ark of bulrushes, is lifted from the Nile by Pharaoh's daughter, and Exodus says simply: "he became her son." She named him for it: "Because I drew him out of the water."
neighbors.difference: Moses's own mother is brought in to nurse him, and he grows up knowing his people. Karna learns whose son he is only on the eve of war. Moses's story leads to a people's freedom; Karna's, to one man's divided heart.
neighbors.shared: the one who takes you in is family too.

neighbors.heading: through you, not from you
neighbors.text: Today one mother let go upstream and another took the baby in downstream, and he carried both into his life. The poet Kahlil Gibran wrote of children: "They come through you but not from you, And though they are with you yet they belong not to you." No child is only the story of the people who made or raised them.
neighbors.difference: Gibran loosens every claim: children belong to Life itself, not to any parent. The epic weighs both claims: Kunti's blood and Radha's care each shape Karna, and he is called Radheya, after the woman who raised him.
neighbors.shared: every child is bigger than any one parent's story.

neighbors.heading: the left hand doesn't know
neighbors.text: Today Vidura saved a family with a riddle, a digger and a boat, and never once stood in the light. Jesus praised help like that. "But when thou doest alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth," he says, "That thine alms may be in secret." Quiet good, he teaches, is seen by God.
neighbors.difference: Vidura hides his help to keep the Pandavas alive in a court that wants them dead. Jesus asks for hidden giving so that the good is done for God, not for praise.
neighbors.shared: the best help often arrives without a name on it.

neighbors.heading: help given in secret
neighbors.text: Today Vidura's help came hidden: a riddle, a tunnel, a boatman with the right words. Muslims prize hidden help too. The Qur'an says giving openly is good, but giving in secret to people in need is better. And a hadith counts among the people God shelters someone who gives so quietly the left hand doesn't know what the right gave.
neighbors.difference: Vidura's secrecy is a shield against a dangerous court. In Islam, secret giving guards the giver's heart against showing off, so the gift is for God alone.
neighbors.shared: quiet kindness still reaches the far bank.

neighbors.heading: the open kitchen
neighbors.text: Today Yudhishthira fed a great crowd before he set foot in his new hall. Sikhs keep a kitchen at the heart of the gurdwara. Langar, the free community meal, goes back to Guru Nanak, and tradition says Guru Amar Das asked every visitor, even an emperor, to sit and eat in it first. Everyone sits together in rows and eats the same food.
neighbors.difference: Yudhishthira's feast honors brahmanas as a royal rite, blessing a new beginning. Langar is an ongoing open table for anyone of any faith or none, cooked and served by volunteers.
neighbors.shared: a place becomes holy when people are fed there.
neighbors.sources: Sikh tradition of langar, from Guru Nanak and Guru Amar Das (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: I was hungry
neighbors.text: Today a new hall was opened by feeding people first, with music and gifts. Catholics count feeding the hungry among the works of mercy. Jesus, describing the last judgment, says: "I was hungry, and you gave me to eat." In his telling, whoever feeds the least of his brothers and sisters has fed him.
neighbors.difference: Yudhishthira feeds people as a rite to begin something new and auspicious. For Catholics, feeding the hungry is a daily work of mercy, and Christ himself is met in the hungry person.
neighbors.shared: the best way to open a new home is to feed someone.
neighbors.sources: Matthew 25:35 (Douay-Rheims) · Matthew 25:40 (paraphrase) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 2447 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: get yourself a teacher
neighbors.text: Today everyone told Yudhishthira yes, and he still sent for the one friend who would tell him the truth. The rabbis gave similar advice. Pirkei Avot teaches: make for yourself a teacher, and acquire a friend. Proverbs adds: "in the multitude of counsellors there is safety." Many Jews still study in chavruta, with partners who push back.
neighbors.difference: Yudhishthira seeks out one person who sees further, Krishna, whom many Hindus worship as God. In Jewish learning the teacher is human, and study partners are meant to question each other, not only defer.
neighbors.shared: the best counsel comes from someone who won't just flatter you.

neighbors.heading: the whole of the path
neighbors.text: Today a king set aside a room full of yes and sent for a friend who would tell him the truth. Buddhists tell of Ananda saying that good friendship is half the holy life. The Buddha corrected him: not half. Admirable friendship, he said, is the whole of the holy life.
neighbors.difference: Yudhishthira turns to Krishna, a friend whom many Hindus worship as God. In the Buddha's teaching the admirable friend is a wise companion on the road, and each person still walks the path themselves.
neighbors.shared: find the friend who tells you the truth, either way.

neighbors.heading: repel it with something better
neighbors.text: Today a guest mocked the host in front of everyone, and Yudhishthira went after him with gentle words instead of guards. Muslims hear this in the Qur'an: "Repel the evil deed with one which is better," and an old enemy may become a close friend. Another verse says that when the foolish speak to God's servants, they answer: "Peace."
neighbors.difference: The epic lets two answers stand side by side: Yudhishthira's gentleness and Bhishma's firmness. The Qur'an names the better answer as God's way for believers, with God's reward, while still allowing wrongs to be resisted.
neighbors.shared: a gentle sentence can keep a guest at the table.

neighbors.heading: kindness that can't be beaten
neighbors.text: Today the host answered an insult with a gentle word, while the elder answered with steel. The Stoic emperor Marcus Aurelius wrote that a genuine kind disposition is invincible: what can even the most violent person do to you, if you stay kind and, when there's a chance, gently set them right? He meant it as daily practice.
neighbors.difference: For Marcus, kindness is reason at work, owed to every person as part of one human community. In the epic, Yudhishthira's gentleness is a host's dharma, and the poem gives Bhishma's sharper answer room too.
neighbors.shared: the first answer to an insult can still be kind.

neighbors.heading: every heart a jewel
neighbors.text: Today a guest fell into a pool, his host's brother laughed, and the hurt grew toward a war. Sikh scripture keeps a warning for that moment. Sheikh Farid's lines say: don't speak even one harsh word, for the True Lord lives in everyone; don't break anyone's heart, because every heart is a priceless jewel.
neighbors.difference: The epic shows the laugh and lets its harm unfold for years, without excusing what Duryodhana does next. Farid grounds the rule in God: wounding a heart wounds the place where the True Lord lives.
neighbors.shared: a laugh at someone's fall can outlast the fall.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1384, Salok of Sheikh Farid (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: restore, don't mock
neighbors.text: Today a man walked into a pool he took for floor, and the laughter behind him became a grudge. Paul wrote about moments like that: "if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted." Help first. You might slip next.
neighbors.difference: Duryodhana's slip is only a mistake about a floor, and Yudhishthira does send dry clothes. Paul is speaking of moral failings among believers: be gentle, because everyone needs God's mercy.
neighbors.shared: the one who slipped today could be you tomorrow.

neighbors.heading: not without giving first
neighbors.text: Today Draupadi served the guests, then her husbands, and ate last, and the sun's vessel kept the forest camp fed. Buddhists keep a saying of the Buddha close to this: if people knew, as he knew, the fruit of giving and sharing, they would not eat without first giving, even if it were their last mouthful.
neighbors.difference: Draupadi's serving keeps a household's duty to its guests, and a god's gift turns on it. For the Buddha, giving trains the giver's own mind, loosening stinginess on the way to freedom.
neighbors.shared: a table feels fuller when someone eats last on purpose.

neighbors.heading: servant of all
neighbors.text: Today Draupadi fed everyone before herself, in a camp that owned nothing. Jesus told his friends that greatness runs the other way: "whosoever will be first among you, shall be the servant of all." Popes have long used a title with the same idea in it: servant of the servants of God.
neighbors.difference: Draupadi serves as the heart of a household keeping the guest-duty of dharma. For Catholics, serving last follows Christ, who said he came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life.
neighbors.shared: the one who serves last holds the whole table together.
neighbors.sources: Mark 10:44 (Douay-Rheims) · Mark 10:45 (paraphrase) · the papal title Servus servorum Dei (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the right time to be angry
neighbors.text: Today a married couple argued in the forest: Draupadi said now is the time for strength; Yudhishthira called forgiveness the strength of the strong. Aristotle saw the same knot.
