Anyone can get angry, he wrote; that's easy. But to be angry with the right person, to the right degree, at the right time, for the right reason and in the right way is hard.
neighbors.difference: Aristotle looks for a middle way, set by reason and good habits. Draupadi and Yudhishthira argue from dharma and old stories of Prahlada and Bali, and the epic leaves both of them standing.
neighbors.shared: the hard part isn't choosing strength or mercy; it's knowing when.

neighbors.heading: a season for everything
neighbors.text: Today Draupadi quoted Prahlada: don't forgive always, don't use force always; there's a time for each. Jews read the same wisdom in Ecclesiastes: "To every thing there is a season," it begins, with "a time to keep silence, and a time to speak," and "a time of war, and a time of peace." Ashkenazi custom reads the book on Sukkot.
neighbors.difference: Prahlada gives a king practical advice: learn to judge which time it is. Ecclesiastes is a poem about seasons people can't always control, and it ends by urging reverence for God.
neighbors.shared: mercy and strength each have their hour; wisdom is telling which.

neighbors.heading: whither thou goest
neighbors.text: Today Damayanti shared her one cloth with Nala and told him she wouldn't leave. Christians read the same stubborn love in Ruth, who refused to leave her mother-in-law: "whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge." Matthew's Gospel names Ruth in Jesus's family line.
neighbors.difference: Damayanti stays with a husband who, that same night, leaves her sleeping. Ruth's loyalty is to Naomi, her mother-in-law, and she takes Naomi's people and God as her own. Ruth is a book Christians share with Jews.
neighbors.shared: love often looks like refusing to take the road away.

neighbors.heading: love and mercy between you
neighbors.text: Today Damayanti wrapped her husband in half her only garment and refused the road home without him. Muslims read marriage this way in the Qur'an: God "created for you helpmeets from yourselves that ye might find rest in them, and He ordained between you love and mercy." Muslims also remember Khadijah, the Prophet's first wife, who stood by him when others didn't.
neighbors.difference: The epic tests Damayanti's faithfulness to the breaking point, and Nala, not in his right mind, leaves. The Qur'an calls the love and mercy of marriage one of God's signs, a gift God places between two people.
neighbors.shared: notice who stays beside you when there's only one cloth left.
neighbors.sources: Qur'an 30:21 (Pickthall 1930) · Khadijah in the hadith and the Prophet's biography (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: what God hath joined
neighbors.text: Today Savitri learned her chosen husband would die within a year, and said she would not choose twice. Catholics see marriage as a choice made once, too. Jesus said: "What therefore God hath joined together, let no man put asunder." The Church teaches that the bond of a sacramental marriage, once fully made, lasts until death.
neighbors.difference: Savitri chooses before any wedding, and her faithfulness follows Satyavan to Death himself. In Catholic teaching the bond holds until death and then ends; a widow may marry again, and hope rests in God.
neighbors.shared: some choices are made once, and then kept.
neighbors.sources: Matthew 19:6 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 1640 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: one light in two bodies
neighbors.text: Today Savitri said she had chosen once and wouldn't choose twice, even knowing the year ahead. Sikhs hold marriage that close. Guru Amar Das wrote that those who only sit together aren't truly husband and wife; husband and wife are one light in two bodies. In the Anand Karaj, a couple walks four rounds around the Guru Granth Sahib.
neighbors.difference: Savitri's choice is a promise kept against a known death, and later she argues her husband back from Yama. In the Sikh wedding, the four rounds join the couple to each other and to God, on one spiritual journey.
neighbors.shared: a choice of the heart is a promise already made.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 788, Guru Amar Das (paraphrase) · the Lavan, Ang 773–774, Guru Ram Das (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: who is rich?
neighbors.text: Today a prince in exile said the happy person cooks simple greens at home and owes nothing. The rabbis asked a twin question: who is rich? Ben Zoma answered, the one who rejoices in his portion, and quoted a psalm: "thou shalt eat the labour of thine hands: happy shalt thou be."
neighbors.difference: Yudhishthira's happy person has outer conditions: a home, no debts, no exile. Ben Zoma's riches are inward: gladness in whatever portion you have, wherever you are.
neighbors.shared: a simple supper can be a whole happiness.

neighbors.heading: the best riches
neighbors.text: Today the yaksha asked who is happy, and the answer was small: greens at home, nothing owed. Buddhists keep a verse that points the same way: "Health is the greatest of gifts, contentedness the best riches; trust is the best of relationships, Nirvana the highest happiness." Contentment, here, is counted as wealth.
neighbors.difference: Yudhishthira's happiness is a householder's: a home, a supper, nothing owed. The Dhammapada honors contentment too, but names nirvana as the highest happiness, a freedom beyond any home, and Buddhist monks and nuns leave home to seek it.
neighbors.shared: enough, held gladly, is already a kind of wealth.

neighbors.heading: be fair among your children
neighbors.text: Today Yudhishthira chose to save Madri's son, not his strongest brother, so both mothers would have a living son. Muslims carry a hadith about fairness at home. When a father gave one son a gift, the Prophet asked whether he had given the same to all his children. He hadn't. The Prophet said: fear God, and be just among your children.
neighbors.difference: Yudhishthira's fairness is a life-or-death choice between two mothers' lines. The hadith is about everyday gifts from a parent, and it places fairness under God's watch.
neighbors.shared: fairness at home is a kind of love everyone can see.

neighbors.heading: choosing against your own side
neighbors.text: Today Yudhishthira, Kunti's son, chose to bring back Madri's son, so the family would stay fair. Philosophers test fairness this way too. John Rawls asked people to design society's rules as if they didn't know which place in it they would end up in. Choose from there, he argued, and you'll choose fairly.
neighbors.difference: Rawls asks us to imagine forgetting where we stand. Yudhishthira knows exactly where he stands, Kunti's living son, and chooses against his own side anyway, out of dharma and loyalty to both mothers.
neighbors.shared: fairness sometimes means choosing what isn't best for your side.
neighbors.sources: John Rawls, A Theory of Justice, the veil of ignorance (paraphrase)

items.lessonTitle: Udyoga: the embassy, Krishna's counsel, Karna and Kunti

neighbors.heading: the carpenter's bread
neighbors.text: Today Krishna turned down a prince's feast and ate in Vidura's plain house. Sikhs tell a story that sounds very close. Guru Nanak, tradition says, refused the banquet of a rich official, Malik Bhago, and ate the coarse bread of Bhai Lalo, a carpenter. Squeezed in the Guru's hand, Lalo's bread gave milk; Bhago's, blood.
neighbors.difference: Krishna's reason is love: he won't eat where there is neither love nor need. Guru Nanak's is honesty: bread earned by hard work, set beside bread squeezed from the poor.
neighbors.shared: where you choose to eat can say more than a speech.
neighbors.sources: Janamsakhi tradition of Bhai Lalo and Malik Bhago (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: I must abide at thy house
neighbors.text: Today Krishna passed by the prince's feast and stayed under Vidura's plain roof. Jesus made a choice like that too. In Jericho, with a crowd around him, he looked up into a tree and said: "Zacchaeus, make haste, and come down; for to day I must abide at thy house." The crowd murmured. The visit changed Zacchaeus.
neighbors.difference: Krishna refuses the table of a man who means harm. Jesus chooses the table of a man the crowd calls a sinner, and the visit becomes the way back: Zacchaeus gives half his goods to the poor.
neighbors.shared: a shared meal can be the start of a changed life.

items.lessonTitle: Bhishma Parva (the Gita re-read in place, 6 sessions)

neighbors.heading: going for refuge
neighbors.text: Today Arjuna put down his bow and said: I am your disciple; teach me; I come to you for refuge. Buddhists know that word well. The Three Refuges begin "Buddham saranam gacchami," I go for refuge to the Buddha, and then to the Dhamma, his teaching, and to the Sangha, the community.
neighbors.difference: Arjuna takes refuge in Krishna, his friend and charioteer, whom he comes to see as God. Buddhists take refuge in the Buddha as the teacher who found the way and showed it, in his teaching, and in each other.
neighbors.shared: admitting you need a teacher can be the bravest moment.
neighbors.sources: Khuddakapatha 1, the Three Refuges (Pali; English paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: lord, teach us
neighbors.text: Today a warrior between two armies stopped fighting and became a student: I am your disciple, teach me. Catholics remember a quieter version of that moment. After watching Jesus pray, one of his disciples asked: "Lord, teach us to pray, as John also taught his disciples." Jesus answered with the Our Father.
neighbors.difference: Arjuna asks what to do with a terrible duty, and hears a teaching about the self that cannot be killed. The disciples ask how to pray, and Jesus gives them words to say together to God as Father.
neighbors.shared: a real teaching often starts with someone brave enough to ask.

neighbors.heading: peace has to be made
neighbors.text: Today Bhishma, lying on his bed of arrows, asked Duryodhana to let the war end with him, and was turned down. Philosophers have wrestled with refusals like that. Immanuel Kant wrote that peace between neighbors isn't the natural state of things; it has to be established, on purpose, by people who choose it and build it.
neighbors.difference: Bhishma's plea is a dying elder's word to his own family, inside dharma. Kant was thinking of nations, and of laws and agreements strong enough to hold even when people don't feel peaceful.
neighbors.shared: peace doesn't just happen; someone has to ask for it.
neighbors.sources: Immanuel Kant, Perpetual Peace (1795), second section (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: seek peace, and pursue it
neighbors.text: Today a dying man used his last strength to plead for peace between cousins. Jews pray a psalm that asks the same: "seek peace, and pursue it." Hillel taught: be among the disciples of Aaron, loving peace and pursuing peace, loving people and bringing them near to the Torah. Pursue means you don't wait for it. You go after it.
neighbors.difference: Bhishma's plea comes at the end, from a bed of arrows, after a war he fought in. Hillel asks people to chase peace every day, in small quarrels, long before anyone picks up a weapon.
neighbors.shared: it's never wrong to ask for peace, even late.
neighbors.sources: Psalm 34:15 (JPS 1917; 34:14 in many English Bibles) · Pirkei Avot 1:12 (paraphrase)

items.lessonTitle: Karna: the wheel stuck, the death

neighbors.heading: the midwives' answer
neighbors.text: Today Krishna told of a man who spoke the truth to robbers, and travelers died for it. Christians wrestle with this knot too. In Exodus, the Hebrew midwives disobey Pharaoh's order to kill baby boys and give him an evasive answer, and the text says: "Therefore God dealt well with the midwives." Augustine still taught that every lie is wrong.
neighbors.difference: Krishna weighs truth by what it does to living beings. Many Christians, following Augustine, hold that a lie is never right, even to save a life, and praise the midwives' mercy rather than their words; others read it differently.
neighbors.shared: truth and kindness are meant to walk together.

neighbors.heading: not a liar who makes peace
neighbors.text: Today Krishna told Arjuna that truth is weighed by what it does to living beings. Muslims hold truthfulness close, and a hadith names a narrow exception that sounds like this: the one who makes peace between people, passing on good words to bring them together, is not a liar.
neighbors.difference: Krishna's teaching is broad: weigh each truth by its effect. In Islam truthfulness is the rule, scholars allow only a few named exceptions such as reconciling people, and many prefer gentle, indirect words to an outright falsehood.
neighbors.shared: honest words are meant to bring people back together.

items.lessonTitle: Shalya: Duryodhana in the lake, the mace fight

neighbors.heading: this day, in paradise
neighbors.text: Today Kripa told a beaten king it wasn't too late for peace, and Duryodhana said no. Catholics treasure a moment when someone said yes at the very end. On the cross, a thief asked Jesus to remember him, and Jesus answered: "Amen I say to thee, this day thou shalt be with me in paradise."
neighbors.difference: Kripa offers peace between cousins and a share of a kingdom; Duryodhana refuses out of loyalty to friends who died. The thief asks for God's mercy, which Catholics teach stays open until the last breath.
neighbors.shared: it isn't too late while you can still ask.

neighbors.heading: the shining bronze
neighbors.text: Today an old teacher told Duryodhana there was still time, and he turned it down. Sikhs tell of a man who turned. Sajjan, tradition says, welcomed travelers by day and robbed them by night. Guru Nanak sang to him of bronze that shines but shows black when it's rubbed. Sajjan heard himself in it, and changed his life.
neighbors.difference: Duryodhana hears plain counsel and refuses, out of loyalty to the dead. In the Sikh story, change comes through the Guru's song, heard by a man in his own house, and an honest life follows.
neighbors.shared: a true word, heard at the right moment, can turn a life.
neighbors.sources: Janamsakhi tradition of Sajjan (paraphrase) · Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 729, Suhi, Guru Nanak (paraphrase)

items.lessonTitle: Shalya: Duryodhana in the lake, the mace fight

neighbors.heading: my creatures are drowning
neighbors.text: Today the war was won, and Yudhishthira told Bhima to take his foot off a fallen king. Jewish tradition holds the same line. Proverbs says: "Rejoice not when thine enemy falleth." And the rabbis tell that when the angels wanted to sing as the Egyptians drowned, God stopped them: my creatures are drowning, and you sing?
neighbors.difference: In the epic the winners stand downcast while flowers fall on the loser, and the argument stays open. In the rabbis' story God grieves for the enemy, and Israel's rescue is still celebrated.
neighbors.shared: even a just win leaves room for grief.

neighbors.heading: victory breeds hatred
neighbors.text: Today the winners of a war couldn't agree how to treat the loser, and flowers fell on the fallen king. Buddhists keep a verse for a field like that: "Victory breeds hatred, for the conquered is unhappy. He who has given up both victory and defeat, he, the contented, is happy."
neighbors.difference: The epic weighs the victory: what was done, why, and what it cost, and lets every side speak. The Dhammapada steps outside the contest, pointing to a peace beyond winning and losing.
neighbors.shared: the one on the ground is still someone's family.

neighbors.heading: a stranger, a traveler
neighbors.text: Today Vidura told a grieving king about a man in a well, still reaching for the honey. Muslims keep a short saying of the Prophet with the same clear eyes: be in this world as if you were a stranger, or a traveler passing through. And the Qur'an calls the life of this world a passing comfort that can deceive.
neighbors.difference: Vidura's story describes everyone, gently, to comfort a king in grief. The hadith is advice for living: hold the world lightly, because the traveler is on the way home to God.
neighbors.shared: time is short, so hold the sweet things gently.

neighbors.heading: the honey in the well
neighbors.text: Today a man hung in a well between a serpent and an elephant, licking honey. Leo Tolstoy found the same parable, which he called an Eastern fable, in his own crisis. In A Confession he pictured himself on that branch, and wrote that the honey no longer tasted sweet. It sent him searching for what makes a life mean something.
neighbors.difference: Vidura uses the story to console a king: everyone hangs there, so don't be swept away by grief. Tolstoy used it as a mirror for his own despair, and spent years looking for an answer.
neighbors.shared: honest about time, and still able to taste the honey.

items.lessonTitle: Shanti and Anushasana: Bhishma's teachings from the bed of arrows (selections)

neighbors.heading: water for every soldier
neighbors.text: Today a pigeon made a fire for the hunter who had caged his mate. Sikhs tell of Bhai Kanhaiya, who carried water across a battlefield to wounded soldiers of both sides. Accused of helping the enemy, he said he saw no enemy, only the Guru's light in every face. Guru Gobind Singh, tradition says, gave him ointment for their wounds too.
neighbors.difference: The pigeon's story shows hospitality to a guest at your door, told to the extreme. Bhai Kanhaiya's service is on a battlefield, healing, because the Guru taught him to see God in everyone.
neighbors.shared: a guest is a guest, even the one who hurt you.

neighbors.heading: if thine enemy hunger
neighbors.text: Today a pigeon warmed and fed the hunter who had caught his mate, and the hunter laid down his nets. Christians hear Paul in it: "if thine enemy hunger, feed him; if he thirst, give him drink: for in so doing thou shalt heap coals of fire on his head." Then: "overcome evil with good."
neighbors.difference: The pigeon's gift is the duty to a guest, told to the extreme, and the hunter is transformed. Paul's teaching rests on Jesus's command to love enemies, and leaves judgment to God.
neighbors.shared: kindness to the one who hurt you can change them.

neighbors.heading: the widow's two coins
neighbors.text: Today a mongoose said a royal sacrifice wasn't worth a poor family's handful of barley. Jesus said something close at the Temple. Watching rich people put in large sums, he saw a poor widow drop in two small coins, and said: "Amen I say to you, this poor widow hath cast in more than all they who have cast into the treasury."
neighbors.difference: In the epic, the poor family gives every portion to a guest who turns out to be Dharma, and they are carried to heaven. Jesus simply notices the widow; the Gospel tells no reward, only his words.
neighbors.shared: the size of a gift isn't measured in coins.

neighbors.heading: a little, worth a thousand
neighbors.text: Today a half-golden mongoose rolled in a king's grand sacrifice and found it lighter than a poor family's barley. Buddhists keep a verse spoken before the Buddha with the same surprise: some give from the little they have, and a gift given from little is worth a thousand times as much.
neighbors.difference: In the epic, Dharma himself comes as the guest and rewards the family with heaven. Buddhist teaching looks to the giver's mind: a gift from little, given gladly, shapes the giver, whatever comes of it.
neighbors.shared: a small gift given fully can outweigh a great show.

items.lessonTitle: the Pandavas' last journey, Yudhishthira's dog, heaven

neighbors.heading: can they suffer?
neighbors.text: Today Indra told Yudhishthira the dog didn't count, and he would rather give up heaven than leave it. The philosopher Jeremy Bentham asked who counts, too. Of animals he wrote: "The question is not, Can they reason? nor, Can they talk? but, Can they suffer?" A creature that can't repay you is still owed care.
neighbors.difference: Yudhishthira's answer is about faithfulness: he won't abandon one who is devoted to him and has nowhere else to go. Bentham's is about suffering: any creature that can feel pain counts, devoted or not.
neighbors.shared: the smallest one on the road still counts.
neighbors.sources: Jeremy Bentham, An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation (1789), chapter 17, footnote

neighbors.heading: the shepherd and the young goat
neighbors.text: Today a king refused heaven rather than leave behind a dog. Jews tell of care for animals too. Proverbs says: "A righteous man regardeth the life of his beast." And a midrash says Moses chased a runaway young goat to a spring, carried it back on his shoulders, and God said: this is who will shepherd my people.
neighbors.difference: Yudhishthira's test is about loyalty: refusing to turn away a creature devoted to him. In the midrash, Moses's care for a young goat shows he is fit to lead people, and Jewish law forbids causing animals needless pain.
neighbors.shared: the way you treat the smallest shows who you are.

neighbors.heading: carried away by night
neighbors.text: Today Vasudeva carried his newborn son through the dark, away from a king who killed children, and left him with another family. Christians tell of a night like it. When King Herod hunted for the child Jesus, an angel warned Joseph in a dream. Matthew says: "he took the young child and his mother by night, and departed into Egypt."
neighbors.difference: Vasudeva gives his son to another mother and walks back alone into chains. Joseph keeps the family together and takes them all into exile. In the Bhagavata the child is the Lord himself; Christians call Jesus the Son of God, made man.
neighbors.shared: a parent's arms can carry a child through the darkest night.

neighbors.heading: a mother lets go
neighbors.text: Today Vasudeva left his newborn son with another family, so a cruel king could not find him. The Qur'an tells of a mother who faced the same fear. God inspired the mother of Moses: nurse him, and when you fear for him, set him in the river, and don't fear or grieve; he will come back to you. (paraphrase) And he did, to nurse at her breast again.
neighbors.difference: In the Bhagavata, the baby is the Lord himself, and his father acts on the Lord's own word. In the Qur'an, Moses is a human prophet, and his mother trusts a promise from God that her son will be returned.
neighbors.shared: letting go of a child to keep them safe is love too.

neighbors.heading: kept in her heart
neighbors.text: Today Yashoda looked into her little boy's mouth and saw everything there is, then went back to being his mother. Catholics treasure a mother like that. When shepherds came to the manger with news of angels, Luke says: "But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart." The Church calls her the Mother of God, still feeding and holding a baby.
neighbors.difference: In the Bhagavata, Krishna's own power veils the vision as a mother's love, and Yashoda forgets. Mary is honored for remembering and pondering. Catholics honor Mary above all the saints, and worship God alone.
neighbors.shared: the child in your arms may hold more than you can see.
neighbors.sources: Luke 2:19 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 495 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the whole world inside
neighbors.text: Today Yashoda looked into her son's mouth and found the whole universe, with her own village and herself inside it. The Guru Granth Sahib keeps a line from the saint Pipa that looks inward the same way: whatever is in the universe is found in the body, and whoever searches will find it. (paraphrase) Sikhs sing it as gurbani, the Guru's word.
neighbors.difference: In the Bhagavata the universe appears inside one child, Krishna, as a sign of who he is. Pipa's line looks inside every body, and for Sikhs the One found there is formless, never born in a body.
neighbors.shared: look closely: there's more inside than anyone can see.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Raag Dhanasari, hymn of Bhagat Pipa (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: "how long?"
neighbors.text: Today the gopis stood in the road and cried out at being left, and the Bhagavata kept every raw word. The Psalms keep words like that too. One psalm begins: "How long, O LORD, wilt Thou forget me for ever? How long wilt Thou hide Thy face from me?" Jewish prayer makes room for that cry, spoken straight to God.
neighbors.difference: The gopis grieve a beloved who has left for another city, promising to come back. The psalmist speaks to a God who is never seen in any form, and before the psalm ends, it turns to trust in God's mercy.
neighbors.shared: love is allowed to say out loud how much it hurts.
neighbors.sources: Psalm 13:2 (JPS 1917; Psalm 13:1 in many Bibles) · Psalm 13:6 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: parted from what's dear
neighbors.text: Today the gopis watched Krishna's chariot go until even its dust was gone. The Buddha named that ache plainly. In his first teaching after his awakening, he counted it among the forms of suffering: being parted from what we love. (paraphrase) He didn't call the grief foolish. He called it true, and something to understand.
neighbors.difference: For the gopis, the ache is love for Krishna, and the Bhagavata treasures it as devotion. The Buddha's way looks at the ache itself, sees that everything that comes together changes, and seeks freedom from clinging.
neighbors.shared: missing someone is one of the oldest things people share.

neighbors.heading: better than sleep
neighbors.text: Today Andal's girls went door to door before dawn, waking the friends who overslept. Muslims hear a dawn call like that. In the Sunni tradition, the call to the morning prayer adds a line the other calls don't have: prayer is better than sleep. (paraphrase) And the Qur'an says the recitation at dawn is witnessed. (paraphrase)
neighbors.difference: Andal's girls go together to Krishna's door, keeping a month-long vow of love for him. The dawn prayer is one of the five daily prayers, offered every day of the year to God alone.
neighbors.shared: a friend who wakes you for what matters is a gift.
neighbors.sources: Sunan Abu Dawud, Book of Prayer, on the call to prayer (paraphrase) · Qur'an 17:78 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a dawn in me
neighbors.text: Today Andal's girls rose before dawn and wouldn't go without the friend still asleep. Henry David Thoreau, living by Walden Pond, made the early hour a practice of his own. He wrote: "Morning is when I am awake and there is a dawn in me." For him, the sunrise mattered less than being truly awake inside it.
neighbors.difference: Andal's dawn is a vow to seek Krishna, kept with friends. Thoreau's mornings were mostly spent alone in the woods, and they were about waking up to life itself rather than going to a god's door.
neighbors.shared: every morning is a chance to wake up a little more.
neighbors.sources: Henry David Thoreau, Walden (1854), "Where I Lived, and What I Lived For"

neighbors.heading: the boy with the bowl of milk
neighbors.text: Today the boy Namdev set milk before Vitthal and waited for him to drink. Sikhs know this story in Namdev's own words, because his songs are in the Guru Granth Sahib. In one hymn he tells of carrying a cup of milk to God, begging him to drink, and God drinking it. (paraphrase) Sikhs sing it as gurbani, the Guru's word.
neighbors.difference: In the Varkari telling, Vitthal reaches out of his image at Pandharpur. Sikhs don't worship images; they honor Namdev's words as part of the Guru, and understand God as formless, met in love and in the Name.
neighbors.shared: simple love, offered with your whole heart, is never too small.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Raag Bhairo, hymn of Bhagat Namdev (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: like a little child
neighbors.text: Today Namdev took God at his word, the way a child takes anyone at their word, and the story rewards him. Christians remember Jesus saying something close. When his disciples turned children away, he stopped them: "Whosoever shall not receive the kingdom of God as a little child, he shall not enter therein." Then he took them up in his arms and blessed them.
neighbors.difference: In Namdev's story, God comes out of the image to drink a child's offering. In the Gospel, Jesus, whom Christians call the Son of God, holds up children's trust as the way to receive God's kingdom.
neighbors.shared: trust like a child's is welcome, never foolish.

items.lessonTitle: Kabir (the dohas, one a day for a week)

neighbors.heading: a lamp unto yourself
neighbors.text: Today Kabir's deer hunted the whole forest for a scent it carried all along. Buddhists remember the Buddha turning his followers back toward home, too. Near the end of his life he told them: "Be ye lamps unto yourselves. Be ye a refuge to yourselves." The path he taught is walked from the inside, not found somewhere far off.
neighbors.difference: For Kabir, what's hidden in every heart is Ram, God. The Buddha points to no God within and teaches that there's no lasting self to find; the refuge is his teaching, the Dhamma, practiced by each person.
neighbors.shared: what you're looking for may be closer than you think.

neighbors.heading: within, and I abroad
neighbors.text: Today Kabir's deer searched the forest for the musk it carried all along. A Catholic saint wrote that same ache into a prayer. Augustine, looking back on his restless youth, told God: "Thou wert within, and I abroad, and there I searched for Thee." The one he hunted for out in the world had been with him the whole time.
neighbors.difference: Kabir says Ram is in every heart. Augustine finds God within, yet never as himself: for Catholics, God is the Maker, closer than a person's own heart and still other than them.
neighbors.shared: sometimes the search ends by turning around.

items.lessonTitle: Tulsidas (the Ramcharitmanas opening and the Hanuman Chalisa, verse by verse)

neighbors.heading: keep good company
neighbors.text: Today Tulsidas called the company of good people a pilgrimage that walks, one that comes down your street. The Roman philosopher Seneca gave a friend the same advice in a letter: "Associate with those who will make a better man of you. Welcome those whom you yourself can improve." He added that it works both ways: people learn while they teach.
neighbors.difference: For Tulsidas, the saints' company carries you toward Rama, and keeping it is part of devotion. Seneca was a Stoic: for him, good company trains character and reason, and devotion isn't the point.
neighbors.shared: the people around you can carry you somewhere good.
neighbors.sources: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 7 (Gummere)

neighbors.heading: the dust of their feet
neighbors.text: Today Tulsidas bowed to the company of good people, a pilgrimage that walks. Jewish teachers prized that company too. In the Mishnah, an early sage taught: let your house be a meeting place for the wise, sit in the dust of their feet, and drink in their words with thirst. (paraphrase)
neighbors.difference: Tulsidas honors the saints as people whose company brings you to Rama. In Jewish tradition, the wise are honored as teachers of Torah, and sitting with them means learning God's teaching together.
neighbors.shared: the wise are worth sitting close to, even on the floor.

neighbors.heading: lowliness of mind
neighbors.text: Today Chaitanya's verse asked for a heart humbler than a blade of grass, giving honor to others and asking none. Paul wrote something close to an early church: "Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory; but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves." Then he pointed to Jesus, who, Christians believe, took the form of a servant.
neighbors.difference: Chaitanya's humility clears the way to sing Hari's name without end. Paul roots humility in Jesus, whom Christians call God's Son: following his lowliness is the reason to be lowly.
neighbors.shared: honor others first, and there's room for everyone to sing.

neighbors.heading: they walk the earth gently
neighbors.text: Today Chaitanya's verse asked for humility like grass and patience like a tree. The Qur'an paints God's servants the same way: "The (faithful) slaves of the Beneficent are they who walk upon the earth modestly, and when the foolish ones address them answer: Peace." Humble steps, and a patient answer to a rude word.
neighbors.difference: Chaitanya's verse makes humility the ground for singing Hari's names. In the Qur'an, humility belongs to being a servant of the One God, who has no partner and no form, called on by his own beautiful names.
neighbors.shared: a gentle step and a calm answer can change a room.

neighbors.heading: you did it to me
neighbors.text: Today Vivekananda turned the thank-you around: serve the person in front of you the way you'd worship God. Catholics hear Jesus say something close. In his picture of the last judgment, he speaks of the hungry, the stranger and the prisoner: "as long as you did it to one of these my least brethren, you did it to me."
neighbors.difference: Vivekananda's reason is Vedanta: the divine is present in every person. Catholics believe Christ is met in the poor because he made himself one with them, while each person stays a person, made by God.
neighbors.shared: the one you help is a gift, not a burden.

neighbors.heading: seva
neighbors.text: Today Vivekananda said helping isn't a favor we do the world; it's a chance we're given. Sikhs call selfless service seva. Guru Nanak sings that whoever serves in this world is given a seat of honor in God's court. (paraphrase) In the langar, the shared kitchen, anyone can serve, and anyone can eat.
neighbors.difference: Vivekananda serves people as the divine itself, as his Vedanta teaches. Sikhs serve because God's light is in everyone, and seva wears away the ego, while God remains the formless One beyond any one person.
neighbors.shared: serving someone can be the best part of your own day.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Sri Raag, Guru Nanak (paraphrase) · Sohila, Guru Nanak, on the light in all (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: let be, and know
neighbors.text: Today Vivekananda pictured the mind as a lake: when the waves settle, you can see the bottom. A psalm asks for stillness too. In a song of earthquakes, roaring seas and nations in uproar, God speaks: "Let be, and know that I am God." Through all that noise, the call is to stop, and to know.
neighbors.difference: For Vivekananda, the still water shows your own true self lying at the bottom. The psalm's stillness looks up and out, toward the God of Israel, the Maker of all, who is never the same as the self.
neighbors.shared: some things only come clear when we stop stirring.

neighbors.heading: a deep, still lake
neighbors.text: Today Vivekananda said you can't see the bottom of a lake while the wind is blowing. The Dhammapada reaches for a lake as well: "Wise people, after they have listened to the laws, become serene, like a deep, smooth, and still lake." Buddhists call that settling samatha, calm, and pair it with clear seeing.
neighbors.difference: Vivekananda says the still water reveals the true self that was there all along. The Buddha taught that clear seeing finds no lasting self at all, and that seeing this is what frees.
neighbors.shared: a settled mind sees more clearly.

neighbors.heading: neither grieve nor exult
neighbors.text: Today the Gita described a person of steady wisdom: sorrow doesn't shake them, pleasure doesn't grab them. The Qur'an teaches a steadiness like it, because everything that happens is already known to God: "That ye grieve not for the sake of that which hath escaped you, nor yet exult because of that which hath been given."
neighbors.difference: The Gita roots steadiness in being content in the Self. The Qur'an roots it in trust that everything is in God's hands and known to him; the steady heart rests in God.
neighbors.shared: a steady heart doesn't swing with every gain and loss.

neighbors.heading: the promontory
neighbors.text: Today the Gita pictured the steady one as the sea, full and unmoved while rivers pour in. The Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius, writing notes to himself, chose a rock instead: "Be like the promontory against which the waves continually break, but it stands firm and tames the fury of the water around it."
neighbors.difference: The Gita's steady person rests in the Self, and for Gandhi offers every act to God. Marcus was a Stoic: his steadiness comes from reason, judging events calmly and doing his duty.
neighbors.shared: the waves keep coming, and you can still stand.

neighbors.heading: the city without sorrow
neighbors.text: Today Tagore prayed for a place where the mind is without fear. The Guru Granth Sahib keeps a song like it by the saint Ravidas. He sings of a city called Begampura, the place without sorrow: no anxiety, no tax, no fear, and no one counted second or third. (paraphrase) Sikhs sing it as part of the Guru's word.
neighbors.difference: Tagore asks God to wake his country into freedom. Ravidas sings of the home he has found in God, and for Sikhs his song stands in the Guru Granth Sahib beside the Gurus' own hymns.
neighbors.shared: everyone deserves a place to live without fear.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Raag Gauri, Bhagat Ravidas, Begampura (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: none shall make them afraid
neighbors.text: Today Tagore prayed: "Where the mind is without fear and the head is held high." A Hebrew prophet, read by Christians in their Old Testament, pictured a world like that: "they shall sit every man under his vine and under his fig tree; and none shall make them afraid." No more war, no more fear, each family at peace.
neighbors.difference: Tagore asks God to wake a people now, into freedom of mind. Micah's picture is God's promise for the last days; Christians hope to see it fulfilled in God's kingdom, which they believe Jesus began.
neighbors.shared: a world without fear is worth praying for.

neighbors.heading: not without sharing
neighbors.text: Today the Gita sorted gifts and honored the one given simply because it's right, expecting nothing back. The Buddha praised giving too. In one teaching he says that if people knew, as he knows, the fruit of giving and sharing, they wouldn't eat without sharing, not even their last mouthful. (paraphrase) Buddhists call giving dana.
neighbors.difference: The Gita's best gift is given because giving is right, with no thought of return. The Buddha speaks openly of giving's good fruit, and teaches giving as a way to loosen clinging.
neighbors.shared: giving is good for the hand that opens.

neighbors.heading: they cannot repay you
neighbors.text: Today the Gita praised the gift given to someone who can do nothing in return. Jesus said something close at a dinner: "But when thou makest a feast, call the poor, the maimed, the lame, and the blind; And thou shalt be blessed, because they have not wherewith to make thee recompense."
neighbors.difference: The Gita weighs a gift by its reason, timing and person. Jesus adds a promise: the guest can't repay, but God will, at the resurrection of the just. For Catholics, giving to the poor is also loving Christ in them.
neighbors.shared: the best gifts don't wait for a thank-you.

neighbors.heading: a portion of thyself
neighbors.text: Today Krishna said a leaf, a flower, a fruit or a little water is enough, if it's given with love. Ralph Waldo Emerson, writing about gifts between people, said something close: "The only gift is a portion of thyself." So, he wrote, let the farmer give his corn, the painter his picture, the girl a handkerchief she sewed herself.
neighbors.difference: Krishna's verse is about offering to God, who accepts the love behind the leaf. Emerson writes about gifts between people, and his point is honesty: give what is truly yours, not a costly stand-in.
neighbors.shared: a small gift with your heart in it is plenty.
neighbors.sources: Ralph Waldo Emerson, "Gifts," Essays: Second Series (1844)

neighbors.heading: much or little
neighbors.text: Today Krishna said a leaf, a flower, a fruit or water is enough, if it's offered with love. The Mishnah says something close about the old Temple offerings. Some brought an ox, some a bird, some a little flour, and the sages taught: whether one gives much or little, what matters is that the heart is turned to Heaven. (paraphrase)
neighbors.difference: Krishna speaks in his own voice and accepts the gift himself. The Mishnah speaks of offerings to the unseen God of Israel, and since the Temple fell, Jewish tradition has set prayer in the offerings' place.
neighbors.shared: it's the heart, not the size, that's being given.

neighbors.heading: two small coins
neighbors.text: Today Krishna ate a poor friend's handful of rice with delight, as if it were a feast. Christians remember Jesus watching people give at the Temple. A poor widow dropped in two small coins, and he said: "this poor widow hath cast more in, than all they which have cast into the treasury." The others gave from plenty; she gave all she had.
neighbors.difference: Sudama's gift goes into Krishna's own hands, and his life changes overnight. The widow's coins go to the Temple treasury, and the Gospel tells of no reward: Jesus simply sees her, and counts her gift the greatest.
neighbors.shared: a small gift given from the heart is seen.

neighbors.heading: even a sheep's foot
neighbors.text: Today Krishna welcomed a poor friend, washed his feet, and ate his humble rice with joy. Muslims remember the Prophet Muhammad's way with small gifts. He said that if he were invited to a meal of a sheep's foot, he would go, and if he were given a sheep's foot as a gift, he would accept it. (paraphrase) No gift too humble, no host too poor.
neighbors.difference: In the Bhagavata, Krishna is the Lord himself, receiving a devotee's offering. Muslims honor Muhammad as a human being and God's messenger, never divine; his example shows how people should welcome each other's gifts.
neighbors.shared: a friend's small gift deserves a big welcome.

neighbors.heading: praise the name
neighbors.text: Today Tulsidas said to set Rama's name on your tongue like a lamp on a doorstep, lighting inside and out. Catholics pray the psalm: "From the rising of the sun unto the going down of the same, the name of the Lord is worthy of praise." The Church teaches that calling on the holy name of Jesus is the simplest way to pray always. (paraphrase)
neighbors.difference: Tulsidas praises Rama's name, and even says the name has helped more people than Rama did in person. Catholics call on the name of Jesus, whom they believe is God made man, and the name leads them to him.
neighbors.shared: a name you love can light up a whole day.
neighbors.sources: Psalm 112:3 (Douay-Rheims; Psalm 113:3 in many Bibles) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 2666-2668 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: remember, remember
neighbors.text: Today the kirtan sang only the name, over and over, a lamp on the tongue. Sikhs call this naam simran, remembering God's name, alone or sung together in the gurdwara. Guru Arjan's Sukhmani opens: remember, remember, keep remembering, and find peace. (paraphrase) Waheguru, wonderful Lord, is a name Sikhs repeat in simran.
neighbors.difference: Tulsidas sings the name of Rama, God come to earth as a prince. For Sikhs, God is never born in a body; the Name points to the formless One, and the Guru's word teaches how to remember.
neighbors.shared: remembering, again and again, is how love stays awake.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan, opening lines (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: if I am not for myself
neighbors.text: Today Shankara's teacher said fear not, there's a road, and then: no one can walk it for you. A Jewish sage put it in three short questions. Hillel used to say: if I am not for myself, who will be for me? And if I am only for myself, what am I? And if not now, when? (paraphrase)
neighbors.difference: Shankara's student must come to know the Self for himself; no one can do it in his place. Hillel's questions sit inside a life of Torah and community: your effort is yours, and you're never only for yourself.
neighbors.shared: a teacher can show the road; your own feet walk it.

neighbors.heading: you must make the effort
neighbors.text: Today the Vivekachudamani said hunger goes away only when you eat; no one can eat your dinner for you. The Buddha said it about his own teaching: "You yourself must make an effort. The Tathagatas (Buddhas) are only preachers." A teacher points the way; walking it is up to each person.
neighbors.difference: Shankara's road ends in knowing the Self as Brahman. The Buddha's road ends in nirvana, and he teaches no lasting Self to know; the freedom is in seeing that clearly.
neighbors.shared: nobody can walk your road for you, but you're never sent alone.

neighbors.heading: the breath of life
neighbors.text: Today an Upanishad told how every power in the body rises and settles with the breath. The Qur'an tells where the first breath came from. God shaped the human being from clay, and said to the angels: "when I have made him and have breathed into him of My Spirit, do ye fall down, prostrating yourselves unto him."
neighbors.difference: In the Upanishad, prana is the chief of the body's powers, the one they all depend on. In the Qur'an, life is God's gift breathed in; the spirit comes from God, but the human being is created, never divine.
neighbors.shared: every breath is a gift worth noticing.

neighbors.heading: the stream of my breathing
neighbors.text: Today an Upanishad told how speech, mind, eye and ear all rise and settle with the breath. The psychologist William James noticed something like it in himself. Looking hard at his own stream of thinking, he wrote that much of what he felt as his inner self turned out to be, mostly, the stream of his breathing. (paraphrase)
neighbors.difference: The Upanishad calls prana a living power that holds the body together, and the story ends in praise. James was describing what he noticed when he paid close attention, and made no claim about a power beyond it.
neighbors.shared: your breath has been with you through every moment.

neighbors.heading: the ambrosial hours
neighbors.text: Today the Laws of Manu hung the Gayatri on the two hinges of the day, dawn and dusk. Sikhs keep the edges of the day too. Guru Nanak's Japji says: in the amrit vela, the ambrosial hours before dawn, speak the True Name and reflect on God's greatness. (paraphrase) Evening has its prayer, Rehras, and bedtime has Sohila.
neighbors.difference: Manu ties the Gayatri, a Vedic verse, to the rising and setting sun. Sikhs sing the Gurus' own hymns at these times, to remember the One God, who is meant to be remembered in every hour.
neighbors.shared: the edges of the day are good places to remember.

neighbors.heading: evening, and morning
neighbors.text: Today the Laws of Manu set the Gayatri at dawn and dusk, the joints of the day. A psalm Christians pray keeps that rhythm: "Evening, and morning, and at noon, will I pray, and cry aloud: and he shall hear my voice." The old Book of Common Prayer sets Morning Prayer and Evening Prayer for every day of the year.
neighbors.difference: Manu's verse is the Gayatri, an old Vedic prayer for a lit mind. The psalmist cries to the God of Israel, and Christians pray those psalms through Jesus, whom they call Lord.
neighbors.shared: a day can be held by prayer at both ends.
neighbors.sources: Psalm 55:17 (KJV) · Book of Common Prayer 1662, Morning and Evening Prayer

neighbors.heading: drop by drop
neighbors.text: Today Patanjali said practice takes root when it's kept a long time, without a break, and with care. The Dhammapada pictures that patience: "Even by the falling of water-drops a water-pot is filled; the wise man becomes full of good, even if he gather it little by little." No single drop fills the pot. Every one counts.
neighbors.difference: Patanjali ties steady practice to repeating Om and turning toward Ishvara, the Lord. The Buddha's path of good asks for no God; its drops are kind acts, honest living and meditation, gathered on the way to freedom.
neighbors.shared: small, faithful steps add up to more than you'd guess.

neighbors.heading: always to pray, and not to faint
neighbors.text: Today Patanjali said practice takes root when it's kept a long time, without a break, and with care. Jesus told a parable for the same reason. Luke says: "he spoke also a parable to them, that we ought always to pray, and not to faint." In it, a widow keeps coming to a judge until he finally hears her.
neighbors.difference: Patanjali's steady japa turns the mind toward Ishvara through the sound Om. The widow's persistence is a picture of trust in God the Father, who, Jesus says, hears those who cry to him day and night.
neighbors.shared: keep coming back; coming back is the practice.

neighbors.heading: bringing it back
neighbors.text: Today Krishna pictured a steady mind as a lamp that doesn't flicker, and said: wherever the mind wanders, draw it back. The psychologist William James prized that same move: "the faculty of voluntarily bringing back a wandering attention, over and over again, is the very root of judgment, character, and will." Wandering is normal. Coming back is the skill.
neighbors.difference: Krishna's steady lamp rests in the Self, and the practice leads toward the divine. James studied attention as a psychologist, a habit of mind that shapes character, and made no claim about where it leads beyond that.
neighbors.shared: every time you bring your mind back, you're practicing.
neighbors.sources: William James, The Principles of Psychology (1890), ch. XI

neighbors.heading: the lamp of the LORD
neighbors.text: Today Krishna pictured a gathered mind as a lamp in a windless place: still burning, no flicker. The Book of Proverbs also calls the inner person a lamp: "The spirit of man is the lamp of the LORD, searching all the inward parts." A steady light that lets a person see within.
neighbors.difference: For Krishna, the steady lamp is a mind gathered in the Self. In Proverbs, the human spirit is a lamp that belongs to God: a light God gives and uses, never God itself.
neighbors.shared: there's a light inside you worth keeping steady.

neighbors.heading: face to face
neighbors.text: Today darshan meant seeing God and being seen. Paul wrote of that same hope: "For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face: now I know in part; but then shall I know even as also I am known." To see God, and to be fully known by him, is the hope he holds out.
neighbors.difference: In darshan, a devotee beholds God in the temple image today. Paul says that in this life we see dimly, and Christians hope to see God face to face in the life to come.
neighbors.shared: being truly seen is one of the deepest kinds of love.

neighbors.heading: as though you see Him
neighbors.text: Today darshan meant seeing God, and being seen. Muslims treasure a hadith in which the angel Gabriel asks the Prophet Muhammad what excellence in faith, ihsan, is. The answer: to worship God as though you see Him, and though you don't see Him, He sees you. (paraphrase)
neighbors.difference: Darshan happens before a sacred image, with the eyes. Islam makes no images of God, who has no likeness; the seeing in ihsan is of the heart, and what's certain is that God sees you.
neighbors.shared: you are seen, even when no one else is looking.
neighbors.sources: Sahih Muslim, Book of Faith, the hadith of Gabriel (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: fear not
neighbors.text: Today the raised palm of abhaya mudra said: do not be afraid. Catholics hear those words in Scripture. When the angel greeted Mary and she was troubled, he told her:"Fear not, Mary, for thou hast found grace with God." And through the prophet Isaiah, God says: "Fear not, for I am with thee."
neighbors.difference: In the abhaya gesture, the god's own hand holds out fearlessness, the quality the Gita names first. In Scripture, "fear not" rests on God's presence: the trust that God is with us.
neighbors.shared: someone is telling you: you don't have to be afraid.

neighbors.heading: fearless, without hate
neighbors.text: Today the raised palm said: do not be afraid, and the Gita named fearlessness first. Sikhs name it at the very start of their scripture. The Mool Mantar, the opening of the Guru Granth Sahib, calls God nirbhau, without fear, and nirvair, without hate. Guru Tegh Bahadur praised the one who frightens no one and fears no one. (paraphrase)
neighbors.difference: On the temple image, a god's hand holds out fearlessness to the devotee. Sikhs keep no image of God; fearlessness is God's own nature, and living by the Guru's word helps a person grow fearless too.
neighbors.shared: fear loosens its grip when you know you're held.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Mool Mantar (paraphrase) · Salok of Guru Tegh Bahadur (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the shepherd and the young goat
neighbors.text: Today Yudhishthira refused heaven rather than leave behind the dog that walked with him. Jewish teachers tell of Moses as a shepherd. A young goat ran off, and he followed it to a pool. He said: I didn't know you were thirsty, you must be tired, and carried it back on his shoulder. God said: then you will shepherd my people. (paraphrase)
neighbors.difference: Yudhishthira's dog turns out to be Dharma himself, testing him. Moses' goat is only a goat, and that's the point: in the midrash, his care for one small animal shows God he can lead a people.
neighbors.shared: how we treat the smallest creature shows who we are.

neighbors.heading: a boundless heart
neighbors.text: Today Yudhishthira would not leave a frightened dog with no other refuge, not even for heaven. The Buddha taught a love that leaves no one out. In the Metta Sutta: just as a mother would guard her only child with her own life, so let a person grow a boundless heart toward every living being. (paraphrase)
neighbors.difference: Yudhishthira's loyalty is dharma, a duty kept to one devoted creature, and the gods honor him for it. Metta is loving-kindness grown toward all beings at once, as part of the path the Buddha taught.
neighbors.shared: no creature is too small to be cared for.

neighbors.heading: a stranger, a traveler
neighbors.text: Today the Gita pictured a lotus leaf that sits in the pond all day and never gets wet. Muslims remember a teaching like it. The Prophet Muhammad took a young companion by the shoulder and said: be in this world as if you were a stranger, or someone passing through on a journey. (paraphrase) Live in the world fully, without letting it hold you.
neighbors.difference: The Gita's leaf stays dry by placing every act in Brahman and letting go of clinging. The hadith looks toward the life to come: a traveler doesn't settle, because home is with God after this world.
neighbors.shared: you can be fully here without being held by it.
neighbors.sources: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Softening of the Hearts, hadith of Ibn Umar (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: given back, not lost
neighbors.text: Today the Gita pictured a lotus leaf that lives in the water and comes out dry. The Stoic teacher Epictetus taught a similar ease with what we hold. Never say of anything, I have lost it, he said; say, I have given it back. (paraphrase) A field, a home, even the people we love: held with care, never owned.
neighbors.difference: The Gita's leaf stays dry by offering every act to Brahman. Epictetus grounds his calm in reason: some things are up to us and some aren't, and freedom means caring rightly for what is.
neighbors.shared: hold things with open hands, and they weigh less.

neighbors.heading: cartloads of books
neighbors.text: Today Shvetaketu came home proud of his studies, and one question made him a beginner again. Guru Nanak sang about learning like that: you can read and read, load carts with books, fill caravans with them, read every year and every breath of your life, and still only one thing counts. (paraphrase) The rest, he says, is the ego's chatter.
neighbors.difference: Shvetaketu's father leads him toward knowing the one reality behind all things. For Guru Nanak, the one thing that counts is God's Name, remembered with love, and all learning is weighed against that.
neighbors.shared: the more you know, the more there is to ask.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Asa di Var, salok of Guru Nanak (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: knowledge puffeth up
neighbors.text: Today Shvetaketu came home sure he knew it all, until his father asked one question. Paul warned a clever church about the same thing: "Knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth. And if any man think that he knoweth any thing, he knoweth nothing yet as he ought to know." Learning is good. Thinking you're finished is the trap.
neighbors.difference: The Upanishad's teaching leads Shvetaketu toward the one reality behind all things. For Paul, love matters more than knowing: the next line says that whoever loves God is known by him.
neighbors.shared: staying a beginner keeps the door open.

neighbors.heading: not mine, not me
neighbors.text: Today a worried merchant asked the goddess for one thing: the knowledge that cuts the knot of I and mine. Buddhists know that knot. In an early teaching, the Buddha asks his first students about the body, feelings and thoughts: do they last? And is what changes rightly seen as this is mine, this I am, this is my self? No, they answer, and the grip begins to loosen.
neighbors.difference: The merchant receives his knowledge as a gift from the goddess, and in Vedanta the knot loosens onto a true Self beyond the small I. The Buddha's teaching points to no lasting self at all, and freedom comes through seeing, not from a deity.
neighbors.shared: loosening the grip of "mine" can bring a worried heart some peace.

neighbors.heading: an understanding heart
neighbors.text: Today the goddess asked two men what they wanted, and one asked for knowledge instead of his old life back. Catholics read a scene like it. God appears to young King Solomon in a dream and tells him to ask for whatever he wants. Solomon asks: "Give therefore to thy servant an understanding heart." God is pleased, and adds the riches he didn't ask for.
neighbors.difference: In the Devi Mahatmya, the goddess grants both requests and the text ranks neither. In the Bible, God praises Solomon for choosing wisdom over long life and riches, and the gift comes from the one God, not a goddess.
neighbors.shared: when the moment comes to ask, what we ask for shows who we are.
neighbors.sources: 3 Kings 3:5-13 (Douay-Rheims; 1 Kings 3 in many Bibles; quoted 3:9)

items.lessonTitle: the goddess of speech in a giant's mouth

neighbors.heading: a slip of the tongue
neighbors.text: Today a giant opened his mouth for a great wish, and out came sleep. Later tellers made it a slip: one sound out of place. Psychology has its own famous take. Sigmund Freud collected everyday slips, the wrong name, the word that jumps out first, and argued they aren't random: often a wish we haven't admitted is the one speaking (paraphrase).
neighbors.difference: In the Ramayana, the word comes from outside: the goddess of speech steps into the giant's mouth, and he's dismayed by his own wish. For Freud, nothing steps in; the slip comes from a part of us we don't see.
neighbors.shared: one word said out loud can show more than we meant.
neighbors.sources: Sigmund Freud, The Psychopathology of Everyday Life (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a word put in the mouth
neighbors.text: Today the goddess of speech stepped into a giant's mouth, and his wish came out changed. The Torah has a mouth like that. A king hires the seer Balaam to curse Israel, and each time he opens his mouth, a blessing comes out: "And the LORD put a word in Balaam's mouth." One of his blessings, "How goodly are thy tents, O Jacob," is still sung at morning prayer.
neighbors.difference: Kumbhakarna's word trips him, and the gods use it to protect the worlds. Balaam's word turns a curse into a blessing. And in the Torah it is the one God who puts the word there, not a goddess of speech.
neighbors.shared: the words that come out of us are not always only ours.

items.lessonTitle: a blade of grass fire cannot burn

neighbors.heading: in him we move
neighbors.text: Today fire couldn't burn a blade of grass and wind couldn't lift it, until the gods learned their power was borrowed. Christians speak of borrowed strength too. Jesus told his friends: "I am the vine, ye are the branches... for without me ye can do nothing." And Paul told the people of Athens that in God "we live, and move, and have our being."
neighbors.difference: In the Kena Upanishad, the power behind fire and wind is Brahman, and a goddess, Uma, explains it. For Christians, the strength comes from the one God, known in Jesus, and Paul's words are about every human life.
neighbors.shared: the strength in our hands was given before we used it.

neighbors.heading: no strength save in God
neighbors.text: Today one blade of grass showed the gods their power was borrowed. The Qur'an tells of a man proud of his rich garden. His friend asks why, entering it, he didn't say: "That which Allah willeth (will come to pass)! There is no strength save in Allah!" Muslims still say a form of it when a load feels too heavy: la hawla wa la quwwata illa billah.
neighbors.difference: The Upanishad's scene has many gods, and their power belongs to Brahman, made known by Uma. In Islam there is one God, with no partner, and the Qur'an keeps a clear line between the Creator and everything created.
neighbors.shared: a little humility makes room to see where strength comes from.

neighbors.heading: in the beginning was the word
neighbors.text: Today a poet bowed to Parvati and Shiva, joined like a word and its meaning, before he wrote a line. Catholics open a Gospel with a Word too: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God." A few verses on: "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us." A meaning, given a voice anyone could hear.
neighbors.difference: Kalidasa's word and meaning are a picture of two, goddess and god, never apart. For Catholics the Word is one divine Person, the Son, who became a man in Jesus; the picture is of God speaking, not of a couple.
neighbors.shared: we hope what we say will carry something true.

neighbors.heading: the Word is the guru
neighbors.text: Today a poet asked the couple who are word and meaning to keep his words true. Sikhs hold the Word close in their own way. Asked who his guru was, Guru Nanak answered that the Shabad, the Word, is the guru, and the attentive mind is the disciple (paraphrase). The Guru Granth Sahib, a book of sung words, sits at the heart of the gurdwara as Guru.
neighbors.difference: For Kalidasa, word and meaning picture Shiva and Parvati, two forms joined. For Sikhs, God is one and without form, and the Word is how that one God is known and sung; the scripture is honored as Guru, not as an image of God.
neighbors.shared: a word, taken to heart, can teach us how to live.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Siddh Gosht, Guru Nanak, Ang 943 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a breath of spice
neighbors.text: Today the goddess of fortune had a doorway made of fragrance. Jews know a doorway like that. As Shabbat ends on Saturday night, the havdalah blessings are said over wine, a braided candle and a box of sweet spices, passed hand to hand so everyone can breathe in. Tradition says the spices comfort the soul as the Sabbath's extra soul departs.
neighbors.difference: In the Sri Sukta, fragrance is a sign of the goddess herself, called near to the house. In havdalah, the spices comfort people, and the blessing thanks the one God who creates sweet smells; the fragrance itself isn't God.
neighbors.shared: a sweet smell at the door can make a house feel blessed.
neighbors.sources: Havdalah at the end of Shabbat (described) · Talmud, Beitzah 16a, the added soul of Shabbat (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: against the wind
neighbors.text: Today a hymn asked for a good name to rest on a household, the way jasmine rests on a doorframe. The Dhammapada has a line about that scent: "The scent of flowers does not travel against the wind, nor (that of) sandal-wood... but the odour of good people travels even against the wind; a good man pervades every place."
neighbors.difference: The Sri Sukta asks a goddess to bring fortune and a good name into the home. The Dhammapada asks no one; the fragrance is a person's own goodness, grown by their own practice.
neighbors.shared: kindness carries farther than any perfume.

items.lessonTitle: the goddess's second address: the body

neighbors.heading: nearer than the jugular vein
neighbors.text: Today the goddess with a jeweled city got a second address: a human body, from the base of the spine to the crown. The Qur'an gives God's nearness an address that close too: "We verily created man and We know what his soul whispereth to him, and We are nearer to him than his jugular vein."
neighbors.difference: The Lalita names map a power rising through the body, and that practice is taught in person by a teacher. In Islam, God is near in knowledge and care but never dwells in a body or becomes part of creation.
neighbors.shared: what we're looking for may be closer than our own breath.

neighbors.heading: the body is sacred
neighbors.text: Today a hymn placed the goddess inside the body: rising from the root of the spine, untying knots, raining nectar down. Walt Whitman, a poet who belonged to no church, found holiness in the body too. In "I Sing the Body Electric" he writes: "If any thing is sacred the human body is sacred."
neighbors.difference: For the Lalita Sahasranama, the body is a map of the goddess's rising, read inside a lineage with a teacher. Whitman needs no lineage or deity: the body, just as it is, is already holy, for anyone.
neighbors.shared: the body we live in deserves reverence, not shame.
neighbors.sources: Walt Whitman, "I Sing the Body Electric," Leaves of Grass

items.lessonTitle: a mother with her child on her lap

neighbors.heading: you are my mother
neighbors.text: Today the goddess was named for the child on her lap: Skandamata, Skanda's mother. Sikhs call God by family names too. In a hymn by Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, the singer says to God: you are my father, you are my mother, you are my kin, you are my brother (paraphrase). The one God is as close as the people who raised us.
neighbors.difference: Hindus honor the goddess as a mother with a form and a story, holding her son. For Sikhs, God is one and without form; mother and father are ways of saying how near and caring God is, never an image.
neighbors.shared: we are held the way a child is held on a lap.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Raag Majh, Guru Arjan, Ang 103 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: as a mother comforts
neighbors.text: Today a fierce goddess sat still with a baby on her lap. The Bible reaches for a mother too. Through the prophet Isaiah, God says: "As one whom his mother comforteth, so will I comfort you." And Jesus, grieving over Jerusalem, says he longed to gather its children "as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings."
neighbors.difference: Hindus worship the goddess herself as a mother, and Navaratri gives her many forms. Christians call God Father and pray through Jesus; a mother's comfort is a likeness for God's love, not a goddess.
neighbors.shared: the strongest love can sit still and hold someone small.

items.lessonTitle: desire takes aim at a god in meditation

neighbors.heading: the arrows of desire
neighbors.text: Today Kama aimed his flower arrows at Shiva, sitting still in meditation. Buddhists know a scene like it. As the Buddha-to-be sits under the tree, Mara comes to break his stillness, with armies, and in some tellings with his daughters, Craving among them. He doesn't move. He touches the earth as his witness, and Mara turns away.
neighbors.difference: Shiva burns desire with the fire of his third eye, and the story moves on to a marriage, with love later restored. The Buddha doesn't destroy Mara; he simply isn't moved, and awakening, not marriage, follows.
neighbors.shared: stillness can be stronger than the loudest pull.
neighbors.sources: Padhana Sutta, Sutta Nipata 3.2 · Samyutta Nikaya 4.25, Mara's daughters · the earth-touching story, Nidanakatha (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: forty days, one answer
neighbors.text: Today desire took aim at a god deep in meditation. Catholics remember a test like it. Jesus fasts forty days in the desert, and the tempter offers him bread, a show of power, and all the kingdoms of the world. Jesus answers each with Scripture, and at last: "Begone, Satan." The Church keeps those forty days each year as Lent.
neighbors.difference: Kama is a god of desire, sent by the gods themselves for a good end, and desire returns in the story as love. In the Gospel the tempter is an enemy, and Jesus refuses him; desire itself isn't the enemy.
neighbors.shared: a quiet heart can feel a strong pull and still say no.

neighbors.heading: the other half
neighbors.text: Today one figure stood split down the middle, and the creator learned the world grows on two halves together. Plato tells a story about halves too. In the Symposium, a guest named Aristophanes says humans were once double, then cut in two, and have been searching ever since: "the desire and pursuit of the whole is called love."
neighbors.difference: Ardhanarishvara is a form of God, and its two halves are never really apart. Aristophanes' story is a playful myth told at a dinner party about people, and its halves are lost and looking.
neighbors.shared: love is the reach toward wholeness.

neighbors.heading: male and female
neighbors.text: Today one figure stood split down the middle, half Shiva, half the goddess, so the world could grow. The Torah's first chapter says: "in the image of God created He him; male and female created He them." One rabbi in the Midrash went further: the first human was made two-sided, male and female, and only later separated into two (paraphrase).
neighbors.difference: Ardhanarishvara is God shown as half woman, Shiva and Shakti in one form. Jewish teaching holds that God has no body; it's the human being, made in God's image, who is male and female.
neighbors.shared: neither half of us was made to stand alone.

neighbors.heading: not one sparrow
neighbors.text: Today Shiva was Pashupati, lord of every creature and the one who loosens the rope. Jesus spoke of a God who watches the smallest creature: "Are not two sparrows sold for a farthing? and one of them shall not fall on the ground without your Father." And of untying: "ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free."
neighbors.difference: In Shaiva Siddhanta, the soul is tied by ignorance, past actions and the changing world, and Shiva loosens the rope. Christians name the knot sin, and believe God frees people in Jesus and calls them his children.
neighbors.shared: no creature is too small to be looked after.

neighbors.heading: lord of the worlds
neighbors.text: Today a name over a temple door meant lord of every creature. Muslims begin each prayer with a name that wide: "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds." And the Qur'an says: "there is not a beast in the earth but the sustenance thereof dependeth on Allah. He knoweth its habitation."
neighbors.difference: Pashupati is one of Shiva's thousand names, and in Shaiva teaching he unties the soul from its rope. In Islam, God is Lord of all, one, with no form or partner, and guidance comes through His word in the Qur'an.
neighbors.shared: every creature, from goats to us, is looked after.

neighbors.heading: wonderful are thy works
neighbors.text: Today the Shiva Sutras said wonder is how you know you're on the way, like a toddler shouting at a dog. Catholics pray a psalm of that astonishment: "I will praise thee, for thou art fearfully magnified: wonderful are thy works." And Jesus set a child among his friends and said they must become like little children to enter the kingdom (paraphrase).
neighbors.difference: For the Shiva Sutras, wonder is recognition: the self finding it was Shiva all along. For Catholics, wonder is a creature's awe before the Creator, itself a gift of God, and the one praising is never the one praised.
neighbors.shared: amazement is a way of saying thank you.
neighbors.sources: Psalm 138:14 (Douay-Rheims; Psalm 139:14 in many Bibles) · Matthew 18:2-3 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: vismad
neighbors.text: Today a short line said wonder marks the stages of yoga. Sikhs have a word for it: vismad, awe. In Asa di Var, sung in the gurdwara in the early morning, Guru Nanak lists wonder after wonder: wondrous the sound, wondrous the knowledge, wondrous the creatures, the colors, the wind, the water, the fire at play (paraphrase).
neighbors.difference: In the Shiva Sutras, wonder is the self recognizing it was Shiva all along. For Sikhs, vismad is awe before the one formless Creator and the creation, felt while singing God's praise.
neighbors.shared: wonder is a sign that we're paying attention.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Asa di Var, salok of Guru Nanak, Ang 463-464 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: make yourself a teacher
neighbors.text: Today the Shiva Sutras said, in two words, the teacher is the way. The rabbis say something close. In Pirkei Avot, the sayings of the fathers, Joshua ben Perachiah teaches: make for yourself a teacher, and acquire for yourself a friend (paraphrase). Torah is learned from a person, voice to voice, and often studied in pairs.
neighbors.difference: In the Shiva Sutras, the guru can be grace itself, Shiva's own power to reveal working through a person. In Judaism a teacher is a human being who passes on Torah; the teacher shows the way to God but is never divine.
neighbors.shared: nobody learns the deepest things alone.

neighbors.heading: the whole of the path
neighbors.text: Today a grandmother's hand guided a child's hand, and a sutra said the teacher is the way. Buddhists tell of Ananda, the Buddha's companion, saying a good friend is half the holy life. The Buddha answers: not half, Ananda. Admirable friendship, a good companion, is the whole of the holy life (paraphrase).
neighbors.difference: The Shiva Sutras' guru may be Shiva's grace itself, revealing the self. In this Buddhist teaching, the good friend is a fellow traveler or teacher, and the Buddha calls himself the good friend who shows the path; no god works through him.
neighbors.shared: the way is easier to find with a hand on ours.

items.lessonTitle: trees with green hair, rain and drought

neighbors.heading: the stars and the trees
neighbors.text: Today the Rudram went outside and bowed to trees with green hair, to rain and to drought. The Qur'an walks outdoors too. In the chapter called the Beneficent, it says simply: "The stars and the trees adore." Again and again it points to rain bringing dead earth back to life, and calls such things signs for people who think (paraphrase).
neighbors.difference: The Rudram bows to Rudra in the tree, the rain and the drought; nothing is outside him. In the Qur'an the trees bow to God; they are His creation and His signs, and God is never in them or the same as them.
neighbors.shared: the trees and the rain can teach us to bow.

neighbors.heading: in the woods
neighbors.text: Today a hymn bowed to the foam at the curb and the grass in a crack. Ralph Waldo Emerson, who gave up the pulpit, found the holy outdoors too. In Nature he writes: "In the woods, we return to reason and faith." Standing on bare ground, he says, all mean egotism vanishes (paraphrase).
neighbors.difference: The Rudram bows even to drought and storm, because nothing is outside Rudra. Emerson finds in the woods the currents of a "Universal Being" running through him, with no temple, hymn or rite.
neighbors.shared: the ground outside your door is worth greeting.

items.lessonTitle: food handed out before the fast is broken

neighbors.heading: the true bargain
neighbors.text: Today a woman who had fasted all night handed out food before she took a bite. Sikhs tell a story of young Nanak. His father gave him money to strike a good deal. On the road he met hungry holy men and spent it all feeding them, calling it the true bargain. Gurdwaras still serve langar, a free meal for anyone who comes, eaten side by side.
neighbors.difference: The Shivaratri morning closes a personal fast and vow to Shiva with giving. Sikh teaching doesn't ask for fasting as a path to God; the shared kitchen is everyday practice, open to everyone, whatever their faith.
neighbors.shared: the first bite can belong to someone else.
neighbors.sources: the Sacha Sauda story, the Janamsakhis (paraphrase) · langar, the gurdwara's shared kitchen (described)

neighbors.heading: the fast that feeds
neighbors.text: Today the fast ended with food handed to the man sweeping the steps before the one fasting ate. The Bible asks what a fast is for. Through Isaiah, God says: "Is not this the fast that I have chosen?... Is it not to deal thy bread to the hungry, and that thou bring the poor that are cast out to thy house?"
neighbors.difference: The Shivaratri vow is kept for Shiva, with worship at dawn before the fast is broken. Christians hear Isaiah alongside Jesus, who said that whatever is done for the hungry is done for him.
neighbors.shared: a fast is finished best by feeding someone.

items.lessonTitle: reasons that only look like reasons

neighbors.heading: test it for yourself
neighbors.text: Today a bank teller held a note up to the light, and Nyaya taught us to test reasons the same way. The Buddha told the Kalamas, villagers confused by teachers who each praised their own views: don't go only by reports, tradition, scripture or clever reasoning. When you know for yourselves that a thing leads to harm, let it go; when it leads to good, take it up (paraphrase).
neighbors.difference: Nyaya tests a reason by its form: does it really connect to what it claims? The Buddha's test in this sutta is what a teaching does in a life, whether it brings harm or welfare, as the wise would judge.
neighbors.shared: a good question isn't an insult; it's how trust is earned.

neighbors.heading: prove all things
neighbors.text: Today Nyaya named reasons that only look like reasons, so we could hold them up to the light. Catholics have Paul's short rule: "prove all things; hold fast that which is good." And John's letter warns: "believe not every spirit, but try the spirits if they be of God." The Church teaches that faith and reason never truly contradict (paraphrase).
neighbors.difference: Nyaya tests a reason by careful rules of inference, alongside perception and trusted testimony. For Catholics, reason is a gift that works alongside faith, and the teaching handed down in the Church guides what is held fast.
neighbors.shared: honest testing makes room for what's true to shine.
neighbors.sources: 1 Thessalonians 5:21 (Douay-Rheims) · 1 John 4:1 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 159 (paraphrase)

items.lessonTitle: a school that opens like a doctor

neighbors.heading: philosophy as medicine
neighbors.text: Today Samkhya opened like a doctor: there is pain, and the remedies in the drawer don't finish the job. Greek philosophers talked the same way.
