Epicurus said a philosopher's words are empty if they heal no human suffering: just as medicine is useless unless it drives out sickness, philosophy is useless unless it drives out the soul's pain (paraphrase).
neighbors.difference: Samkhya's cure is knowing the difference between nature and the witness, purusha, so pain no longer clings. Epicurus's cure is simple living, friendship, and losing the fear of the gods and of death; he sees no witness beyond the body.
neighbors.shared: wisdom is worth most when it eases someone's pain.
neighbors.sources: Epicurus, fragment preserved in Porphyry, To Marcella 31 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: healers of souls
neighbors.text: Today Samkhya began the way a doctor does, naming the pain before the cure. Maimonides was a physician and a rabbi, and he wrote like one. As the sick in body taste bitter as sweet, he says, those sick in soul come to love bad ways; let them go to the wise, who are healers of souls (paraphrase). A psalm praises God "Who healeth the broken in heart."
neighbors.difference: Samkhya's healing is knowledge that frees the witness from nature's show. For Maimonides, healing the soul means growing a balanced, good character through Torah and its commandments, before the one God who heals.
neighbors.shared: naming the pain honestly is the first step toward care.
neighbors.sources: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilchot De'ot 2:1 (paraphrase) · Psalm 147:3 (JPS 1917)

items.lessonTitle: the second before you hit send

neighbors.heading: a soft answer
neighbors.text: Today a hand hovered over the send arrow, and Patanjali said: cultivate the opposite. The Bible has words for that second. The letter of James says: "let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath." Proverbs adds: "A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger." Jesus went further: bless those who curse you (paraphrase).
neighbors.difference: Patanjali's method is inner: follow the angry thought to its cost, then grow the opposite, so the mind can be still. For Christians, the gentler reply is also love for the neighbor, even an enemy, with grace helping where effort runs out.
neighbors.shared: the second before we answer can change the whole day.

neighbors.heading: repel it with what is better
neighbors.text: Today an angry reply waited, half typed, and the Yoga Sutras said: grow the other side. The Qur'an says: "Repel the evil deed with one which is better, then lo! he, between whom and thee there was enmity (will become) as though he was a bosom friend." And the Prophet said the strong one isn't the wrestler, but the one who holds himself back in anger (paraphrase).
neighbors.difference: Patanjali's opposite thought is a discipline for stilling the mind on the way to freedom. In Islam, holding back anger and answering with good is obedience to God, rewarded by Him, and meant to turn an enemy into a friend.
neighbors.shared: a better answer can turn a rival into a friend.
neighbors.sources: Qur'an 41:34 (Pickthall 1930) · Sahih al-Bukhari 6114, Book of Good Manners (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: one is your master
neighbors.text: Today Patanjali traced every chain of teachers back to Ishvara, teacher even of the first ones. Catholics trace a chain too: bishop to bishop, back to the apostles, who learned from Jesus. And Jesus told them: "Neither be ye called masters; for one is your master, Christ." Every teacher in the line is first a student.
neighbors.difference: For Yoga, Ishvara is a special witness never caught in the world, known through the sound Om. For Catholics, the first teacher is Jesus, God made man, who lived, died and rose, and whose teaching the Church hands on.
neighbors.shared: behind every good teacher stands someone who taught them.
neighbors.sources: Matthew 23:10 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 77, apostolic succession (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the wondrous teacher
neighbors.text: Today Patanjali asked who taught the first teacher. Sikhs ask it too. Their Gurus form a line, from Guru Nanak through ten human Gurus to the scripture itself. A name Sikhs say for God, Waheguru, holds the word guru inside it, often heard as the wondrous teacher. And tradition says Guru Nanak's own teacher was God.
neighbors.difference: For Patanjali, Ishvara is a special purusha, one witness among many, never touched by the world. For Sikhs, God is the one Creator, beyond time and form, and the Word given through the Gurus is living guidance.
neighbors.shared: every line of teachers begins with someone who listened first.
neighbors.sources: the ten Gurus and the Guru Granth Sahib (described) · Waheguru (described) · Guru Nanak at the Vein river, the Janamsakhis (paraphrase)

items.lessonTitle: a branch that points to the moon

neighbors.heading: you shall see my back
neighbors.text: Today a branch pointed to the moon, and the Brahma Sutra pointed past the world to its source. The Torah has a pointing scene. Moses asks to see God's glory and is told: "Thou canst not see My face, for man shall not see Me and live." Set in a cleft of the rock, he hears: "thou shalt see My back; but My face shall not be seen."
neighbors.difference: Vedanta's pointer leads from the world to Brahman, which some of its teachers say is your own self. In Judaism, God is always the Creator, never the self; Moses comes as close as a person can and stays a person.
neighbors.shared: we can point toward what no hand can hold.

neighbors.heading: the finger and the moon
neighbors.text: Today a branch helped a child find the moon, and a line of scripture became a pointer. Buddhists use the same picture. A Mahayana sutra warns that someone shown the moon with a finger may stare at the finger instead (paraphrase). The Buddha also called his teaching a raft: for crossing over, not for carrying on your head once you've landed (paraphrase).
neighbors.difference: For Vedanta, the pointer leads to Brahman, the source of the world. For Buddhists, words point toward awakening and the end of suffering, and the Buddha didn't teach a creator as the world's source.
neighbors.shared: words are a pointing hand; the seeing is ours to do.
neighbors.sources: Lankavatara Sutra, the finger and the moon (paraphrase) · Alagaddupama Sutta, Majjhima Nikaya 22, the raft (paraphrase)

items.lessonTitle: a rumor at the bus stop

neighbors.heading: verify it
neighbors.text: Today a rumor at the bus stop became not yet known. The Qur'an asks for the same pause: "If an evil-liver bring you tidings, verify it, lest ye smite some folk in ignorance and afterward repent of what ye did." And for the friend who snapped: "Shun much suspicion; for lo! some suspicion is a crime."
neighbors.difference: Nyaya checks a report by the means of knowing, asking whether the speaker is reliable. The Qur'an asks it too, as a command from God with moral weight: careless words can wrong a person and be a sin.
neighbors.shared: a pause before believing a story is a kindness.

neighbors.heading: not things, but opinions
neighbors.text: Today a friend snapped, and a thought tried to stick: so that's who they really are. The Stoic teacher Epictetus, once enslaved, saw that moment clearly: "Men are disturbed not by the things which happen, but by the opinions about the things." When someone insults us, he said, it's our own judgment that stings (paraphrase).
neighbors.difference: The darshanas ask how we know and what a thing is made of, within a tradition that looks to the Veda and to freedom. Epictetus asks what is up to us, so we can live in agreement with nature, with no scripture.
neighbors.shared: a second look can be kinder than the first.

items.lessonTitle: the guest of honor washes feet

neighbors.heading: dust of the feet
neighbors.text: Today the honored guest washed the dust of the road from other people's feet. In a gurdwara you can see something close. Volunteers take visitors' shoes at the door, clean them and hand them back, as seva, selfless service. Gurbani asks for the dust of the feet of the holy company, the humblest place, as a blessing (paraphrase).
neighbors.difference: For his devotees, Krishna at the guests' feet is God choosing a humble task. For Sikhs, seva is how anyone, of any rank, sets ego aside before the one God; the server is a servant, never divine.
neighbors.shared: no job is too low for love.
neighbors.sources: seva at the gurdwara's shoe stall (described) · Guru Granth Sahib, on the dust of the saints' feet (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a towel and a basin
neighbors.text: Today the guest of honor, whom his devotees call God, took the job at the guests' feet. Christians know that picture. At the Last Supper Jesus takes a towel and a basin and washes his friends' feet. Then he says: "If I then, your Lord and Master, have washed your feet; ye also ought to wash one another's feet."
neighbors.difference: Krishna washes feet as one job among many at a royal feast, and the text mentions it in passing. For Christians, the washing comes the night before Jesus dies, a sign of love that gives itself away.
neighbors.shared: the one who kneels to serve stands close to love.

neighbors.heading: right livelihood
neighbors.text: Today a proud ascetic learned dharma from a merchant who never cheated on the weight. Buddhists put work right on the path: right livelihood is one step of the Eightfold Path. The Buddha says a lay follower doesn't trade in weapons, living beings, meat, intoxicants or poison, and early texts praise one who won't cheat with scales and measures (paraphrase).
neighbors.difference: Tuladhara's dharma is friendship to all beings, in a story where a voice from the sky sends the ascetic to learn. In Buddhism, right livelihood belongs to a path walked by one's own effort toward awakening.
neighbors.shared: an honest counter can be a holy place.
neighbors.sources: Vanijja Sutta, Anguttara Nikaya 5.177 (paraphrase) · Brahmajala Sutta, Digha Nikaya 1 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a just weight
neighbors.text: Today a merchant's even scale taught a great ascetic what dharma is. The Bible keeps a scale in view too: "A deceitful balance is an abomination before the Lord: and a just weight is his will." Catholics honor Saint Joseph the Worker, a carpenter, and the Church teaches that ordinary work, done well, can be a path to holiness (paraphrase).
neighbors.difference: In the Mahabharata, the merchant's dharma is harmlessness and an even mind toward all beings. For Catholics, honest work is offered to God and joined to the work of Christ, who spent years as a carpenter's son.
neighbors.shared: holiness can live in a fair price and a kept promise.
neighbors.sources: Proverbs 11:1 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 2427 (paraphrase)

items.lessonTitle: three strangers and a fourth in the dark

neighbors.heading: three chairs
neighbors.text: Today a shelter with room for one to lie down made room for two to sit and three to stand. Henry David Thoreau, in his small cabin at Walden Pond, kept the same arithmetic of welcome: "I had three chairs in my house; one for solitude, two for friendship, three for society." A small room, he found, could still hold good company.
neighbors.difference: In the Alvars' story, the fourth one pressing in is Vishnu with Lakshmi, and the lamps are hymns to him. Thoreau's guests are people, and what fills his cabin is conversation and the woods, with no god named.
neighbors.shared: a small room grows when we make space for each other.

neighbors.heading: the presence between
neighbors.text: Today three soaked strangers squeezed into a dark shelter, sang, and felt someone unseen press in among them. The rabbis say something like it. In Pirkei Avot, Rabbi Hananiah ben Teradion teaches: when two sit together and words of Torah pass between them, the Shekhinah, God's presence, rests between them (paraphrase).
neighbors.difference: The Alvars see Vishnu and Lakshmi in form, golden, as the lamps of song burn. In Judaism, the Shekhinah has no shape or image; it's God's nearness, felt in study and company, not shown in an image.
neighbors.shared: when we gather around good words, we're never only two.

items.lessonTitle: remembrance like a thread of oil

neighbors.heading: pray without ceasing
neighbors.text: Today oil poured in one unbroken thread, and Ramanuja said that's what knowing God looks like. Paul's letter gives Christians three words: "Pray without ceasing." Some Christians, especially in the Orthodox churches, take it to heart with a short prayer repeated with the breath until it keeps going on its own: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me.
neighbors.difference: Ramanuja's loving remembrance is offered to Vishnu, Narayana, and grows until it's like seeing. For Christians, unceasing prayer is a life lived with God through Jesus, kept up by grace when attention wanders.
neighbors.shared: love keeps remembering, even in a busy day.
neighbors.sources: 1 Thessalonians 5:17 (KJV) · the Jesus Prayer, Orthodox tradition (described)

neighbors.heading: much remembrance
neighbors.text: Today a thread of oil poured without breaking, and Ramanuja called it firm remembrance. The Qur'an's word for it is dhikr: "O ye who believe! Remember Allah with much remembrance." And: "Verily in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest!" Muslims keep it on prayer beads, after the daily prayers, and in the quiet between tasks.
neighbors.difference: Ramanuja's steady remembrance is meditation on Vishnu, with form and qualities, deepening until it's like seeing. Dhikr remembers the one God, who has no form or likeness, through His names and the words of the Qur'an.
neighbors.shared: a heart that keeps remembering finds somewhere to rest.

items.lessonTitle: the glasses on top of your head

neighbors.heading: thou wert within
neighbors.text: Today someone tore the house apart for glasses sitting on their head. Saint Augustine knew that search. Looking back on years of hunting for God outside himself, he wrote: "Too late loved I Thee, O Thou Beauty of ancient days, yet ever new!... Thou wert within, and I abroad, and there I searched for Thee."
neighbors.difference: For Shankara, the self you're searching for is Brahman, so the finding is recognition. For Augustine, God is closer to him than he is to himself, yet always God, not Augustine; the finding is love answered by grace.
neighbors.shared: what we long for may be nearer than our searching.

neighbors.heading: why search the forest?
neighbors.text: Today Shankara asked how you can look for what you already have. Guru Tegh Bahadur, the ninth Guru, sang it this way: why go searching in the forest? The Lord lives in everything and stays with you always, like fragrance in a flower, like a face in a mirror. Look within, he sings (paraphrase).
neighbors.difference: Shankara says the self you seek is Brahman itself, already and always. Sikhs hear God dwelling within every heart, found through the Guru's Word and remembering the Name, as a devotee before the one Lord.
neighbors.shared: the search can end where it began, in our own heart.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Raag Dhanasari, Guru Tegh Bahadur, Ang 684 (paraphrase)

items.lessonTitle: emptying the sea with a blade of grass

neighbors.heading: water on stone
neighbors.text: Today Gaudapada pictured emptying the sea with a blade of grass, one drop at a time, to steady the mind. The rabbis tell how Akiva began. At forty he had never studied. At a well he saw a stone hollowed by dripping water and thought: if soft water can carve stone, words of Torah can carve my heart (paraphrase). He became one of the great teachers.
neighbors.difference: Gaudapada's patience steadies a mind toward no grasping at all, resting in the self that was never touched. Akiva's patience fills a heart with Torah, learned letter by letter, in the service of the one God.
neighbors.shared: small, faithful drops can change what looked impossible.

neighbors.heading: drop by drop
neighbors.text: Today a blade of grass emptied the sea, one patient drop at a time. The Dhammapada turns the picture around and fills a pot instead: "Even by the falling of water-drops a water-pot is filled; the wise man becomes full of good, even if he gather it little by little." The Buddha also told a monk to tune effort like a lute string, not too tight or loose (paraphrase).
neighbors.difference: Gaudapada's steady mind rests in the self that was never touched. The Buddha's teaching points to awakening without a lasting self, and its patience is gathering good and seeing clearly, drop by drop.
neighbors.shared: patience, not hurry, is how the big things get done.
neighbors.sources: Dhammapada 122 (Max Müller 1881) · Sona Sutta, Anguttara Nikaya 6.55 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: we have wronged ourselves
neighbors.text: Today Vasishtha went straight to Varuna and asked, what did I do? Muslims keep a prayer for that moment. The Qur'an gives the words Adam and Eve said after their wrong: "Our Lord! We have wronged ourselves. If Thou forgive us not and have not mercy on us, surely we are of the lost!"
neighbors.difference: Vasishtha speaks to Varuna, one of the many gods the hymns praise, and names drink, anger and dice as what led him astray. In the Qur'an, Adam and Eve call the wrong their own, and turn to the one God, who forgives them.
neighbors.shared: when something breaks, you can ask out loud to be set right.

neighbors.heading: the nightly question
neighbors.text: Today Vasishtha named his weak spots out loud: drink, anger, dice, not thinking. The Roman philosopher Seneca kept a habit like that. Each night, he wrote, once the lamp was out and the house was quiet, he went over his whole day and asked himself: what bad habit have you cured today? What failing have you resisted? In what way are you better?
neighbors.difference: Vasishtha brings his wrongs to Varuna, who sees what people do, and asks to be released. Seneca brings them to himself, as his own judge, and hopes simply to do better tomorrow.
neighbors.shared: naming your weak spots out loud is the first step to mending.

items.lessonTitle: the Nasadiya Sukta (the hymn of creation — "who really knows?")

neighbors.heading: the Creator alone knows
neighbors.text: Today the hymn asked who really knows where all this came from. Guru Nanak asks it too, in Japji Sahib: what was that time, what moment, what day, what season, when the world was made? The pandits didn't find it. The qazis didn't find it. The Creator who made this creation, he says, alone knows.
neighbors.difference: The hymn ends with "or perhaps that one does not know," and leaves the question open. Guru Nanak answers it: no scholar can find the moment, but the one Creator, who made all of it, knows.
neighbors.shared: the biggest questions deserve wonder, not a rushed answer.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Japji Sahib, pauri 21, Ang 4, Guru Nanak (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: where wast thou?
neighbors.text: Today the hymn said even the gods came after the world's making, so who was there to see? In the Bible, God asks Job almost the same question, out of a whirlwind: "Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth? declare, if thou hast understanding." Job, who wanted answers, goes quiet: "I will lay mine hand upon my mouth."
neighbors.difference: The hymn asks the question and leaves it open, even about the one who watches from the highest heaven. In Job, the question comes from God himself, the Maker who was there, and the point is that a person wasn't.
neighbors.shared: not knowing, said honestly, can sit right next to awe.

neighbors.heading: first among meters
neighbors.text: Today Krishna named the Gayatri among meters as a place where his glory shows. The Buddha honored that verse too, by its other name, the Savitri. In a verse kept in the Pali texts, he names the foremost of each kind: the fire offering among sacrifices, the Savitri foremost of verses, the king among people, the ocean among rivers, the moon among stars, the sun among all that shines.
neighbors.difference: Krishna says "I am" the Gayatri: God shining through the best of each kind. The Buddha's list names no creator; each thing is simply foremost of its kind, and the list ends with the Sangha, his community, as the best place to give.
neighbors.shared: some words are so well made that many traditions stop to honor them.
neighbors.sources: Sutta Nipata 568–569, Sela Sutta (paraphrase); also Majjhima Nikaya 92

neighbors.heading: seen through what is made
neighbors.text: Today Krishna named the best of each kind, a meter, a month, a season, as places his glory shows. Catholics also look through the world to God. The Book of Wisdom says: "For by the greatness of the beauty, and of the creature, the creator of them may be seen, so as to be known thereby." And a psalm sings: "The heavens shew forth the glory of God."
neighbors.difference: For many Hindus, Krishna says "I am" these things: God showing himself in them. For Catholics, creation points to its Creator like a signpost; the meter, the month and the heavens are made by God, and are never God.
neighbors.shared: the beautiful things of the world can turn your eyes upward.
neighbors.sources: Wisdom 13:5; Psalm 18:2 (Douay-Rheims; Psalm 19:1 in many Bibles)

items.lessonTitle: hymns to Agni, Indra, Ushas, Varuna

neighbors.heading: a dawn in me
neighbors.text: Today Ushas woke every living thing. Henry David Thoreau loved the morning, and he borrowed the Vedas to say why: "The Vedas say, 'All intelligences awake with the morning.'" Then he turned it inward: "Morning is when I am awake and there is a dawn in me." For him, the hour on the clock mattered less than being awake to it.
neighbors.difference: In the hymn, the dawn is a goddess, praised and spoken to, the same one seen by every generation. For Thoreau, morning is mostly a state of mind: a person can sleep through sunrise, or find a dawn at noon.
neighbors.shared: every morning is a fresh invitation to wake up.
neighbors.sources: Henry David Thoreau, Walden (1854), "Where I Lived, and What I Lived For"

neighbors.heading: new every morning
neighbors.text: Today the hymn watched the dawn come again, one in a long line of mornings. Jewish tradition gives a prayer for waking, Modeh Ani, said before getting out of bed: thank you, living King, for giving back my soul with compassion. Its last words echo Lamentations: "They are new every morning; great is Thy faithfulness."
neighbors.difference: In the Rig Veda the dawn herself is a goddess, and she wakes the world. In Jewish prayer, the light is something God creates; it's God who returns the soul, and whose mercies are new each day.
neighbors.shared: waking up is worth a thank you, every single day.
neighbors.sources: Lamentations 3:23 (JPS 1917) · Modeh Ani, Jewish morning prayer (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: pray over the sick
neighbors.text: Today a healer spoke over a broken bone while giving a healing herb. Christians also bring words to the bedside. The letter of James says: "Is any sick among you? let him call for the elders of the church; and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord." Prayer and oil: words, and something you can touch, together.
neighbors.difference: The Atharva hymn speaks to the plant and the bone directly. In James, the prayer goes to the Lord, and the oil is used in his name; the healing is asked of God.
neighbors.shared: an aching body is never too ordinary for care and kind words.

neighbors.heading: a cure for every illness
neighbors.text: Today the hymn sat at a bedside with an herb that knits bones. Muslims treasure a saying of the Prophet Muhammad, as his companions remembered it: God has not sent down any disease without also sending down its cure. In that saying, seeking medicine is no failure of faith. And the Qur'an calls its own words "a healing and a mercy for believers."
neighbors.difference: The Atharva healer speaks to the fever, the herb and the bone directly. In Islam, words of healing are spoken to God alone; the herb and the doctor are means, and the cure is God's gift.
neighbors.shared: medicine and caring words can work side by side.

neighbors.heading: hands on the sick
neighbors.text: Today the healer blessed their own two hands before touching the sick. Hands matter to Catholics too. The Gospel of Mark says of those who believe: "they shall lay their hands upon the sick, and they shall recover." In the anointing of the sick, the priest lays his hands on the person, prays over them, and anoints them with oil.
neighbors.difference: The Atharva healer praises their own hand as all-healing. For Catholics, the hands only serve; the healing is asked of Christ, and it may come as strength and peace rather than a cure.
neighbors.shared: a kind touch, offered with a prayer, is a gift.
neighbors.sources: Mark 16:18 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 1519–1520 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the child Guru among the sick
neighbors.text: Today the hymn blessed a healer's kind hands. Sikhs remember a healer who was still a child. Tradition says Guru Har Krishan, the eighth Guru, went among the sick of Delhi during an epidemic and tended them, and the pool at Gurdwara Bangla Sahib remembers him. Sikhs still name him in the Ardas, their daily prayer: think of Guru Har Krishan, seeing whom all sorrow departs.
neighbors.difference: The Atharva hymn praises the healer's own hands. Sikhs remember the Guru's care as seva, service done in the One Creator's name; tradition says he fell ill himself while serving.
neighbors.shared: caring for the sick is holy work, whoever's hands do it.
neighbors.sources: Sikh tradition (paraphrase) · the Ardas, opening lines (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: i will awake the dawn
neighbors.text: Today the classical routine asked a healthy person to rise before sunrise, to protect life. Jewish law opens its guide to the day at the same hour. The Shulchan Aruch begins: be strong as a lion to rise in the morning to serve your Creator, so that you are the one who wakes the dawn. The picture comes from a psalm: "I will awake the dawn."
neighbors.difference: The Ayurvedic verse frames early rising as care for the body, and tradition adds prayer and study. The Shulchan Aruch frames it first as service: the reason to get up is the Creator, and the day starts with prayer.
neighbors.shared: the first quiet minute of the day is worth guarding.

neighbors.heading: the last watch of the night
neighbors.text: Today the routine began before sunrise, while the street is still quiet. The Buddha gave his students a rhythm like that. In one teaching he lays it out: in the first watch of the night, walk and sit, clearing the mind; in the middle watch, lie down mindfully; then, in the last watch, rise, and again walk and sit, clearing the mind. He called it devotion to wakefulness.
neighbors.difference: The Ayurvedic verse rises early to protect the body's life, and Hindu tradition makes the hour one for prayer. The Buddha's early hour has no god to greet; it's for watching the mind and loosening what clouds it.
neighbors.shared: a quiet hour before the world wakes is a gift to yourself.

neighbors.heading: the one who greets first
neighbors.text: Today a medical text said to speak kindly and be the first to greet. Muslims hear that too. The Prophet Muhammad said, as his companions remembered it, that the people closest to God are those who greet others first. And the Qur'an teaches: "When ye are greeted with a greeting, greet ye with a better than it or return it."
neighbors.difference: The Ashtanga Hridaya counts being first to greet among the habits of a healthy, happy life. In Islam, the greeting, peace be upon you, is itself a small prayer for the other person, and offering it first is an act of faith.
neighbors.shared: don't wait to see if it'll be warm. be warm first.

neighbors.heading: happiness takes practice
neighbors.text: Today the Ashtanga Hridaya said every being seeks happiness, and happiness doesn't come without right living. Aristotle drew the same link. In his Ethics, happiness is the soul at work in keeping with virtue, across a whole life. And he says we become good the way we learn a craft, by doing: "we become just by doing just acts."
neighbors.difference: The Ayurvedic text ties happiness to dharma, a right order bigger than any one person, and lists kindness beside brushing your teeth. Aristotle grounds it in human nature and character, built by habit, with no scripture behind it.
neighbors.shared: being kind every day is part of being well.
neighbors.sources: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics I.7 (paraphrase) and II.1 (W. D. Ross translation)

neighbors.heading: food that harms the mind
neighbors.text: Today Charaka and the Gita both said: eat in measure, not too much and not too little. Guru Nanak warns about eating without care, in a hymn in the Guru Granth Sahib. The pleasure of other foods brings ruin, he sings: foods that, once eaten, hurt the body and let wrong thoughts run through the mind.
neighbors.difference: Charaka's measure is set by your own digestive fire, a way of listening to the body. For Guru Nanak, the deeper food is God's Name; any food that crowds that out, harming body or mind, is too much.
neighbors.shared: how you eat shapes more than your body.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Sri Rag, Guru Nanak, Ang 16 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: as much as is sufficient
neighbors.text: Today Charaka and the Gita both said: eat in measure. The book of Proverbs keeps the same kitchen wisdom: "Hast thou found honey? eat so much as is sufficient for thee, lest thou be filled therewith." And Paul gives every meal a direction: "whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God."
neighbors.difference: Charaka measures by each person's digestive fire, and the Gita ties measure to yoga's end of sorrow. For Christians, measure is part of thanks: the meal is a gift from God, eaten for his glory.
neighbors.shared: enough is a good place to stop.

neighbors.heading: if they knew giving
neighbors.text: Today the Upanishad said to cook enough so there's food to give. The Buddha said something close. In one teaching he says, in paraphrase: if people knew, as I know, the fruit of giving and sharing, they wouldn't eat without having given, even if it were their last bite, their last mouthful, and there were someone to receive it.
neighbors.difference: The Upanishad asks you to honor the guest like a god. The Buddha names no god at the door; for him, giving loosens the grip of stinginess on the giver's own mind, and that is part of its fruit.
neighbors.shared: a kitchen that cooks for one more is a generous kitchen.

neighbors.heading: you gave me to eat
neighbors.text: Today the Upanishad said let the guest be a god to you, and never turn away a knock. Catholics hear Jesus speak from the other side of the door: "I was hungry, and you gave me to eat... I was a stranger, and you took me in." And: "as long as you did it to one of these my least brethren, you did it to me."
neighbors.difference: In the Upanishad, the guest is honored like a god. For Catholics, the stranger is a fellow human being, not God, and Christ says that what is done for them is done for him.
neighbors.shared: there should always be one more plate for whoever knocks.

items.lessonTitle: the breath again — every claim checked

neighbors.heading: a little flesh and breath
neighbors.text: Today breath settled a quarrel over who holds the body up. The Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius took stock of himself the same way: "Whatever this is that I am, it is a little flesh and breath, and the ruling part." And he watched breath closely: air, never the same, every moment sent out and drawn in again.
neighbors.difference: In the Prashna, breath wins the quarrel: it is the greatest power, fire and sun and rain. Marcus would hand that crown to the ruling part, reason; breath, for him, is air passing through.
neighbors.shared: watching your breath come and go is a way of knowing yourself.
neighbors.sources: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations 2.2 (George Long translation, 1862; second line paraphrased)

neighbors.heading: the breath of life
neighbors.text: Today breath got up to leave, and every sense had to follow. The Torah also sees life hanging on breath: "Then the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul." And the last psalm ends: "Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD."
neighbors.difference: In the Prashna, breath is the greatest power in the body, born from the self, shining as fire and sun. In Genesis, breath is God's gift, breathed in from outside; the body is dust until God gives it life.
neighbors.shared: each breath is a gift worth noticing.

items.lessonTitle: the breath again — every claim checked

neighbors.heading: a living sacrifice
neighbors.text: Today the Gita turned breathing into an offering, one gift in a row of many. Christians also offer ordinary life. Paul writes: "I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service." Not one rite at an altar: a whole day, given.
neighbors.difference: The Gita offers breath as one form of yajna, beside study, giving and restraint. Paul's offering answers the mercies of God in Christ; for Christians, Christ's own sacrifice comes first, and a life is given in thanks.
neighbors.shared: the ordinary things you do all day can be a gift.

neighbors.heading: my living and my dying
neighbors.text: Today Krishna said some people offer their very breath, in and out, as a gift. The Qur'an gives a believer words for offering everything: "Lo! my worship and my sacrifice and my living and my dying are for Allah, Lord of the Worlds." Not only prayer and sacrifice, but living itself, each ordinary hour, turned toward God.
neighbors.difference: The Gita honors many offerings, each a way of knowing sacrifice. The Qur'an gathers all of life toward the one God, and the next verse adds: "He hath no partner."
neighbors.shared: an ordinary day, given with your whole heart, is holy.

neighbors.heading: what are these among so many?
neighbors.text: Today Krishna ate one scrap from an empty pot, and the hungry sages felt full. The Gospel of John tells of a crowd and almost nothing to feed it: "There is a boy here that hath five barley loaves, and two fishes; but what are these among so many?" Jesus gives thanks, and everyone eats. Then: "Gather up the fragments that remain, lest they be lost."
neighbors.difference: For many Hindus, Krishna is God himself, satisfying the soul of the world with one leaf. Catholics read the loaves as a sign Jesus gave, pointing ahead to the Eucharist, where he gives himself as bread.
neighbors.shared: what little you have is never too little to share.
neighbors.sources: John 6:9, 11–12 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 1335 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: everyone eats from one kitchen
neighbors.text: Today Draupadi served every guest first and ate last. Sikhs built a kitchen on that idea. In the langar, the Guru's free kitchen, anyone who comes is fed, sitting side by side on the same floor. Tradition says Guru Amar Das asked visitors to eat in the langar before meeting him: first the shared meal, then the company.
neighbors.difference: Draupadi's pot is a gift from the sun that lasts until she eats, and Krishna saves the day with a wonder. The langar needs no wonder: volunteers cook and serve, and rich and poor sit as equals.
neighbors.shared: a guest at the door is a guest at the table.
neighbors.sources: Sikh tradition of the langar and Guru Amar Das (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: arguing for life
neighbors.text: Today Savitri walked behind Death and spoke of the good until he gave back what she asked. The Torah has a pleader too. Abraham hears that Sodom will be destroyed, and steps forward: "Wilt Thou indeed sweep away the righteous with the wicked?" Then, boldly: "shall not the Judge of all the earth do justly?" He bargains from fifty all the way down to ten.
neighbors.difference: Savitri speaks to Yama, the god of death, for her husband, and wins his life. Abraham speaks to God, the one Judge, for the righteous of a whole city, and the story doesn't end with the city spared.
neighbors.shared: love can speak up, even to the one who decides.

neighbors.heading: a mustard seed
neighbors.text: Today Savitri wouldn't let Death take her husband without a conversation. Buddhists tell of a mother who couldn't let go either. Kisa Gotami carried her dead child to the Buddha, asking for medicine. He told her to bring a mustard seed from a house where no one had died. She knocked on door after door, and found none.
neighbors.difference: Savitri's words win her husband back from Yama. Kisa Gotami's search doesn't bring her son back; her peace comes from seeing that death touches every house, and she lays him down and becomes a nun.
neighbors.shared: no one walks to the hardest door completely alone.
neighbors.sources: the story of Kisa Gotami, from the commentaries on the Dhammapada and the Therigatha (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: nearer than your own vein
neighbors.text: Today Shakuntala told the king: you think no one saw, but the sun, the moon and your own heart did. The Qur'an says no one is ever unwitnessed: "We verily created man and We know what his soul whispereth to him, and We are nearer to him than his jugular vein." Even each word, it adds, has "an observer ready."
neighbors.difference: Shakuntala calls on the sun, moon, wind and fire, and his own heart, as witnesses. In the Qur'an, the first witness is God himself, the Maker of sun and moon, who knows even what the soul whispers.
neighbors.shared: the truth is seen, even when no one else is in the room.

neighbors.heading: the man within the breast
neighbors.text: Today Shakuntala told the king that his own heart saw what he did. The philosopher Adam Smith gave that inner witness a name: the impartial spectator, "the man within the breast." When we're tempted to put ourselves first, he wrote, this inner judge makes us see ourselves as a fair onlooker would, and shows us how small our own claims really are.
neighbors.difference: Shakuntala names the sun, moon, wind and fire as witnesses beside the heart. Smith's spectator lives only inside a person: a conscience learned from living among others, with no sky watching.
neighbors.shared: your own heart can be the fairest judge in the room.
neighbors.sources: Adam Smith, The Theory of Moral Sentiments, Part III (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: mad for the King
neighbors.text: Today Mira danced with bells, and people called her mad. Guru Nanak heard names like that too. In a hymn in the Guru Granth Sahib he sings: some call me a ghost, some a demon, some say Nanak is just a poor man. Then he takes the word for himself: Nanak has gone mad for his King, and knows no one but the Lord.
neighbors.difference: Mira's Lord has a name and a form: Giridhar, Krishna who lifted the mountain, loved as her own. Guru Nanak's King is the formless One, never born, praised through the Name rather than any image.
neighbors.shared: love that won't sit still is nothing to be ashamed of.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Raag Maru, Guru Nanak, Ang 991 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: dancing with all his might
neighbors.text: Today Mira danced in public, and her family said she'd ruined them. The Bible has a dancer who embarrassed his house too. "And David danced before the LORD with all his might," and his wife Michal, watching from a window, "despised him in her heart." Paul later wore the insult proudly: "We are fools for Christ's sake."
neighbors.difference: Mira dances for Krishna, her Lord and beloved. David dances before the ark of the God of Israel, and Paul's foolishness is following Jesus, the crucified one, whom Christians call Lord.
neighbors.shared: joy that moves your feet is a kind of prayer.

items.lessonTitle: Lal Ded — a season of the tradition's women

neighbors.heading: a rock in the wind
neighbors.text: Today Lal Ded let the curses and the flowers come, and stayed untouched. The Buddha used a picture for that steadiness. In the Dhammapada: "As a solid rock is not shaken by the wind, wise people falter not amidst blame and praise." In another teaching, praise and blame are named among eight worldly conditions that come to everyone.
neighbors.difference: Lal Ded sang as a seeker of Shiva, and her steadiness comes from turning within. The Buddha's rock stands on wisdom alone: seeing that praise and blame both come and go, with no God to lean on.
neighbors.shared: what others say about you doesn't get to decide who you are.

neighbors.heading: none the holier for praise
neighbors.text: Today Lal Ded put curses and garlands on the same scale. A classic Catholic book of devotion, The Imitation of Christ, says it like this: you are none the holier for being praised, nor the worse for being blamed. What you are, you are, and words can't make you greater than you are in the sight of God.
neighbors.difference: Lal Ded stays untouched by turning within. For Thomas à Kempis, the only true measure is God's sight, and the way to steadiness is humility before him, not rising above praise and blame by one's own strength.
neighbors.shared: garlands and insults weigh the same on a steady heart.
neighbors.sources: Thomas à Kempis, The Imitation of Christ, Book II, chapter 6 (paraphrase)

items.lessonTitle: Lal Ded — a season of the tradition's women

neighbors.heading: too much, too little
neighbors.text: Today Lal Ded said: eat in measure, and you'll become even. Aristotle said something very close about food. Too much exercise or too little ruins strength, he wrote, and food above or below a certain amount ruins health, while what's in proportion builds and keeps it. Virtue of character, for him, sits like that: a middle between too much and too little.
neighbors.difference: Lal Ded's even plate opens bolted doors, a way inward that some readers hear as a way to God. Aristotle's middle builds character and a good human life; it needs no door beyond that.
neighbors.shared: neither heaped nor empty: enough is a wise place to stand.
neighbors.sources: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II.2 and II.6 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the middle path
neighbors.text: Today Lal Ded warned that going without food can make a person proud. The Jewish teacher Maimonides warned the same. In his code he says the right way is the middle measure in every trait. Some people, he notes, give up meat and wine to be holy, but that is a wrong road; what the Torah forbids is enough.
neighbors.difference: Lal Ded's measure is a seeker's discipline that opens the doors within. For Maimonides, the middle path is walking in God's own ways, as the Torah commands, and food is a gift to enjoy within its laws.
neighbors.shared: holiness doesn't need an empty plate.
neighbors.sources: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilchot De'ot 1:4–6 and 3:1 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: she loved much
neighbors.text: Today a hunter broke the rules of worship, and Shiva stopped his hand in love. The Gospel of Luke has a careful host and a rule-breaker too. At a Pharisee's dinner, a woman washes Jesus' feet with her tears and dries them with her hair. The host is shocked. Jesus answers: "Her sins, which are many, are forgiven; for she loved much."
neighbors.difference: Kannappa gives his own eyes to an image of Shiva, and Shiva's hand comes out of the stone. In Luke, the woman kneels before Jesus himself, and his answer is about forgiveness: love and mercy meeting face to face.
neighbors.shared: love that doesn't know the rules can still be welcome.

neighbors.heading: the devotion reaches
neighbors.text: Today a hunter brought meat and water carried in his mouth, and Shiva cared about the love, not the rules. The Qur'an says something close about offerings: "Their flesh and their blood reach not Allah, but the devotion from you reacheth Him." What God receives is the heart behind the gift.
neighbors.difference: Kannappa offers to Shiva's image, and Shiva's hand reaches out of the stone. In Islam, nothing is offered to an image, and God needs nothing from the offering; the meat is shared with the poor.
neighbors.shared: a sincere heart is the part of the gift that arrives.

neighbors.heading: as a mother comforts
neighbors.text: Today Varkaris called God mauli, mother. Catholics call God Father, and the prophets also reach for a mother's love. Isaiah hears God say: "As one whom the mother caresseth, so will I comfort you." And: "Can a woman forget her infant...? and if she should forget, yet will not I forget thee."
neighbors.difference: Varkaris call Vitthal mauli outright, and the word runs on to saints and strangers. The Church teaches that God is neither man nor woman; a mother's tenderness is an image of his love, and he is prayed to as Father.
neighbors.shared: you don't need the right words to run home.
neighbors.sources: Isaiah 66:13; Isaiah 49:15 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 239 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: you are my mother
neighbors.text: Today a gray-bearded pilgrim called God mauli, mother. Sikhs sing that closeness too. A hymn by Guru Arjan in the Guru Granth Sahib says: you are my father, you are my mother, you are my kin, you are my brother. You are my protector everywhere, so what fear or worry could touch me?
neighbors.difference: Vitthal is a form of Krishna, standing on his brick at Pandharpur. For Sikhs, the One sung as mother and father has no form and is never born, so the closeness comes through the Name, not an image.
neighbors.shared: the one you run to can feel like family.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Raag Majh, Guru Arjan, Ang 103 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a judge with no favorites
neighbors.text: Today Kalhana said a history must be told like a judge, free of love and hate. The Torah asks the same of every judge: "Ye shall do no unrighteousness in judgment; thou shalt not respect the person of the poor, nor favour the person of the mighty." And the prophet Nathan told King David his wrong to his face: "Thou art the man."
neighbors.difference: Kalhana judges the kings of the past, and hopes the reader comes away calm, letting go of power. In the Torah, fair judgment is God's command, and a prophet names a king's wrong so it can be set right.
neighbors.shared: the truth deserves to be told straight, even about the powerful.

neighbors.heading: four wrong turns
neighbors.text: Today Kalhana wanted his history straight, bent by neither love nor hate. The Buddha named four ways a judgment goes wrong: through desire, through hatred, through confusion, and through fear. Whoever doesn't stray from what's right by any of these, he said, grows in good name like the moon as it waxes.
neighbors.difference: Kalhana tells a long story of kings and wants it to leave the taste of peace. The Buddha's four wrong turns are for anyone deciding anything, and the cure is a mind cleared of grasping.
neighbors.shared: a fair heart sees past both love and grudge.

neighbors.heading: keep the covenant
neighbors.text: Today Bali kept his word, though his own teacher warned it would cost him everything. The Qur'an asks for the same faithfulness: "Keep the covenant. Lo! of the covenant it will be asked." And: "O ye who believe! Fulfil your undertakings." A promise, in Islam, is a trust, and God will ask about it.
neighbors.difference: Bali keeps his word to the boy who is Vishnu in disguise, and Vishnu later stands guard at his door. In Islam, a promise is kept because the one God will ask about it, whoever it was made to.
neighbors.shared: your word is worth keeping, even when it costs you.

neighbors.heading: good faith
neighbors.text: Today Bali gave up everything rather than take back a promise. The Roman thinker Cicero wrote that the foundation of justice is good faith: truth, and faithfulness to promises and agreements. He praised Regulus, a captured Roman general sent home on his word to bargain, who went back to his captors, knowing what waited, because he had sworn to return.
neighbors.difference: Bali keeps his word to God in disguise, and God himself becomes his guard. Regulus keeps his word to his enemies, and Cicero praises him for honor alone, with no reward promised.
neighbors.shared: a kept promise is a kind of quiet courage.
neighbors.sources: Cicero, On Duties I.23 and III.99–100 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a bath that pleases
neighbors.text: Today Ravidas said: if the mind is pure, the Ganga is in this bowl. Sikhs know his voice well; his hymns are kept in the Guru Granth Sahib. And Guru Nanak sings a close cousin of that line in Japji Sahib: I would bathe at a holy river if it pleased the Lord; without that, what good is bathing?
neighbors.difference: In the story, the Ganga herself reaches out of the water to take Ravidas's coin; the river is honored. For Guru Nanak, no river makes a bath holy by itself; what counts is living in the One's will.
neighbors.shared: the holy can find you at your own workbench.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Japji Sahib, pauri 6, Guru Nanak (paraphrase) · hymns of Bhagat Ravidas in the Guru Granth Sahib

neighbors.heading: not on this mountain
neighbors.text: Today Ravidas stayed at his bench and said the holy river could be in his bowl. Jesus said something like it to a woman at a well who asked which mountain was the right place to worship: "the hour cometh, when ye shall neither in this mountain, nor yet at Jerusalem, worship the Father." True worshippers, he said, worship "in spirit and in truth."
neighbors.difference: Ravidas honors the Ganga, and the river reaches out to meet him. Jesus points past every holy place to the Father, and offers the woman "living water" of his own: for Christians, Christ himself.
neighbors.shared: the holy isn't kept from anyone's ordinary place.

neighbors.heading: the second arrow
neighbors.text: Today a king and a merchant asked why knowing something is gone doesn't stop the mind going back. The Buddha answered with arrows. When pain comes, he said, an untaught person grieves and struggles, and so feels two arrows: one in the body, and a second in the mind. A trained person feels the first arrow only.
neighbors.difference: Medhas says the pull is the Goddess as Mahamaya, and the same power that binds the mind sets it free. The Buddha points to no goddess; the second arrow is our own clinging, and seeing it clearly loosens it.
neighbors.shared: a mind that keeps going back to hurt deserves patience, not scolding.

neighbors.heading: the good which i will
neighbors.text: Today a king and a merchant asked: we know these things are gone, so why doesn't knowing help? Saint Paul knew that ache: "For I do not that good which I will; but the evil which I hate, that I do." Then he cries out: "who shall deliver me...?" And answers: "The grace of God, by Jesus Christ our Lord."
neighbors.difference: Medhas names the pull Mahamaya, the Goddess's own power, which also frees. Paul names it sin dwelling in him, and the way out is grace through Christ.
neighbors.shared: you're not the only one whose heart lags behind what it knows.

neighbors.heading: nothing human is foreign
neighbors.text: Today a hungry king gave his last water to an outcaste and asked to carry the sorrow of all beings. The Roman playwright Terence gave one of his characters a line people still quote for that open door: I am human, and nothing human is foreign to me. Centuries later, Arthur Schopenhauer argued that compassion, feeling another's suffering as your own, is the root of real goodness.
neighbors.difference: Rantideva's gift is devotion: the guests turn out to be gods, and he asks them for nothing. For Terence and Schopenhauer, the reason to help is simply that the thirsty person is human, like you.
neighbors.shared: the thirsty stranger is one of us.
neighbors.sources: Terence, The Self-Tormentor, Act I (paraphrase) · Arthur Schopenhauer, On the Basis of Morality (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the fast that feeds
neighbors.text: Today Rantideva ended a long fast by feeding everyone who came, down to his last water. Isaiah asks what a fast is for: "Is not this the fast that I have chosen?... Is it not to deal thy bread to the hungry, and that thou bring the poor that are cast out to thy house?" Jews read these words aloud on Yom Kippur, the day of fasting.
neighbors.difference: Rantideva asks to take on the sorrow of all beings, and the guests turn out to be gods. In Isaiah, feeding the hungry is God's own command, and the poor are neighbors to care for, not gods in disguise.
neighbors.shared: a fast means most when someone else gets fed.

neighbors.heading: the crumbs under the table
neighbors.text: Today the epics' women spoke up right when they were expected to stay quiet. The Gospel of Mark has a woman like that. A Greek mother begs Jesus to heal her daughter, and he answers with a hard saying about the children's bread. She answers back: "Yes, Lord: yet the dogs under the table eat of the children's crumbs." He sends her home, and her daughter is healed.
neighbors.difference: The epic women speak to kings, husbands and even Death. The woman in Mark speaks to Jesus, whom Christians call Lord, and her bold answer is the very thing he honors: "For this saying go thy way."
neighbors.shared: speaking up at the hard moment can be an act of faith.

neighbors.heading: she who pleads
neighbors.text: Today the epics' women spoke when silence was expected. The Qur'an names a whole surah for a woman like that: Al-Mujadila, she who pleads. It opens: "Allah hath heard the saying of her that disputeth with thee (Muhammad) concerning her husband, and complaineth unto Allah. And Allah heareth your colloquy." Tradition names her Khawla.
neighbors.difference: Shakuntala and Sita argue with kings and husbands, and the epics keep their words. Khawla brings her complaint to the Prophet and to God, and the answer changes the law: a husband can't cast off his wife with a harsh old oath without making amends.
neighbors.shared: a voice raised for what's right is heard.
neighbors.sources: Qur'an 58:1–4 (Pickthall) · the story of Khawla bint Tha'laba, Islamic tradition (paraphrase)
